ent-w9-module-q20-20:
From 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia. Motility disorders are diagnosed by manometry, not endoscopy. Each pattern pairs peristalsis with how the LES behaves:

  • Achalasia (I) = aperistalsis + impaired LES relaxation (A): the LES fails to relax, giving a bird's-beak on barium swallow.
  • Scleroderma (II) = aperistalsis + hypotensive LES (B): scarring weakens both, so reflux, strictures and Barrett's follow.
  • Distal esophageal spasm (III) = simultaneous premature contractions (C), which are non-propulsive.
  • Jackhammer (IV) = high-amplitude repetitive contractions (D).
  • None (V) = weak, slowly propagating contractions (E), which match none of the four.

The LES separates the two aperistaltic disorders: it is tight in achalasia and slack in scleroderma.

ent-w9-module-q22-22.html:
From 03 - Oropharyngeal Dysphagia. The lecture lists what oropharyngeal dysphagia is associated with: increased morbidity and mortality, increased healthcare costs, and decreased well-being and quality of life. Its complications drive that burden: aspiration, aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, dehydration and death. Prevalence ranges from 6 to 50%, and over 70% of stroke patients are affected.

  • A, B, C are all on the lecture's list.
  • D reverses the effect, since quality of life falls.

ent-w9-module-q25-25:
From 06 - Pediatric Neck Masses. A thyroglossal duct cyst is left behind as the thyroid descends from the foramen cecum at the tongue base. The tract stays tethered to the hyoid and tongue base, so the cyst elevates with tongue protrusion. That is the bedside sign, and it is why the Sistrunk procedure removes the central hyoid.

  • B: a TGDC is the classic midline mass. A lateral congenital mass suggests a branchial cleft cyst.
  • C: lymphatic malformations are congenital. 60% are apparent at birth, and nearly 90% present before age 2.
  • D: the foramen cecum lies at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue, not in the anterior third.
ent-w9-module-q26-26:
From 06 - Pediatric Neck Masses. The lecture gives two treatments for lymphatic malformations. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice, though incomplete excision recurs in 15-50% of cases. The other is sclerotherapy, which injects an inflammatory agent to scar the lesion.

  • A: radiation is not among the listed treatments.
  • C: these lesions are usually soft, fluctuant and lobulated, not solid.
  • D: they typically sit in the posterior triangle and can occur anywhere in the body. The midline mass of childhood is the thyroglossal duct cyst.
ent-w9-module-q27-27:
From 07 - Pediatric Airway Pathology. A child's airway is narrowest at the cricoid cartilage, which is the subglottis. The cricoid is a complete ring and cannot expand, so a little subglottic swelling, as in croup, narrows the lumen sharply.

  • A: croup is the most common cause of stridor in children, not tonsillar hypertrophy.
  • B: the cricoid is a full circle. The horseshoe (C-shaped) cartilages are the tracheal rings.
  • D: croup is viral (parainfluenza, RSV, influenza) and peaks between 6 months and 3 years, not in neonates.

The lecture does not give the age at which the adult pattern takes over; the figure of about 8 years comes from the question.
ent-w9-module-q28-28:
From 07 - Pediatric Airway Pathology. Vegetable matter makes up 70-80% of foreign bodies aspirated by children.

  • A: aspiration peaks at 1-3 years and is more common in boys. It is not a neonatal problem.
  • C: the quiet middle phase makes observation dangerous. After the acute choking episode, the reflexes fatigue and the child can look well for hours to weeks before obstruction, erosion or infection sets in. A positive history, exam or chest x-ray (gas trapping) is each enough on its own for rigid bronchoscopy.
  • D: coins are more typically swallowed into the esophagus than aspirated.

ent-w9-module-q29-29.html:
From 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck. An unvaccinated toddler with fever, drooling and stridor has epiglottitis until proven otherwise. The lecture attributes it to Haemophilus influenzae type B (C). It is rare now because of Hib vaccination, which is why the stem says the child is unvaccinated. It is an airway emergency: secure the airway and do not agitate the child.

  • C. diphtheriae (A): also seen in the unvaccinated, but it causes a grey pharyngeal membrane and myocarditis, not this picture.
  • F. necrophorum (E): Lemierre's syndrome, a thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein that follows pharyngitis.
  • S. aureus (G) and viridans strep (I): skin and oral flora behind deep neck and dental infections.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives B, but B, D, F and H are not organisms. They are the module's own marking labels (“Incorrectly selected”, “Correctly unselected”), scraped in as options. The answer that 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck supports is C, Haemophilus influenzae B. The option list needs cleaning in the bank.

ent-w9-module-q3-3:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. A warm, tender, diffusely enlarged parotid with pus at Stensen's duct means the gland itself is infected. That is acute suppurative sialadenitis of the parotid, or parotitis. It follows salivary stasis and retrograde spread of bacteria, most often S. aureus.

  • Sialolithiasis (B): pain and swelling that worsen with meals, usually in the submandibular gland. A stone can set off an infection, but a hot gland with pus is the infection itself.
  • Parotid mass (C): usually a painless, discrete lump, not a hot, diffusely enlarged gland.
  • Metastatic skin cancer (D): a firm mass over or in the parotid, without pus.
ent-w9-module-q4-4:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Acute sialadenitis begins with salivary stasis, so treatment gets saliva flowing and treats the infection. That means gland massage, warm compresses, hydration, sialagogues (sour foods that stimulate flow) and antibiotics, IV if needed. If there is no improvement in 3 days, look for complications such as a deep neck infection.

  • A treats the bacteria but leaves the stasis, so it is incomplete.
  • C: incision and drainage is for a complicating abscess, not first-line.
  • D: the compresses should be warm, not cold, and hydration and sialagogues are missing.

ent-w9-module-q5-5.html:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. The lecture's head and neck cancer history looks for symptoms of a mucosal primary in the upper aerodigestive tract:

  • Odynophagia (B) and dysphagia (F): oral and pharyngeal symptoms.
  • Hoarseness (E): persistent hoarseness beyond 3 weeks suggests a laryngeal primary.
  • Weight loss (G): a constitutional symptom, alongside night sweats and fever.
  • Ear pain (H): referred otalgia with a normal ear exam, classically from an oropharyngeal primary.

Sneezing, cough, acid reflux and rash (A, C, D, I) are common, non-specific symptoms, and the lecture does not link them to malignancy.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives B, E, G, H and leaves out dysphagia (F). 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses lists dysphagia next to odynophagia among the oral and pharyngeal symptoms to ask about, so F belongs among the answers. The answer the material supports is B, E, F, G, H.

ent-w9-module-q6-6:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Clara fits the HPV-positive profile: younger, healthy, educated, of higher socioeconomic status, and a non-smoker and non-drinker. HPV-16 causes 90% of HPV-related head and neck SCC, and the palatine tonsils and root (base) of the tongue are the most commonly affected subsites.

  • A: not every head and neck cancer is smoking-driven. Salivary tumours are not linked to smoking except Warthin's tumour, and skin cancers follow sun exposure.
  • B: HPV also drives oropharyngeal cancer, the fastest-rising cancer in non-smokers.
  • C: HPV-positive disease presents at a lower T-stage and has a better prognosis.

ent-w9-module-q9-9.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. The key reads: label A = sternocleidomastoid, B = trapezius, C = middle scalene, D = anterior scalene. Use their relationships to place each one:

  • Sternocleidomastoid: the large diagonal muscle that divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. Most of the neck's nerves lie deep to it.
  • Trapezius: the back edge of the posterior triangle, running out to the scapula.
  • Anterior scalene: in the floor of the posterior triangle, with the phrenic nerve on its anterior surface.
  • Middle scalene: just posterior to it, flexing the neck laterally. The brachial plexus emerges between the two scalenes.

flags.title: The diagram is not in the bank
flags.html: The labelled diagram is not in the bank, so the key's letter-to-structure mapping cannot be checked against it. That the brachial plexus passes between the anterior and middle scalenes comes from general anatomy, not the note.

ent-w9-new-q1-1.html:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Pain and submandibular swelling that worsen with eating are salivary colic from sialolithiasis, and the submandibular gland is the most common site. The stone causes stasis, and its complications follow from obstruction and infection:

  • Acute suppurative sialadenitis (II).
  • Ductal stricture (III).
  • Abscess (IV), when the sialadenitis progresses.
  • Fistula (V), the gland draining through the skin. The lecture gives it as a complication that may need surgery.

Necrosis (I) is not a listed complication of either condition.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives D (I, II, V), which includes necrosis and leaves out stricture and abscess. The vault's sialolithiasis note lists fistula, acute sialadenitis and ductal stricture as complications. Its acute sialadenitis note adds abscess and deep neck space infection. Neither mentions necrosis, so the material supports C (II, III, IV, V).

ent-w9-new-q21-21:
From 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck. Lemierre's syndrome is an infectious thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically caused by the oral anaerobe Fusobacterium necrophorum. A pharyngitis comes first; about a week later the patient develops fever and rigors, looks toxic, and has neck pain over the vein. Septic emboli to the lungs cause the respiratory distress.

  • A: an angio-invasive aseptate mould is Mucor, the cause of rhinocerebral mucormycosis.
  • B: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole treats Lemierre's. Mucormycosis needs surgical debridement plus liposomal amphotericin B.
  • D: even with that treatment, mucormycosis has a very high mortality.

ent-w9-new-q8-8.html:
From the achalasia column of the esophagus table in 01 - Approach to Abdominal Pain & Distension (Week 13). The table splits treatment in two. Surgical myotomy is curative; balloon dilation, botulinum toxin and calcium channel blockers are symptom management. Cutting the LES muscle permanently relieves the obstruction, which is why laparoscopic Heller myotomy is the definitive answer. Its cost is reflux afterwards, usually requiring long-term PPIs.

  • Pneumatic dilation (B): effective, but the table places it under symptom management.
  • Botox (C): wears off in 6-7 months.
  • POEM (D): an endoscopic myotomy of the same muscle.

flags.title: More than one option is defensible
flags.html: The vault's achalasia note labels pneumatic dilatation and POEM “definitive” alongside Heller myotomy, and POEM is itself a myotomy. A is the surgical myotomy the Week 13 table calls curative, so it is the intended answer, but D is hard to rule out on this material.

ent-wb-ent0-q13.html:
From 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses. Hoarseness raises the question of a laryngeal primary, and the lecture's cancer history covers each element offered:

  • Duration (A): the red flag is persistent hoarseness, which the lecture defines as more than 3 weeks.
  • Associated symptoms (B): referred otalgia and dysphagia point to an upper aerodigestive tract primary.
  • Risk factors (C): smoking is the main one. Trauma and previous surgery are structural causes of voice change to rule out, for example neck surgery that puts the recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk.

flags.title: The duration does not match the lecture
flags.html: The lecture's threshold for persistent hoarseness is more than 3 weeks, not the 2 weeks in option A. B and C match 04 - Adult Head & Neck Masses, and D is the intended answer, but A is not supported as written.

ent-wb-ent0-q15:
From 07 - Pediatric Airway Pathology. All three statements come straight from the lecture:

  • A: croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is the most common cause of stridor in children, and 3-5% of children develop it.
  • B: it is viral, usually parainfluenza, RSV or influenza.
  • C: because it is viral, it is most common in spring and fall.

It peaks between 6 months and 3 years, with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor and a steeple sign. Epiglottitis is the bacterial (Hib) alternative, and it is now rare.

ent-wb-ent0-q23.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. The sternocleidomastoid splits the neck into two triangles. The anterior triangle is bounded above by the inferior border of the mandible, medially by the midline of the neck, and laterally by the anterior border of the SCM. A is the only option with that set.

  • B gives the posterior triangle: posterior border of the SCM, the trapezius, and the clavicle.
  • C, D, E combine landmarks that do not enclose either triangle. The external jugular vein runs across the SCM and is not a boundary.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The note describes the carotid triangle's boundaries, but not those of the anterior or posterior triangles; those are from general anatomy. Note too that option A's “back of sternocleidomastoid” is loose: the anterior triangle is bounded by the SCM's anterior border. Verify before relying on it.

ent-wb-ent0-q34.html:
From 05 - Infections of the Head and Neck. Pharyngitis is most often viral, caused by the common upper respiratory tract viruses (rhinovirus, coronaviruses, influenza, parainfluenza), with EBV and CMV as further viral causes.

  • Strep pyogenes (D): group A strep is the main bacterial cause and the one worth catching, but it is the minority.
  • Strep pneumoniae (C): causes sinusitis, otitis media and pneumonia, not typical pharyngitis.
  • Candida (A): yeast is only an occasional part of the oral flora.
  • E. coli (E): not a throat pathogen.

review.t: Infections of the Head and Neck

ent-w9-module-q10-10.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. Each nerve runs with the vessel serving the same territory:

  • Vagus nerve (II) with the common carotid artery (A): both lie in the carotid sheath, with the vagus between the internal jugular vein and the carotid.
  • Superior laryngeal nerve (III) with the superior thyroid artery (B): the first branch of the external carotid runs down to the larynx and thyroid beside the nerve's external branch. That is why ligating the artery at thyroidectomy can injure the nerve, giving a weak, tired voice from cricothyroid palsy.
  • Hypoglossal nerve (I) with the lingual artery (C): both go to the tongue, the nerve passing deep to the posterior digastric into the oral cavity.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The note describes each nerve and artery separately but does not pair them. That the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery, and is at risk when it is ligated, is from general anatomy. Verify it before relying on it.

ent-w9-module-q19-19.html:
From 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia. Achalasia is a failure of the LES to relax, together with impaired peristalsis: a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction. Every effective treatment therefore disrupts the LES, whether by pneumatic dilation, Botox, or myotomy (Heller or POEM), as listed in the vault's achalasia note.

  • A: the LES is tight, not hypotensive. What gets regurgitated is undigested food retained above it. A hypotensive LES is the scleroderma pattern.
  • B: the manometric (Chicago) classification has three achalasia subtypes, not four.
  • D: impaired LES relaxation defines the disorder, so it is always present.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The number of achalasia subtypes (three, by the Chicago classification) is not in the notes and comes from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

ent-w9-module-q23-23.html:
From 03 - Oropharyngeal Dysphagia. The lecture is explicit: the main reason for any dysphagia work-up is to assess the risk of aspiration, because it can be life-threatening. Food or liquid that passes below the vocal cords causes aspiration pneumonia (from oropharyngeal anaerobes) or pneumonitis. The work-up (bedside swallow, modified barium swallow, FEES) is built around finding it.

  • Weight loss (D) is a real complication, but it is slower and less dangerous.
  • Fewer food choices (A) and longer meals (B) affect quality of life but are not dangerous.

ent-w9-module-q24-24.html:
From 03 - Oropharyngeal Dysphagia. Every option is on the lecture's lists:

  • Direct symptoms come from the failed swallow itself: coughing (A) and choking (B), as well as drooling, nasal regurgitation and food sticking in the throat.
  • Indirect symptoms are its consequences: weight loss (C), repeated chest infections and pneumonia (D), and voice changes (E), along with changes in articulation and speech.
  • Malnutrition (F) is listed with dehydration among the complications.

Coughing or choking at meals and recurrent pneumonia both point to aspiration, which the work-up is designed to detect.

ent-w9-new-q14-14.html:
From 06 - Pediatric Neck Masses. The lecture's exam box reads consistency as a differential: firm means infection or malignancy, fluctuant means cyst or abscess, and fixed means malignancy.

  • A: most pediatric neck masses are congenital (over 50% by some sources) or inflammatory. Unlike in adults, malignancy is the minority.
  • B: in children, lymph nodes over 2 cm are not normal and need a work-up.
  • D: ultrasound is a routine early step. It separates solid from cystic masses, whereas MRI often needs sedation in children.

cardio-w1-module-q19-19:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology. Each normal heart sound marks a set of valves closing. Valves opening make no sound. S2 ("dub") is the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves closing at the end of systole, which is where diastole begins.

  • A: mitral and tricuspid closure is S1 ("lub"), at the start of systole.
  • B, D: opening is silent in a normal heart. An opening snap is abnormal, heard in mitral stenosis.
cardio-w1-module-q2-2:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. Digoxin is the one drug on this list with no effect on overall mortality in HFrEF. Its benefit is fewer admissions for pulmonary edema, which lowers morbidity. Higher doses and drug levels do not help symptoms and may increase mortality.

  • B, C, E: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and beta blockers are all mortality-reducing HFrEF therapy.
  • D: the lecture cites the 3-year heart failure trials, in which adding an MRA (spironolactone) to usual therapy improved mortality.
cardio-w1-module-q3-3:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. ACE inhibitors block ACE, and ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Bradykinin builds up and causes vasodilation, which gives the two class effects dry cough and angioedema. That makes perindopril the likely culprit.

  • A: furosemide causes volume and electrolyte problems, not airway swelling.
  • B: spironolactone's adverse effects are hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
  • D: metoprolol's are bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue and bronchospasm.
  • E: atorvastatin is not linked to angioedema in the lecture.

ARBs leave bradykinin alone, which is why they replace an ACE inhibitor that caused cough or angioedema.

cardio-w1-module-q4-4.html:
Diffuse, symmetric proximal muscle pain and weakness (thighs, shoulders, lower back) with a raised creatine kinase is the picture of statin-associated myopathy. The most severe form, rhabdomyolysis, can injure the kidneys. That points to atorvastatin. The Cardiac Pharmacology note lists this question with atorvastatin as the answer, but it does not explain statin toxicity.

  • A: furosemide causes volume depletion and hypokalemia. The cramps from low potassium are not a CK-raising myositis.
  • B: spironolactone causes hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
  • C: enalapril causes cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia and renal impairment.
  • D: metoprolol causes fatigue and bradycardia, not a muscle injury with a raised CK.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

cardio-w1-module-q5-5:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. A dry, chronic cough is the signature adverse effect of ACE inhibitors. Blocking ACE stops bradykinin being broken down, and the bradykinin that builds up irritates the airway. That points to lisinopril. The fix is to switch to an ARB, which does not affect bradykinin.

  • A: furosemide gives electrolyte and volume problems.
  • B: spironolactone gives hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
  • D: metoprolol can cause bronchospasm through beta-2 blockade, which is wheeze in reactive airways, not an isolated chronic cough.
  • E: atorvastatin's hallmark is myopathy.
cardio-w1-module-q6-6:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. Hyperkalemia comes from blocking aldosterone, at any point in the pathway. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and MRAs all predispose to it; nitrates do not. The lecture's warning adds that hyperkalemia admissions rose as MRA prescribing rose.

  • A (ramipril): less angiotensin II means less aldosterone.
  • C (valsartan): blocking the AT1 receptor lowers aldosterone in the same way.
  • D, E (spironolactone, eplerenone): these block the aldosterone receptor directly, so potassium is retained.
  • B (nitroglycerin): an NO donor that relaxes vascular smooth muscle. Its adverse effects are headache, hypotension and reflex tachycardia, not potassium.
cardio-w1-module-q31-31:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. Compliance = change in volume / change in pressure. A compliant ventricle holds more blood at a given pressure. A stiff one, from hypertrophy, ischemia or scar, has a higher end-diastolic pressure at the same volume. Dilated cardiomyopathy increases compliance.

  • A: wall tension and contractility relate to systolic force, not filling.
  • C: preload and stroke volume is the Frank-Starling relationship.
  • D: heart rate and stroke volume together give cardiac output.
  • E: wall tension and wall thickness belong to the Laplace law.
cardio-w1-module-q38-38:
From 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology. In the ventricular myocyte, phase 0 is voltage-gated Na+ channels opening, so Na+ rushes in. Phase 2 (plateau) is slow voltage-gated Ca2+ channels letting Ca2+ in, which balances K+ efflux.

  • B: K+ moves out of the cell (efflux), and it repolarizes the cell rather than depolarizing it.
  • C: calcium moves in, and in phase 3 the Ca2+ channels close while K+ channels stay open.
  • D: the phase 4 resting potential (about -90 mV) is set mainly by K+ permeability through leak channels, plus the Na+/K+ pump, not by outside calcium.
  • E: phase 3 makes the interior more negative as K+ leaves.
cardio-w1-module-q39-39:
From 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology. SA node cells have no stable resting potential. More Na+ and Ca2+ leak into them than into other cells, so their potential drifts up from about -55 to -60 mV to the -40 mV threshold on its own. That positive leak is the basis of automaticity.

  • A: the heart needs no nerve input to beat. Autonomic input only changes the rate, and vagal input slows it.
  • B: oxygen content does not open sodium channels.
  • D: the resting potential is still negative inside, just less negative than in a myocyte.
  • E: the order is reversed. The SA node drives the AV node, which takes over only if the SA node fails.
cardio-w1-new-q16-16:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum. The visceral pericardium lines the heart and the roots of the great vessels. The parietal layer lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium, and serous fluid in the cavity between them reduces friction.

  • A: the lecture calls the sac triple-layered: fibrous, then the two serous layers. Only the serous pericardium is double.
  • B: the parietal and visceral layers make up the serous pericardium, not the fibrous one.
  • D: parietal lines the fibrous pericardium, not the heart.
  • E: the serous pericardium secretes the fluid. The fibrous layer is dense, inelastic tissue that anchors the heart to the diaphragm.
cardio-w1-new-q19-19:
From 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology. A is true: the SA node is the primary pacemaker, firing fastest at about 100 bpm. C is true: a greater leak of positive ions into its cells is what lets it self-excite.

  • B is false: the AV node, a secondary pacemaker, can take over if the SA node fails, and lower pacemakers can take over after that. If those fail too, the patient needs an artificial pacemaker.
  • Because B is false, E (all of the above) fails, which leaves D.
cardio-w1-new-q20-20:
From 02 - Introduction to ECG. The inferior leads have the left leg as the positive electrode and look up at the diaphragmatic surface. They are II, III and aVF, and a normal QRS is positive in them because depolarization travels down toward them.

  • I (left arm positive): a lateral lead, grouped with aVL.
  • V5: a precordial lateral lead, grouped with V6.

This matches the STEMI map: inferior leads II, III and aVF point to the RCA, and reciprocal change shows in I and aVL.
cardio-w1-new-q22-22:
From 02 - Introduction to ECG. A normal PR interval is 120-200 ms, three to five small boxes. Under 120 ms suggests the impulse is bypassing the AV node, as in WPW. 200 ms or more is 1st-degree AV block.

  • B: a normal QRS is 80-120 ms. 120 ms or more is a wide complex, as in BBB, VT, hyperkalemia or TCA overdose.
  • C: QT and PR measure different things, ventricular systole and AV nodal delay, so they are unrelated.
  • D: 1st-degree AV block is a prolonged PR, not a wide QRS.
  • E: ST depression suggests ischemia or a reciprocal change. ST elevation and Q waves mark infarction.
cardio-w1-weekly-q7-7:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. The lecture groups these ageing changes together. Increasing age brings a lower maximal heart rate (roughly 220 - age), lower maximal oxygen consumption, and a stiffer aorta and stiffer, less compliant ventricles.

  • A: true. Maximal heart rate falls with age.
  • B: true. The aorta stiffens.
  • C: true. A stiffer ventricle has lower compliance.
  • D: true. VO2 max declines.

All four are right, so the answer is E. Stiffer ventricles are also why older hearts rely more on the atrial kick.
cardio-wb-cardio0-q16:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology. Start at the end of diastole and follow the valves.

  • iv. Atrial systole: the last 10-15% of filling, and the S4 if the ventricle is stiff.
  • iii. Isovolumetric contraction: all valves closed and pressure rising, during the QRS.
  • ii. Rapid ejection: the aortic valve opens.
  • vi. Reduced ejection: the T wave.
  • vii. Isovolumetric relaxation: the first phase of diastole, after the aortic valve closes (S2).
  • i. Rapid filling: the mitral valve opens, and an S3 is heard here.
  • v. Reduced filling: the ventricle approaches its end-diastolic pressure.

Only D keeps both isovolumetric phases where they belong. Ejection must come right after isovolumetric contraction, and filling right after isovolumetric relaxation. A, B, C and E each break one of those pairings.

cardio-w2-module-q19-19.html:
From 04 - Aortic Stenosis. Once severe AS becomes symptomatic, survival collapses. The classic figures are 50% survival at 5 years with angina, 3 years with syncope, and 2 years with dyspnea (heart failure). The shortest survival is with dyspnea, the sign the LV has started to fail. The Surgical Management note says the same: dyspnea/HF carries the worst prognosis.

  • A (angina): about 5-year median survival, the best of the triad.
  • B (syncope): about 3 years, worse than angina but better than heart failure.
  • C (palpitations): not part of the angina-syncope-dyspnea prognostic triad.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q17:
From 01 - Intro to Valvular Disease, Heart Sounds, and Clinical Assessment.

  • S1: the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves close.
  • S2: the ventriculo-arterial (aortic and pulmonary) valves close.
  • S3: early diastole, from rapid filling into a volume-loaded ventricle, as in MR or severe systolic dysfunction. It can be normal in the young.
  • S4: late diastole, from atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle, as in hypertension, LVH or CAD. It is always pathological.

B and D swap S3 and S4. C and D swap S1 and S2. E calls S3 respiratory splitting, but splitting is a feature of S2 (A2 and P2), not an extra sound.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q38.html:
From 08 - Pediatric Cardiology Case Review. The lecture's benign-versus-pathologic table: an innocent murmur is a mid-systolic (ejection) murmur, or continuous for a venous hum. It is grade 1-3, never with a thrill, and soft, musical, vibratory or blowing. It is heard at a characteristic precordial site, such as the LLSB for Still's or the LUSB for peripheral PA stenosis. Anything outside that pattern argues against an innocent murmur.

  • C (diastolic), H (pansystolic): these timings appear only in the pathologic column.
  • D (grade IV or more): grade IV means a thrill, and innocent murmurs never have one.
  • E (harsh): a harsh quality marks a pathologic murmur.
  • F (heard only in the back): innocent murmurs are loudest at their usual precordial site.
  • A, B, G: systolic, musical and ejection are exactly the innocent pattern.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q81:
From 02 - Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease. A MUGA scan tags red cells with technetium, images the blood pool in systole and diastole, and calculates EF from the volume curve. The lecture calls it highly accurate for heart function and EF, and it is used to follow EF after MI and during anthracycline chemotherapy. Cardiac MRI is the overall gold standard, but it is not an option here.

  • B (MIBI): a perfusion scan for ischemia and infarction. It can estimate EF, but that is not what it is for.
  • C (TEE): used for valves and endocarditis when a transthoracic echo is inadequate.
  • D (CT angiogram): coronary anatomy, a rule-out test with an NPV of 99%.
  • E (dobutamine stress echo): detects inducible ischemia.

cardio-w3-module-q10-10.html:
From 05 - Complications of Acute MI. An RV infarct comes from a proximal RCA occlusion. The RCA supplies the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 90%, so sinus bradycardia and AV block are both expected. Infarcted myocardium also leaves a scar that can support re-entrant VT. So none of A, B or C is unlikely. The module's own answer, recorded in the Myocardial Infarction note, is "None of the above": no listed manifestation is the least likely one.

The bank's option D reads "All of the above", which would mean all three are unlikely. That is the opposite of what the lecture teaches.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The module answer recorded in 04 - Myocardial Infarction (module questions, complications) is None of the above. The bank's option D says All of the above. Read as written, it claims bradycardia, AV block and VT are all unlikely in an RV infarct, which 05 - Complications of Acute MI contradicts: the RCA supplies the SA node in 60% and the AV node in 90%. The option text was probably transcribed wrongly. Check it against the source module.

cardio-w3-module-q11-11:
From 05 - Complications of Acute MI. Early post-MI pericarditis comes within 5 days, most often at days 1-3, as inflammation clears the damaged tissue. It presents with a rub and pleuritic pain. The lecture's treatment is high-dose ASA and colchicine.

  • A (morphine): relieves pain but does not treat the inflammation.
  • C (oral corticosteroids): not the lecture's treatment, and in general they are avoided early after MI because they can impair healing of the infarct.
  • D (intrapericardial lidocaine): not a treatment.

Dressler syndrome is the late, immune-mediated form, weeks to months later.
cardio-w3-module-q12-12:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture opens the CABG section with the point that the risk of a cardiac event rises sharply with the number of sites in the body carrying atherosclerosis. More total burden means worse survival: an inverse correlation.

  • A: atherosclerosis is systemic. The same process causes PAD, aneurysm and stroke.
  • B: after an MI, the risk of another is 5-7 times the primary-prevention risk (Cardiac Rehab).
  • D: the lecture does not rank causes of death. C is the statement it directly supports.
  • E: the survival gain from CABG is small in one- or two-vessel disease. The benefit is largest with left main disease and abnormal LV function (the CABG section of 04 - Myocardial Infarction).

cardio-w3-module-q13-13.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction (CABG section). Arterial conduits outlast veins. The lecture's figures: 12-year survival is 70% with one internal thoracic artery but 82% with bilateral internal thoracic arteries, and no internal thoracic artery graft is listed as a predictor of late mortality. The trend is toward more arterial grafts to improve patency and cut repeat operations.

  • A: endoscopic vein harvest gives less pain, infection and edema, with quality identical to open harvest.
  • B: CABG improves survival, most in left main disease and abnormal LV function, as well as angina.
  • C: overall mortality is about 2%, and complications are uncommon: stroke is the worst, and mediastinitis runs about 1.5%. They do not confine the benefit to a small subset.

cardio-w3-module-q14-14:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. CABG is not curative. Afterward the lecture lists ASA for life, clopidogrel or ticagrelor, statins, beta blockers and an ACE inhibitor at a cardioprotective dose, plus lifestyle change. The CABG section of 04 - Myocardial Infarction adds referral to cardiac rehab.

  • B: the strongest distractor. SYNTAX found no difference in all-cause death at 10 years overall. But CABG gave a survival benefit in three-vessel disease and in diabetics, and the lecture says the choice depends on the individual patient. So "equally effective for most" overstates the evidence.
  • C: choosing between PCI, CABG and medicine is a joint cardiology and surgery decision, and that collaboration improves outcomes.
  • D: drugs do not replace exercise, weight loss and smoking cessation. Lifestyle and medication are prescribed together.
cardio-w3-module-q15-15:
From 06 - Cardiac Rehab & Secondary Prevention. The lecture's figure: after an MI, the risk of another MI is 5-7 times the risk before the first one. That jump is why secondary prevention (rehab, antiplatelets, statin, ACE inhibitor, beta blocker) is so aggressive.

  • A (1-3x) and B (3-5x): understate the risk.
  • D (7-10x): overstates it.
cardio-w3-module-q16-16:
From 06 - Cardiac Rehab & Secondary Prevention. In clinical trials, exercise-based cardiac rehab cut mortality by a relative 18-26%. The module question rounds that to 20-30%.

  • A, B, C (0-20%): understate the trial effect. Rehab is a class I, level A recommendation.
  • Don't mix this up with real-world programs, which report larger effects: about 50% in the Toronto and SJH hybrid programs, and 40-60% fewer readmissions or deaths after MI, PCI or CABG.
cardio-w3-module-q18-18:
From 06 - Cardiac Rehab & Secondary Prevention. An exercise prescription follows F.I.T.T.: Frequency, Intensity, Time (duration), Type, set between a warm-up and a cool-down. For the aerobic conditioning phase, that is 3-5 times a week, 40-80% of heart rate reserve, 20-40 minutes, of aerobic activity. Patients can change one element at a time.

  • B: F is Frequency. Exercising with friends is not part of it.
  • C: Time means duration, not time of day.
  • D: I is Intensity, set from heart rate reserve, not interest level.

cardio-w3-module-q8-8.html:
From 05 - Complications of Acute MI. Of these options, only sinus bradycardia is an arrhythmic complication. It is the most common arrhythmia in inferior STEMI: up to 40% in the first 2 hours and 20% by the end of day 1. Increased vagal tone drives it, and it usually resolves within 24 hours. The RCA, which infarcts in inferior MI, also supplies the SA node in 60% of people.

  • B (elevated JVP): part of the RV-infarct triad with hypotension and clear lungs. It is a hemodynamic complication, not an arrhythmia.
  • C (peripheral edema): a sign of right-sided congestion.
  • D (pulmonary edema): a mechanical complication of a very large infarct, typically an anterior STEMI. It is not an arrhythmia.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys D (pulmonary edema), but 05 - Complications of Acute MI classes pulmonary edema as a mechanical complication of large, usually anterior, infarcts. It names sinus bradycardia as the most common arrhythmia of inferior STEMI. The module answer recorded in 04 - Myocardial Infarction (module questions, complications) is also sinus bradycardia, which is A.

cardio-w3-new-q11-11.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. Acute chest pain in the ER is ACS until proven otherwise. The first test is a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, and it decides the pathway. A STEMI goes to reperfusion by primary PCI. An NSTEMI or unstable angina is stabilized, then has angiography within 24-48 hours, sooner if high risk. So the next steps are ECG and coronary angiography.

  • A (Persantine-MIBI): a pharmacological stress test for stable patients who cannot exercise.
  • C (cardiac CTA): a rule-out test for CAD in stable, low-to-intermediate-risk patients, not for an acute presentation.

The Imaging lecture's escalating case follows the same order. Chest pain with shortness of breath on one flight of stairs after a high-risk study leads to a coronary angiogram.

cardio-w3-new-q2-2.html:
From 02 - Pathology of Ischemic Heart Disease. The lecture says atheroma can be very focal. One short, tight segment limits flow through the whole vessel, so a small focus can be a big problem. That makes B false.

  • A: true. CAD mostly affects the proximal epicardial arteries, which is why lesions are reachable by surgery or catheter.
  • D: true. Fibrofatty plaques are more vulnerable and prone to thrombose than calcified or fibrous ones.
  • C: also false by the lecture. Focal stenosis is the easier kind to treat, and severe disease in multiple vessels "makes it much more challenging to treat".

flags.title: Two statements are false
flags.html: B is false, as keyed. But 02 - Pathology of Ischemic Heart Disease also makes C false: focal stenosis is easier to treat surgically, and multi-vessel disease is "much more challenging to treat". The question has two false statements and only one keyed answer.

cardio-w3-new-q8-8:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. CABG improves survival as well as symptoms when a large territory of LV is at risk. The lecture's list: left main, left main equivalent (70% or more in the proximal LAD plus the circumflex), triple-vessel, and double-vessel disease that includes the LAD.

  • B (RCA stenosis): single-vessel disease outside the LAD, which gives the smallest survival gain. The 04 - Myocardial Infarction figure shows the benefit is small for one- or two-vessel disease. PCI or medical therapy fits better.
  • A: triple-vessel disease is where SYNTAX showed a CABG survival benefit.
  • C: LAD plus circumflex is two-vessel disease with the LAD, which is left main equivalent when both are proximal.
  • D: left main equivalent is a listed indication.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q92.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction (CABG section). The lecture lists predictors of operative (early) mortality after CABG: urgency of operation, older age, redo operation, female sex, LV ejection fraction, left main stenosis, diabetes, and cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease. Older age and LVEF also carry over into late mortality. Stroke, the worst complication, and aortic atherosclerosis both rise with age, which is the case for age as the dominant early risk.

  • A, C, D, E (LVEF, sex, extent of CAD, diabetes) are all on the same operative-mortality list, so the lecture does not separate them from age.

flags.title: The lecture does not rank these predictors
flags.html: 04 - Myocardial Infarction lists age alongside LVEF, sex, left main disease and diabetes as predictors of operative mortality. It never names one as the strongest. The workbook key (age) is peer-written, and the lecture neither confirms nor contradicts it.

cardio-w4-module-q10-10:
From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification. Heart failure is a clinical syndrome, not a disease. "Ischemic cardiomyopathy" is defined clinically: HF with LVEF under 40% in a patient with prior MI and/or severe CAD. It is not a pathological category. Pathologically, "cardiomyopathy" means a structurally and functionally abnormal myocardium in the absence of CAD, hypertension, valve disease or congenital disease sufficient to explain it. So an ischemic cause excludes it by definition, and the statement is false.

Ischemic heart disease is still the most common cause of HF, about 65% of patients.
cardio-w4-module-q11-11:
From 03 - Heart Failure Clinical Features and Evaluation. Where the congestion lands depends on which ventricle fails. Right-sided failure backs blood up into the systemic veins, giving raised JVP, hepatic congestion (and ascites), and peripheral edema.

  • A (PND): left-sided. Fluid redistributes into the lungs at night.
  • B (orthopnea): left-sided. Lying flat worsens pulmonary congestion.
  • C (crackles): left-sided. They are pulmonary edema from LV backup.

cardio-w4-module-q12-12.html:
From 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure and 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. Perfusion is warm or cold (how well the heart supports the body) and volume is wet or dry (congestion). The module answer is cold and wet: poor perfusion at rest plus volume overload. 09 calls that profile cardiogenic shock, and every late-stage patient is cold.

  • A (cold and dry): underperfused but not congested, so one axis is spared.
  • D (warm and wet): congested but perfusing. Diuresis treats it.
  • C (warm and dry): the compensated profile, with the best prognosis.

cardio-w4-module-q16-16:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. A VAD is a foreign body giving non-physiological, pulseless flow. The lecture lists its complications from most to least common: driveline infection, GI bleeding, stroke or intracranial hemorrhage, device thrombosis, pump malfunction. Its module answer to this question is stroke and driveline infection. Most patients develop a driveline infection, because the driveline tunnels through the skin to external batteries and a controller.

  • B (electrocution): not a listed complication. The power supply is external and low-voltage, and the driveline carries power and data only to the pump.

cardio-w4-module-q19-19.html:
From 05 - Physiology of Hypertension. The module answer is salt, obstructive sleep apnea and excessive alcohol. Each is on the lecture's lists:

  • B (salt): the first "self-inflicted" aggravating cause.
  • D (OSA): the commonest secondary cause, about 10%, through raised aldosterone and norepinephrine. It can mimic pheochromocytoma biochemically.
  • F (alcohol): alcohol or substance use accounts for about 5% of secondary hypertension.
  • A (eggs), E (water), G (lectures): none appear. The last is a joke option.
  • C (adiposity): not on the lecture's cause or aggravating-factor lists, and the module leaves it out.

flags.title: Excess adiposity is contestable
flags.html: The key follows the module answer recorded in 05 - Physiology of Hypertension, which leaves out excessive adiposity. Obesity is generally accepted as a contributor to raised blood pressure, so C is arguable. The lecture notes simply do not list it. Treat the key as the module's intended answer, not a claim that adiposity plays no part.

cardio-w4-module-q6-6: From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification. The lecture gives three major causes of HF with reduced LV function: ischemic heart disease (~65%), cardiomyopathy ("non-ischemic", ~25%), and primary valvular or congenital disease (~10%). Ischemic disease is the most common, and these patients often have a past MI with myocardial scar. HF is "usually an index of the end stages of a disease", which is what "end stage" ischemic disease means here. The module answer in 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure is true, about 65% in the community.
cardio-w4-module-q9-9: From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification. Myocarditis sits under inflammatory cardiomyopathy, which the lecture splits into infectious and non-infectious causes (sarcoidosis is its non-infectious example). The module answer in 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure is false: myocarditis can be infectious, toxic or unspecified. The point is that myocarditis is defined by inflammation of the myocardium, not by its trigger. Toxic cardiomyopathy has its own list of culprits (anthracyclines, trastuzumab, interferons), and many cases never get a cause.
cardio-w4-new-q13-13:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. The lecture lists three components of transplant assessment, and every option falls under one of them:

  • A: does the patient want transplant or advanced options?
  • B: is the condition advanced enough? That means severe symptoms, backed by cardiopulmonary exercise testing and invasive hemodynamics.
  • C, D, E: are there contraindications? These are significant comorbidities (e.g. cancer in the last 5 years, lung, kidney or liver disease), psychosocial factors, immunological issues, surgical considerations (a prior sternotomy) and age.

Donors are scarce, so justice matters. Ontario rarely has more than 50 people on the waitlist.
cardio-w4-new-q14-14:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. The lecture's VAD complications, most to least common, are driveline infection (E), GI bleeding (A), stroke or intracranial hemorrhage (B), device thrombosis, and pump malfunction (C). They follow from a foreign body giving continuous, pulseless flow.

  • D (myocardial infarction) is not on the list. The pump offloads the ventricle and replaces its output, and the lecture never names coronary events as a VAD complication.

Remember that a VAD patient has no pulse, which is expected with continuous flow.

cardio-w4-new-q16-16.html:
From 06 - Management of Hypertension. The lecture builds the multi-drug regimen in numbered steps:

  • Step 1 (C): a RAAS inhibitor, ACEI or ARB, chosen by the odds of a cough.
  • Step 2 (A): a diuretic or a CCB, chosen by serum K+ and volume status (pedal edema). Normal or low K+ with little edema points to a DHP CCB. High K+ or marked edema points to a thiazide-like diuretic.
  • Step 3 (D): add whichever of the two was not chosen.
  • Step 4 (B): spironolactone, doxazosin or a beta blocker, by K+ and heart rate. Low K+ gives spironolactone, high K+ gives doxazosin, and HR over 85 gives a beta blocker.
  • Step 5 (E): four drugs control 95% of patients, so if BP is still high, check adherence first (directly observed therapy).

cardio-w4-new-q6-6:
From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification. NYHA class describes function, so it waxes and wanes as symptoms are controlled. A class IV patient can therefore improve to class III with treatment. The AHA/ACC stages, by contrast, only move forward.

  • A: HFpEF is EF ≥ 50%. EF ≤ 40% is HFrEF (systolic), and 41-49% is HFmrEF.
  • B: stage B is structural heart disease without symptoms. Clinical HF (past or current symptoms) is stage C.
  • D: ascites, raised JVP and poor appetite come from systemic venous congestion, which is right-sided failure. Left-sided failure gives dyspnea, orthopnea and PND.
cardio-w4-new-q9-9:
From 04 - Heart Failure Treatments. First-line HFrEF therapy is triple therapy:

  • A (ACE inhibitor): indicated in virtually all patients with LV dysfunction.
  • D (beta blocker): for all stable mild-to-moderate HF.
  • E (MRA): indicated outright in NYHA III-IV.
  • B (ARNI): sacubitril/valsartan replaces the ACEI or ARB in patients who stay symptomatic despite optimized GDMT. That makes it a second step.
  • C (ARB): first line only when the patient cannot tolerate an ACEI. Otherwise it is second line after optimizing the ACEI and beta blocker.

cardio-w4-weekly-q2-2.html: From 02 - Heart Failure Causes and Classification and 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure. HFpEF is a filling problem. The ventricle cannot relax and fill normally, and because its volume is small the ejection fraction is kept at EF ≥ 50%. That is what option A means. It makes up about 60% of HF. There is no strong evidence base for treating it, so management targets the risk factors that come with it: blood pressure, heart rate and diabetes. That list of comorbidities is the point of option B. D completes the typical profile, so E, all of the above, is keyed. Note that the extracted options merged B and C into one line and dropped the "≥" sign from A.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The notes support A and B, but they do not describe HFpEF patients as more often elderly and female (option D). That part is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

cardio-w4-weekly-q5-5.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction (the Week 3 overview chart, AAA repair section). Repair of an AAA is prophylactic, so it balances the risk of rupture against operative risk. An infrarenal degenerative AAA is repaired at ≥ 5.5 cm in men and 5 cm in women. Four RCTs showed no survival benefit from repairing smaller aneurysms, even with EVAR. Other indications are growth of more than 1 cm in a year, symptoms, saccular morphology, and rupture, in a patient fit for operation. Below 5 cm the plan is watch and wait with yearly imaging.

  • B, C, D each give a threshold that is either too low or ignores women's lower cut-off.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q107:
From 04 - Heart Failure Treatments. The lecture recommends triple therapy for systolic HF:

  • an ACE inhibitor, or an ARB if the ACEI is not tolerated
  • a beta blocker
  • an MRA such as spironolactone

After titrating these to target doses, the next moves depend on NYHA class, heart rate and EF: switch to an ARNI, add ivabradine if sinus HR ≥ 70, or consider an ICD if EF is under 35%. D leaves out the MRA, and it is the MRA that makes the combination triple therapy. A, B and C alone are each one-third of it.
cardio-wb-cardio0-q97:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. All three statements are taken from the lecture:

  • A: palliative care has traditionally focused on predictable trajectories like cancer. HF is unpredictable, so palliative care should be considered earlier, though it is often raised late.
  • B: HF commonly takes a "palli-active" approach: destination VAD, home inotropes, home IV diuretics and telehomecare.
  • C: no advanced therapy cures HF, not even transplant. The main goal is improving symptoms, which can prolong life but not always.

cardio-w1-module-q17-17.html:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. Bronchodilation is β2-mediated smooth muscle relaxation, so you want a β2 agonist. The lecture profiles fenoterol as +++ β2, + β1 and no α effect, and its module answer for "most helpful for bronchodilation" is fenoterol (C).

  • A (isoproterenol): equal β1 and β2 agonism. The lecture picks it for bradycardia.
  • B (methoxamine): an α1 agonist, a vasoconstrictor with no bronchial action.
  • D (labetalol): α blockade plus β1 and β2 blockade. Blocking β2 causes bronchospasm, so it would do the opposite.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives D (labetalol), but 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology describes labetalol as blocking β1 and β2 receptors, and β2 blockade causes bronchoconstriction. The lecture's own module answer for this question is fenoterol, which is C.

cardio-w1-module-q20-20:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology. Veins and venules are the capacitance vessels. They are thin-walled, very distensible and low-pressure, and they hold about 70% of the blood volume. Venoconstriction lowers their capacitance and pushes blood back to the heart, which is a key compensation for hypovolemia.

  • A (arteries): a high-pressure conducting and distributing system, not a reservoir.
  • B (arterioles): resistance vessels that set flow and pressure.
  • D (capillaries): exchange vessels with a huge surface area but little volume.
  • E (lymphatics): return interstitial fluid. They do not hold circulating blood.

flags.title: More than one point is defensible
flags.html: A loop has two isovolumetric limbs, and both valves are closed along each: contraction (C to D) and relaxation (F to A). F sits on the relaxation limb, so it is hard to rule out. The module answer recorded in 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology is C, the end-diastolic point where isovolumetric contraction begins.

cardio-w1-module-q24-24.html:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology (pressure-volume loop). On the loop, read the corners as valve events. Filling runs along the bottom (A to C). At C, end-diastole, the ventricle starts to contract, the mitral valve closes and the aortic valve is still shut. From C to D is isovolumetric contraction: both valves are closed and pressure rises with no change in volume. The module answer recorded in 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology is C.

  • A, B: diastolic filling, with the mitral valve open.
  • D, E: the aortic valve opens at D and ejection runs through E.
  • F: sits just after the aortic valve closes, at the start of isovolumetric relaxation. See the flag.

cardio-w1-module-q33-33:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum. Follow the flow backwards. The femoral artery leads up the aorta, and the aorta arises from the left ventricle through the aortic valve. A catheter advanced retrograde from the aorta therefore crosses the aortic valve into the LV first. The anatomy module answer recorded in 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology is left ventricle.

  • A (left atrium): lies upstream of the LV, behind the mitral valve, so the catheter would reach it only after the LV.
  • C, D (right atrium, right ventricle): reached by venous access (femoral vein to IVC), not arterial.
cardio-w1-module-q37-37:
From 01 - Cardiac Electrical Physiology. The lecture says how much an ion affects membrane potential depends on three things together: its charge, the membrane's permeability to it, and its relative concentration on each side. Only E has all three. That is why K+, which is charged, concentrated inside the cell (140 vs 4 mEq/L) and far more permeable through leak channels, sets the resting potential near -90 mV.

  • A, D: an impermeable ion cannot move, so it cannot carry charge across.
  • B: a neutral particle moves no charge, whatever its gradient.
  • C: with no gradient there is no net diffusion.
cardio-w1-module-q9-9:
From 08 - Cardiac Pharmacology. Every autonomic ganglion is nicotinic and cholinergic. Sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic fibres both release acetylcholine. The adrenal medulla behaves like a modified sympathetic ganglion: preganglionic fibres synapse directly on its chromaffin cells, and the medulla then releases epinephrine into the blood. The lecture's module answer is acetylcholine.

  • A (norepinephrine): released by sympathetic postganglionic fibres.
  • B (epinephrine): what the medulla secretes, not what stimulates it.
  • D, E (dopamine, serotonin): not the preganglionic transmitter.
cardio-w1-new-q10-10:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology.

  • A is true: the pulmonary and systemic circuits are in series. The left heart pumps what the right heart delivers, so RV and LV outputs must match.
  • B is true: the systemic circuit is high pressure (about 120/80). The pulmonary circuit is low pressure (about 20/10), which is why the RV is less muscular.
  • C is false: the systemic organs are arranged in parallel, so flow can be redistributed. Exercise dilates vessels in skin and muscle, and dehydration cuts skin and kidney perfusion to retain water.

So the answer is D (A and B), and E fails because of C.
cardio-w1-new-q13-13:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. Cardiac output is the blood pumped in one minute, HR × SV (normal about 5 L/min). Stroke volume is then set by preload, afterload and contractility, which gives the lecture its structure.

  • A, D: MAP is a result of CO and resistance (BP = CO × PVR), not a determinant of CO.
  • B: flow and resistance describe pressure along a vessel. CO itself is the flow.
  • E fails because only C is right.
cardio-w1-new-q14-14:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. The force-frequency relationship (Bowditch or treppe phenomenon) says that a higher heart rate increases the force of cardiac muscle contraction, up to a maximum rate (about 180/min in normal muscle).

  • A: arteriolar resistance is vascular tone, not a heart-rate effect.
  • B: describes the skeletal muscle pump that aids venous return. That is a different mechanism, not a cardiac one.
  • D: the lecture says the effect is weak in failing ventricles, not atria.
  • E fails because only C is right.
cardio-w1-new-q15-15:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. Preload is end-diastolic volume, so its determinants are whatever changes how much blood is in the ventricle at the end of filling. The lecture lists blood volume, venous tone, ventricular compliance, afterload, contractility (more ejected means less residual volume) and atrial contraction (the atrial kick). Diastolic time matters too: tachycardia shortens diastole and leaves less time to fill (04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology).

  • D (systolic time) is the exception. Systole is the ejection phase, and it is not listed as a determinant of filling volume.
cardio-w1-new-q17-17:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum. The short vessel is the left main coronary artery, which quickly divides into the LAD and circumflex. The LAD itself is long: it runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex, supplying the anterior two-thirds of the septum. So B is the false statement.

  • A (true): coronary flow, especially to the LV, happens mainly in diastole (05 - The Heart as a Pump). This is why tachycardia starves the LV.
  • C (true): sympathetic input increases SA pacing and force and dilates the coronaries. Vagal input does the reverse.
  • D (true): the SA node sits in the right atrium.
  • E fails because A is true.
cardio-w1-new-q21-21:
From 02 - Introduction to ECG. At 25 mm/s, one large box is 0.2 s. For a regular rhythm, count large boxes between beats and use the sequence 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 (or divide 300 by the number of boxes). Five boxes = 1.0 s per beat = 60/min. Measuring P to P gives the atrial rate, which equals the ventricular rate when every P conducts.

  • B (300): one box.
  • D (150): two boxes.
  • E (75): four boxes.
  • C (95): not a value in the sequence.
cardio-w1-new-q9-9:
From 04 - Introduction to Cardiac Physiology. Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × oxygen content. Oxygen content is the O2 bound to hemoglobin (saturation × Hb × 1.34) plus dissolved O2 (pO2 × 0.3). Most of it is carried on hemoglobin. The lecture adds that tissue-level microvascular perfusion still matters: in sepsis, CO and saturation can be fine while cells starve.

  • A: stroke volume is already part of CO, and neither term measures oxygen.
  • B: lung O2 concentration only matters through arterial content, and aortic pressure is not in the equation.
  • D: no oxygen term.
  • E fails because C is right.
cardio-w1-weekly-q2-2:
From 05 - The Heart as a Pump. Cardiac index = CO / body surface area, which relates heart performance to body size. Work it in two steps, converting mL to L:

  • CO = HR × SV = 78 × 0.076 L ≈ 5.9 L/min.
  • CI = 5.9 / 1.92 ≈ 3.1 L/min/m².

B (5.9) is the trap: that is cardiac output, before dividing by BSA. C and D come from no correct arrangement of the numbers. Weight and height are distractors here, because BSA has already been worked out for you.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q115.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum and 02 - Introduction to ECG. The lecture's territories are: the LAD runs the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum. The circumflex runs in the coronary sulcus to the posterior heart and supplies the lateral LV through the L marginal artery. The RCA, through the posterior descending artery, supplies the inferior and posterior wall and the posterior third of the septum.

The anterolateral LV is the lateral wall, the circumflex's territory (leads I, aVL, V5-V6), with overlap from the LAD anteriorly. So the answer the material supports is C, with B as the anterior overlap.

  • A, D: the RCA and PDA supply the inferior and posterior wall, the opposite side of the ventricle.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives D (posterior descending artery), which 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum places in the posterior interventricular groove, supplying the posterior third of the septum. It does not reach the anterolateral wall. The material supports C (circumflex), with the LAD overlapping anteriorly. The four workbook keys for the LV areas (q115-q118) read D, A, B, C. They look cycled out of order, perhaps from a matching item or a figure that did not survive extraction. Check them against the source workbook.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q116.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum and 02 - Introduction to ECG. The lecture's territories are: the LAD runs the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum. The circumflex runs in the coronary sulcus to the posterior heart and supplies the lateral LV through the L marginal artery. The RCA, through the posterior descending artery, supplies the inferior and posterior wall and the posterior third of the septum.

The posterolateral LV is where the circumflex ends up: it runs in the sulcus to the posterior heart and gives off the L marginal. The answer the material supports is C.

  • A (RCA): supplies the inferior and posterior wall through the PDA. It reaches the posterolateral wall only in some dominant patterns, which the lecture does not cover.
  • B (LAD): anterior.
  • D (PDA): inferior, near the septum.

The material supports C (circumflex). The four workbook keys for the LV areas (q115-q118) read D, A, B, C. cardio-wb-cardio0-q117.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum and 02 - Introduction to ECG. The lecture's territories are: the LAD runs the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum. The circumflex runs in the coronary sulcus to the posterior heart and supplies the lateral LV through the L marginal artery. The RCA, through the posterior descending artery, supplies the inferior and posterior wall and the posterior third of the septum.

The posteroinferior LV is the inferior and posterior wall (leads II, III, aVF). That belongs to the RCA, through the posterior descending artery, in the 85% who are right-dominant (04 - Myocardial Infarction). The material supports A, or D for the branch itself.

  • B (LAD): runs the anterior groove, so it is the wrong surface.
  • C (circumflex): lateral wall, and it gives rise to the PDA only in left-dominant hearts (15%).

It places the posterior descending artery, a branch of the RCA, in the posterior groove, and 02 - Introduction to ECG assigns the inferior wall to the RCA. cardio-wb-cardio0-q118.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum and 02 - Introduction to ECG. The lecture's territories are: the LAD runs the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum. The circumflex runs in the coronary sulcus to the posterior heart and supplies the lateral LV through the L marginal artery. The RCA, through the posterior descending artery, supplies the inferior and posterior wall and the posterior third of the septum.

The anteromedial LV is the anterior wall and the anterior septum (V1-V4). That is the LAD, running down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex. The material supports B.

  • C (circumflex): lateral and posterior, away from the septum.
  • A, D (RCA, PDA): inferior and posterior wall, and only the posterior third of the septum.

The circumflex supplies the lateral wall. The material supports B (LAD). The four workbook keys for the LV areas (q115-q118) read D, A, B, C. cardio-wb-cardio0-q83.html:
From 09 - Endocarditis (atherosclerosis risk factors). The lecture's major non-modifiable risk factors are older age, male sex (estrogen is protective) and family history. Smoking is a major modifiable one. So A, B and C are all risk factors.

Family history only counts when the disease is premature in a first-degree relative: male under 55, female under 65. That cut-off comes from the key; the lecture only says "50-60s".

  • D: the father died at 65, past the male cut-off, so this is not premature CAD and it is the answer.
  • E: the mother died at 51, under 65, so it counts.

cardio-w2-module-q20-20.html:
From 04 - Aortic Stenosis. In AS, timing, not intensity, grades severity. As the LV begins to fail it can no longer generate enough force for turbulent flow, so a severe stenosis can sound quiet. Loudness (D) is therefore not a sign of severe AS. The other three are:

  • Pulsus parvus et tardus (A): a weak, delayed pulse that can fall after S2.
  • Soft S2 (B): the stiff aortic valve barely closes, so only P2 is heard.
  • Late-peaking ejection murmur (C): the tighter the valve, the longer ejection takes and the later the peak.

07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease records the same module answer.

cardio-w2-module-q21-21.html:
From 05 - Aortic Regurgitation. Asymptomatic chronic AR is operated on only once the LV is failing or markedly dilated. The lecture's three quantitative triggers are LVEF < 50%, LVESD > 50 mm and LVEDD > 65 mm, so A, C and D all qualify (the bank's option text has lost the < and > signs).

  • LVH (B) is the expected compensation for volume overload in every chronic AR, since it normalises wall stress. It carries no timing information, and 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease states outright that LVH alone is not a criterion.

cardio-w2-module-q22-22.html:
From 05 - Aortic Regurgitation. Acute AR is a sudden leak into a normal-sized, non-compliant LV, and the lecture names its two causes: endocarditis (leaflet destruction or perforation) and aortic dissection. LV pressure spikes, is transmitted to the LA and lungs, and causes pulmonary edema and hypotension, so surgery is emergent.

  • Bicuspid valve (A), hypertensive root dilatation (B) and degenerative calcific disease (C) all progress over years. They cause chronic AR, where the LV has time to dilate and hypertrophy.

cardio-w2-module-q26-26.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The revised Jones criteria need a recent group A strep pharyngitis plus 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor criteria. Fever is on the minor list, with arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP and a prolonged PR interval.

  • Major: migratory arthritis, carditis/valvulitis, CNS involvement (Sydenham chorea), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum. 06 - Mitral Stenosis lists the same majors.

Watch the pairs: arthritis is major but arthralgia is minor, and carditis is major but a long PR is minor.

cardio-w2-module-q28-28.html: From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. True. Malar flush is a sign of mitral stenosis: rosy cheeks, which the lecture attributes to cutaneous vasodilatation. The note's module-answer table records the same answer. It sits with the other MS signs: a diastolic murmur at the apex, a loud S1 that softens as the valve stiffens, a loud P2 from pulmonary hypertension, and AF from LA dilation.

cardio-w2-module-q35-35.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The mitral apparatus is the annulus (fibrous ring), the two leaflets, the chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles anchored in the LV. Dysfunction of any part causes MR, so A, C and D all affect mitral function.

  • Moderator band (B): the septomarginal trabecula of the right ventricle, running from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle of the RV. It carries conduction fibres (the right bundle) and has nothing to do with the mitral valve (03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum).

cardio-w2-module-q36-36.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture splits MR in two. Primary MR is intrinsic valve pathology. Secondary (functional) MR is a structurally normal valve distorted by dilatation or dysfunction of the surrounding structures: a dilated LV or annulus, or ischemic papillary muscles.

  • Intrinsic pathology (A) is the definition of primary MR.
  • Leaflet prolapse (C) is myxomatous disease, a primary cause.
  • Prosthetic failure (D) is listed among the acute causes of MR, not as the meaning of 'secondary'.

cardio-w2-module-q37-37.html:
From 07 - Mitral Regurgitation. The MR murmur is a high-pitched, blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. So 'best heard at the left lower sternal border' (B) is the false statement. That location belongs to tricuspid regurgitation or a VSR, and TR, unlike MR, gets louder with inspiration.

  • Holosystolic (A): true. The LV leaks into the LA for the whole of systole.
  • Left lateral decubitus (C): true. It brings the apex to the chest wall.
  • Soft in acute MR (D): true. LA and LV pressures equalise quickly in a non-compliant LA.

cardio-w2-module-q38-38.html:
From 07 - Mitral Regurgitation. The echocardiogram is the gold standard for MR, and for every valve lesion. It shows the etiology, severity, LV size and systolic function, LA size, pulmonary pressures and RV function, all of which decide surgical timing.

  • ECG (A) and CXR (B): non-specific. They show only the consequences (LA enlargement, AF, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema), not the valve itself.
  • Cardiac CT (D): gives anatomy but is inferior to echo and MRI for valve function, and adds radiation (07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease).

cardio-w2-module-q39-39.html:
From 07 - Mitral Regurgitation. The lecture's surgical indications are symptomatic chronic severe primary MR (A), and asymptomatic severe primary MR with mild or moderate LV dysfunction (B), which is operated on before the ventricle is too far gone. Surgery is not favourable once LV dysfunction has become severe, so C is the false statement: a badly damaged LV does poorly after the regurgitant 'pop-off' into the LA is closed.

  • Repair over replacement (D): true when anatomy allows. There is no prosthesis, no anticoagulation and less endocarditis.

cardio-w2-module-q40-40.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. Severe symptomatic MR with a normal LV is a surgical indication. The lecture's rule is leaky valves are repaired, tight valves are replaced, so surgical repair (B) is the treatment of choice when anatomy is favourable. Repair keeps the native valve (better hemodynamics and durability, no anticoagulation, less infection) and restores life expectancy.

  • Medical management (A): does not change the course of MR.
  • Replacement (C): for valves that cannot be repaired.
  • Transcatheter repair (D): MitraClip has expanding evidence, but it is for patients who are poor surgical candidates.

cardio-w2-module-q42-42.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. Severe AS has a long latent period, then survival collapses once symptoms start. The lecture's figures for 50% survival are 5 years after angina, 3 years after (exertional pre)syncope, and 2 years after heart failure, and 04 - Aortic Stenosis gives the same numbers. Heart failure (dyspnea) carries the worst prognosis.

  • B is the only option built on the 5/3 pattern, which is why it is keyed.
  • A and C are too short and too long throughout.

flags.title: The keyed option misquotes the lecture
flags.html: Option B, as the bank has it, attaches 5 years to dyspnea and 1 year to heart failure. 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease and 04 - Aortic Stenosis both give 5 years angina, 3 years syncope, 2 years heart failure, with dyspnea standing for heart failure. B is the closest option, but learn the lecture's numbers rather than the option's.

cardio-w2-module-q43-43.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. All three listed findings are indications for mitral surgery in severe MR. The lecture's surgical candidates are severe symptomatic MR, declining LV function, a dilating LV, new-onset atrial fibrillation and severe pulmonary hypertension. The note's module-answer table gives 'all of: dyspnea on exertion, new-onset AF, newly dilated LV'.

  • Dyspnea on exertion (A) makes the MR symptomatic.
  • New AF (B) and a newly dilated LV (C) are markers of LA and LV strain. Operating early, before NYHA III-IV symptoms and LV decline, preserves survival.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives E, which in the bank's lettering is 'None of the above'. 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease supports all of the above (F here). The options skip from C to E, so a D was probably lost in transcription, and the source's E was 'All of the above'. The lettering needs fixing in the bank.

cardio-w2-module-q44-44.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture lists the acute complications of TAVI/valve implantation. Injury to adjacent structures can hit the membranous septum (heart block, VSD, LV-RA fistula) or the anterior mitral leaflet (MR). Inadequate seating of the prosthesis causes coronary obstruction/MI or a paravalvular leak (C), the answer the note records.

  • SA node block (A): the conduction risk is at the AV node and His bundle beside the membranous septum, not at the SA node.
  • Papillary muscle rupture (B): a mechanical complication of inferior MI, not of valve implantation.

cardio-w2-module-q45-45.html:
From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. All three are disadvantages of a prosthesis compared with repair. The lecture's theoretical risks of a prosthetic valve are:

  • Structural valve deterioration (A): bioprostheses wear out in about 15 years.
  • Inferior hemodynamics (B): the prosthesis leaves a smaller orifice and a residual gradient, whereas most repairs leave more valve area.
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis (C): foreign material in the bloodstream, whereas repair keeps native tissue in contact with blood.

Add thrombosis, thromboembolism and, for mechanical valves, lifelong anticoagulation. The note's module-answer table records 'all of'.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives E, which in the bank's lettering is 'None of the above'. 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease supports all of the above (F here). As in the previous question, the options skip from C to E, so the source's E was probably 'All of the above' before a D was lost. The lettering needs fixing in the bank.

cardio-w2-module-q46-46.html: From 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture's warning box lists the risk factors for early bioprosthetic deterioration: younger age, end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, disordered calcium homeostasis and diabetes. So A-D are all correct. The common thread is accelerated calcification of the tissue leaflets. That is why the lecture's 40-year-old on dialysis with rheumatic MS gets a mechanical valve: favour mechanical in these patients if anticoagulation is acceptable.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q24.html:
From 05 - Aortic Regurgitation. AR comes from either the leaflets or the aortic root. The lecture's leaflet causes include rheumatic heart disease (A), bicuspid and other congenital valves (E), endocarditis, and connective-tissue and inflammatory disease such as lupus, ankylosing spondylitis and rheumatoid arthritis (C). Root causes are idiopathic ectasia, hypertension, Marfan and bicuspid aortopathy.

  • LV dilation (D) is a consequence of chronic AR: volume overload dilates the LV. It is not a cause of AR. (A dilated LV causes secondary mitral regurgitation.)
  • Endocarditis (B) is the classic cause of acute AR, but the lecture also lists it among the leaflet causes.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The workbook keys B, endocarditis, presumably because endocarditis is the textbook cause of acute AR. But 05 - Aortic Regurgitation (and 07 - Surgical Management of Cardiovascular Disease) list endocarditis among the leaflet causes of AR. Left ventricular dilation is never a cause of AR, only its result. The answer the material supports is D.

cardio-w3-module-q17-17.html:
From 06 - Cardiac Rehab & Secondary Prevention. The lecture separates trial evidence from real-world evidence. In clinical trials, exercise-based rehab gives an 18-26% (about 20-30%) relative risk reduction in mortality. In real-world programs after MI, PCI or CABG, the reduction in readmission or death is about 40-60%: Toronto CR and the SJH hybrid program each report about 50%, with an NNT of 6.

  • 20-40% (C) is the trial range, the answer to the paired module question.
  • 0% (A) and 0-20% (B) understate an effect the lecture rates class I, level A.

cardio-w3-module-q5-5.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. Every statement matches the lecture's post-MI secondary-prevention table, so the answer is E (the bank has dropped the < before '40%'):

  • Beta-blockers (A): start within 12-24 h unless decompensated HF, hypotension or bradycardia. They cut O2 demand and reinfarction and improve survival.
  • ACE inhibitors (B): start within 24 h, especially with anterior MI, HF or EF ≤ 40%. They limit remodeling and reduce mortality.
  • Eplerenone (C): with EF ≤ 40% plus diabetes or symptomatic HF, on top of an ACEI and beta-blocker.
  • Statins (D): high intensity in all patients, even with normal cholesterol; target LDL < 1.8 mmol/L.

cardio-w3-module-q9-9.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. Ventricular septal rupture is a mechanical complication of a large transmural MI with late presentation, and is rare in the era of primary PCI. All three factors describe the same patient: a big infarct that was never reperfused and so necroses through the full thickness of the septum. The note's module answer is 'all of the above'.

  • Apical VSR follows an anterior (LAD) MI; basal VSR follows an inferior (RCA) MI.
  • The clue is a new harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border with a step-up in RV O2 saturation, which separates it from papillary muscle rupture (soft apical murmur).

cardio-w3-new-q3-3.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The culprit artery sets the wall that infarcts:

  • LAD (I) - anterior MI (C): ST elevation in the anterior leads V3-V4 (V1-V6 if it extends septal and lateral). The LAD supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.
  • RCA (II) - inferior MI (A): ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. In the 85% who are right-dominant, the RCA gives the posterior descending artery.
