  • Left circumflex (III) - posterior MI (B): often missed on a 12-lead. Look for ST depression in V1-V3 or add V8-V9.

cardio-w3-new-q4-4.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. A STEMI that is not reperfused evolves through a fixed sequence, which the key A-E-F-B-D-C traces through the panels:

  • Normal baseline.
  • Hyperacute T waves: broad, peaked, asymmetric. These come first and precede ST elevation.
  • ST elevation: transmural injury in the ischemic zone.
  • Q waves develop as necrosis spreads from subendocardium to epicardium and the wall becomes full-thickness infarct.
  • ST normalises, T inverts.
  • ST and T normal, Q wave persists for life.

A Q wave means necrosis, not ischemia, which is why it is the last thing to go and never does.

flags.title: Only partly covered by the vault notes
flags.html: 04 - Myocardial Infarction covers ST elevation during ischemia and the permanent Q wave after full-thickness infarction, and the hyperacute T wave feature note places those T waves before ST elevation. No lecture note lays out the full six-stage sequence. The middle stages above are from general principles, and the letters could not be checked against the panels, which are unlabelled in the bank.

cardio-w3-new-q5-5.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The lecture splits contraindications to thrombolysis into absolute and relative. The absolute ones include:

  • Any prior intracranial bleed (C), however long ago.
  • Ischemic stroke within 3 months (D): 2 months qualifies. After 3 months it becomes relative.
  • Intracranial malignancy (E).

The others:

  • Pregnancy (A) and therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin (B): relative contraindications.
  • BP 160/90 (F): not a contraindication at all. Only BP > 180/110 is, and even that is relative.

The other absolute ones are closed head or facial trauma within 3 months, active bleeding (except menses), and aortic dissection or acute pericarditis.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q82.html:
From 02 - Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease. The lecture singles out left ventricular function as the strong predictor of outcome and survival. LVEF is normal above 50%, and prognosis falls once it drops below 30-35%. 04 - Myocardial Infarction shows 6-month mortality climbing steeply below an LVEF of about 45%. After an MI, echo or MUGA to assess LV function is the test that best predicts long-term survival.

  • Framingham (A): estimates the risk of developing CAD in people without it.
  • Angiography (C): shows anatomy. The amount of myocardium lost predicts outcome better.
  • Age (D): a risk factor, but weaker than LVEF.

cardio-w4-module-q13-13.html:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. 'Cold' means low perfusion from low cardiac output. 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure lists the signs of hypoperfusion: cold, sweaty extremities, oliguria, confusion, dizziness and a narrow pulse pressure.

  • Narrow pulse pressure (A): a small stroke volume gives a small systolic-diastolic gap.
  • Worsening renal function (B): the kidney is underperfused. This is the 'end-organ dysfunction' of I NEED HELP.
  • Slow heart rate (C): wrong direction. Low output drives a compensatory tachycardia through sympathetic activation.

The note's module answer matches: A and B.

review.t: Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

cardio-w4-module-q14-14.html:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. Stage D (end-stage) heart failure adds therapies that standard care does not use: inotropes as a bridge, ventricular assist devices, transplant and hospice. An LVAD (A) is initiated as a bridge to transplant or as destination therapy.

  • ICD (B), spironolactone (C) and beta-blockers (D): standard guideline therapy for HFrEF, started at stage C, long before end stage. In end stage, beta-blockers are often reduced, and needing to reduce them is itself a marker of advancing disease.

review.t: Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

cardio-w4-module-q15-15.html:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. A patient approaching end-stage HF 'tells you': I NEED HELP. All three options are on the list:

  • LVEF 20% (A): 'E', a very low ejection fraction (< 20%).
  • Reduced beta-blocker dose (B): 'P', prognostic medications that have to be cut or cannot be uptitrated.
  • Recent inotropes (C): 'I', previous or ongoing dobutamine, milrinone or dopamine.

The rest: persistent NYHA III-IV or high BNP, worsening renal or liver function, ICD shocks, 2 or more admissions in 12 months, escalating diuretics, and SBP < 90.

review.t: Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

cardio-w4-module-q17-17.html:
From 09 - Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant. Palliative care grew up around conditions with a predictable trajectory, like cancer. Heart failure instead runs through repeated decompensations and partial recoveries, with sudden death possible at any point, so its unpredictable trajectory (C) makes the timing hard. The note's module answer matches.

  • Considered too early (D): the reverse. The lecture says it should come earlier but is usually considered late.
  • Confused with cancer care (A), no definition of HF (B) and disagreeing practitioners (E): not what the lecture gives. HF has clear definitions (ESC and AHA criteria).

review.t: Heart Failure Advanced Therapies and Transplant

cardio-w4-module-q20-20.html:
From 06 - Management of Hypertension. The lecture's logic is that treatment intensity follows global CV risk, and that thresholds come from outcome trials. Low-risk patients are not treated until SBP is 160 or more because trials lasting 7-8 years cannot accumulate enough events to show benefit below that. So treatment is justified where experimental evidence shows that treating similar patients reduces CV risk (C).

  • Above the population mean (A): a statistical label, not evidence of benefit.
  • Absolute BP over global risk (B): the reverse of the lecture.
  • Drugs are harmful (D): no. Lowering BP cuts CHF by 60% and stroke by 40%.
  • One medication (E): most patients need a 3-drug combination.

cardio-w4-module-q7-7.html:
From 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure. The lecture puts HFpEF (diastolic failure: a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle that fills poorly, EF ≥ 50%) at 60% of heart failure and HFrEF at 40%. It repeats the split in its high-yield summary. On those figures the statement would be true. What the lecture calls most common is the ischemic etiology (65%), which produces mainly HFrEF, and that may be what the source's 'false' was reaching for.

  • HFpEF is driven by hypertension, age, AS and infiltrative disease, and has no evidence-based therapy beyond diuretics and treating risk factors.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key says False, but 01 - Physiology of Heart Failure gives HFpEF as 60% of HF, which makes the statement True. The note's own module-answer table records the source's 'False' next to that same 60% figure and marks it 'as written in source'. Take the lecture's figure over the key.

cardio-w4-weekly-q4-4.html:
From 05 - Physiology of Hypertension. The lecture's 'fate' column of secondary causes includes thyroid disease (screen with TSH) and 'other endocrine' causes: pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome and acromegaly. All four options qualify:

  • Pheochromocytoma (D): catecholamine excess. Rare (0.1%), and OSA can mimic it biochemically.
  • Acromegaly (A): GH and IGF-1 excess.
  • Hyperthyroidism (B) and hypothyroidism (C): the lecture lists thyroid disease without restricting it to one direction, and both raise BP.

Primary aldosteronism (5%) is the commonest endocrine cause and is also worth screening for.

cardio-wb-cardio0-q101.html:
From 05 - Complications of Acute MI. All four are on the lecture's list of MI complications:

  • Heart failure (A): early as pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock, especially after a large anterior (proximal LAD) MI, and late from remodeling.
  • Pulmonary edema (B): an early mechanical complication, graded by Killip class.
  • Cardiac tamponade (C): LV free-wall rupture into the pericardium after a large transmural MI with late presentation. Usually fatal.
  • Acute MR (D): papillary muscle ischemia or rupture, typically posteromedial after an inferior MI. It gives a soft apical pansystolic murmur.

04 - Myocardial Infarction groups the same complications as ischemic, mechanical, arrhythmic and pericardial.

cardio-w5-module-q30-30.html:
From 02 - Bradycardia and 04 - Tachycardia. The key maps the strips in order, A to G onto i to vii. Each one has its own discriminator:

  • A, PAC: an early narrow beat with an abnormal P, then a pause.
  • B, 1st degree AV block: PR > 200 ms with every P conducted.
  • C, 2nd degree AV block: some P waves without a QRS, so beats come in groups.
  • D, 3rd degree block: AV dissociation. P waves march through a slow, regular, wide ventricular escape.
  • E, VF: chaotic baseline, no organised QRS.
  • F, atrial flutter: continuous sawtooth flutter waves between narrow QRSs.
  • G, PVCs: early, wide, bizarre QRSs with no preceding P.

The stem says 8 strips, but only 7 are shown and 7 are listed.

gi-w10-module-q15-15:
From 02 - Gastrointestinal Motility. Each colonic contraction pattern has one job:

  • Haustral contraction (A) = absorption of water and electrolytes (i): a segmentation-type squeeze of the waste bolus, mainly in the ascending colon, that wrings out water.
  • Tonic contraction of the ileocecal valve (B) = preventing bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine (iii): like every sphincter it is tonically closed, stopping bacteria-laden colonic contents refluxing into the relatively sterile ileum.
  • Tonic contraction of the external anal sphincter (C) = voluntary control of defecation (iv): it is striated muscle, so relaxing it is a learned, voluntary act.
  • Mass movement (D) = sustained peristalsis that expels feces (ii): 1-3 large pushes a day toward the rectum, triggered by the gastrocolic reflex after a meal.
gi-w10-module-q18-18:
From 05 - Development of the GI Tract. Sort each structure by what it grows from:

  • Foregut tube (i): the organs themselves. The duodenum (A; the first part is foregut), stomach (D), pancreas (E; dorsal and ventral buds off the duodenal endoderm), bile duct (F), liver (G) and gallbladder (J), which all come from the hepatic diverticulum.
  • Ventral mesentery (ii): the liver grows into it, and it splits into the falciform ligament anterior to the liver (H) and the lesser omentum behind it, which comprises the hepatogastric (C) and hepatoduodenal (I) ligaments.
  • Dorsal mesentery (iii): as the stomach rotates it elongates, folds down four layers thick and fuses into the greater omentum (B).

The trap is the liver: it develops within the ventral mesentery, but it is a foregut outgrowth, not the mesentery itself.
gi-w10-module-q19-19:
From 05 - Development of the GI Tract. Every option is a midgut event or structure:

  • A. 270-degree rotation: 90 degrees around the SMA while herniated into the umbilical cord at week 6, then another 180 degrees as it returns by week 10.
  • B. Rapid growth of the cranial limb: the cranial limb elongates and folds into the loops of jejunum and ileum.
  • C. Vitelline duct: the U-shaped midgut loop communicates with the yolk sac through it.
  • D. Third part of the duodenum: the duodenum distal to the bile duct is midgut, supplied by the SMA; only the part proximal to it is foregut.

With all four true, E is the answer.

gi-w10-module-q22-22.html:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. The figure is a hanging leg raise, which is flexion of the trunk and pelvis toward each other. The lecture describes the rectus abdominis as the strap-like muscle running vertically down the anterior wall, so it is the one whose fibres line up with that movement and does the principal work.

  • A. External oblique and B. internal oblique run diagonally. The bank's own neighbouring question credits the external oblique with lateral flexion.
  • D. Transversus abdominis runs horizontally, so it compresses the abdomen rather than flexing the trunk.
  • E fails because the question asks for the principal mover, not every muscle that fires.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w10-module-q23-23.html:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. The figure is a plank: an isometric hold where the trunk must stay rigid against gravity. The lecture's objective is the role of the wall's layers in maintaining intra-abdominal pressure, and that is what a plank asks of them, so all four work together.

  • Rectus abdominis (C) resists the trunk sagging into extension.
  • External (A) and internal (B) obliques brace the trunk against rotation and side-bending.
  • Transversus abdominis (D), running horizontally, cinches the abdomen and raises intra-abdominal pressure.

Contrast question 22: a movement (a leg raise) has one principal mover, while a static hold recruits the whole wall. Hence E.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w10-module-q24-24:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. The lecture lists the layers superficial to deep exactly in this order:

  • Skin (F), then the two layers of superficial fascia: fatty Camper's (A) above membranous Scarpa's (G).
  • The three flat muscles, outside in: external oblique (C), internal oblique (I), transversus abdominis (H).
  • Then transversalis fascia (B), extraperitoneal fat (D) and finally the parietal peritoneum (E).

The usual slips are swapping Camper's and Scarpa's (fatty is superficial), or putting extraperitoneal fat outside the transversalis fascia. The fat sits between that fascia and the peritoneum.

gi-w10-module-q27-27.html:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture is explicit about which modalities carry ionizing radiation:

  • A. Radiographs/X-ray: yes, a small dose.
  • C. CT: yes. It is an x-ray tube rotating on a gantry, so the dose is much more than a plain film. That matters most in young children, who are up to 10 times more susceptible to radiation-induced cancer.
  • B. Ultrasound: no radiation. It uses sound waves.
  • D. MRI: no radiation, which is exactly why the lecture recommends it in pregnancy, for young Crohn's patients and for appendicitis in pregnancy.

On the lecture's account, the radiation-using modalities are A and C only.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key includes D (MRI), but 07 - GI Imaging lists “no radiation (can be used in pregnancy)” as MRI's first advantage. Only x-ray and CT use ionizing radiation, so the answer the lecture supports is A and C.

gi-w10-module-q28-28.html:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture ends with a table of initial investigations that maps almost one to one onto this question:

  • Ultrasound (i): appendicitis in a 10-year-old (D) avoids radiation in a child, and biliary colic or cholecystitis (B) is a fluid-filled structure.
  • X-ray (ii): bowel perforation (A; free air under the diaphragm on the upright view) and volvulus (C), because the need is a quick look at the gas pattern.
  • MRI (iii): nothing. It is rarely the initial modality.
  • CT (iv): diverticulitis (F), a 70-year-old with pain and weight loss (E; cancer imaging), post-operative abscess (G), and cirrhosis (H).

flags.title: The lecture also accepts ultrasound for cirrhosis
flags.html: 07 - GI Imaging lists liver cirrhosis under both ultrasound and CT in its initial-investigations table, while the key places H under CT only. Expect either to be defensible.

gi-w10-module-q29-29:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's small-versus-large-bowel table has four discriminators on plain film:

  • Small bowel (i): sits centrally (D), with a normal diameter under 3 cm (C). Its folds, the plicae circulares, are continuous and cross the whole lumen, and it rarely contains feces.
  • Colon (ii): forms a peripheral picture frame. Its folds are the thick, interrupted haustra (A) that do not span the lumen, it usually contains fecal material (B), and it runs up to 6 cm, or 9 cm at the cecum.

Learn the numbers as a 3-6-9 rule: small bowel 3, colon 6, cecum 9.
gi-w10-module-q32-32:
From 09 - GERD. GERD is a clinical diagnosis. Endoscopy is reserved for alarm features, Barrett's risk, refractory symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty or abnormal imaging.

  • A: scope. Dysphagia is an alarm feature, and so is new-onset symptoms at 60 or older.
  • C: scope. Failing a PPI trial makes it refractory GERD, an indication in its own right.
  • E: scope. Known Barrett's esophagus needs periodic surveillance for dysplasia, and five years have passed. The notes do not give an interval.
  • B: no. A 30-year-old with typical symptoms and no alarm features gets an empiric PPI trial.
  • D: no. Symptoms are controlled and a scope at 50 was normal, so nothing new has triggered one.
gi-w10-module-q34-34:
From 09 - GERD. The lecture lists why 10-40% of patients fail a standard-dose PPI, and four of the options are on it:

  • A. CYP2C19 ultra-rapid metabolizer: increased PPI metabolism.
  • B. Taking it sporadically: medication timing and adherence. PPIs need daily dosing 30-60 minutes before breakfast.
  • C. Bile reflux: non-acid reflux, which acid suppression cannot touch.
  • D. Systemic sclerosis with residual acid reflux: the lecture's own example of residual acid reflux.

E is not a recognized reason. A patient whose reflux is non-acid fits C, but “low acid levels” is not itself a cause of PPI failure on the lecture's list.
gi-w10-module-q38-38:
From 10 - GI Secretion. CCK is released by duodenal I cells when fat reaches the chyme, and its actions all serve fat digestion:

  • A. Enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion: it acts on the acinar cells. Secretin, by contrast, drives the bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion.
  • B. Relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, letting bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum.
  • C. Delays gastric emptying, buying time to digest the fat.
  • D. Contracts the gallbladder.

E is not a CCK action. The lecture places CCK among the inhibitory intestinal hormones, alongside somatostatin, secretin and GIP. Gastrin is driven by ACh on G cells and by distension, not by CCK.
gi-w10-module-q44-44:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. The discriminator is chronic active. The lecture states that the most common cause of chronic (active) gastritis is H. pylori: its toxins cause inflammation in the lamina propria.

  • A. Alcohol, B. bile reflux and D. NSAIDs are chemical injuries. They produce acute or reactive gastritis through reduced mucin and prostaglandin deficiency, not a chronic active inflammatory infiltrate.
  • E. Tylenol (acetaminophen) is not an NSAID and is not listed as a cause of gastritis.
gi-w10-module-q45-45:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. An ICU patient after major trauma is under severe physiologic stress. The lecture lists burns, CNS trauma, shock and sepsis. Stress injures the stomach by microvascular ischemia, producing acute gastritis/reactive gastropathy, which looks the same microscopically as chemical injury.

  • B. Chronic active gastritis points to H. pylori, not a days-old insult.
  • C. Intestinal metaplasia is the end of long-standing chronic gastritis.
  • D. MALT lymphoma is a chronic H. pylori complication.
  • E. No abnormality fits poorly with new hematemesis.
gi-w10-module-q46-46:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. H. pylori produces urease, which splits urea into ammonia and bicarbonate to alkalinize its microenvironment. The breath test exploits this: the patient swallows labelled (C13) urea, and only urease-positive organisms release the labelled carbon for the patient to exhale.

  • A. Adhesins anchor it to epithelial cells.
  • B. Endocrine effects (lower somatostatin, higher gastrin) raise acid.
  • C. Flagella let it burrow into the mucus.
  • D. Toxins inflame the lamina propria.

All four are real virulence features, but none produces anything you can measure in breath.
gi-w10-module-q47-47:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. The deciding property is malignant potential.

  • A gastric ulcer CAN be malignant, so the lecture says it should always be biopsied and followed to healing.
  • A duodenal ulcer is almost NEVER malignant. It arises from duodenitis in the first part of the duodenum, is usually H. pylori-driven, and is not routinely biopsied.

Location also predicts mechanism. Gastric ulcers usually reflect weakened defences and are linked to NSAIDs; duodenal ulcers reflect increased acid damage.
gi-w10-module-q48-48:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. This is the lecture's benign (peptic) gastric ulcer description, feature for feature: punched out, round, smooth edges, flat margins, and folds radiating to the edge.

A malignant ulcer is the mirror image: oval, an irregular edge, heaped-up margins, and folds that stop short of the edge. The heaped-up margin is tumour growing at the rim, and the interrupted folds are infiltration of the wall around it. A smooth, flat rim with converging folds means the mucosa around the crater is intact.
gi-w10-module-q49-49:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. Every feature here is on the lecture's malignant-ulcer list: oval, irregular edge, heaped-up margins, folds that do not radiate to the edge.

Tumour growing at the rim heaps the margin up and makes the edge irregular. Infiltration of the surrounding wall stops the gastric folds from converging on the crater. A benign peptic ulcer is the reverse: punched out, round, smooth edges, flat margins, radiating folds. That malignant potential is why gastric ulcers are biopsied and followed to healing.

gi-w10-module-q50-50.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastric pathology chart). PUD complications are HOPP, and each has its own presenting clue:

  • Obstruction presents with emesis. An ulcer near the pylorus scars and swells until the gastric outlet narrows, so vomiting is the tell.
  • A. Hemorrhage presents with melena or hematemesis.
  • C. Penetration into the pancreas or liver presents as back pain.
  • D. Perforation presents as an acute abdomen with free air, a surgical emergency. Peptic ulcer causes about half of all perforations (04 - Abdominal Pain).

gi-w10-module-q58-58:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. H. pylori lives in the stomach, colonizing the gastric mucosa via flagella and adhesins. Yet it is more strongly tied to duodenal ulcers. The lecture pairs duodenal ulcers with H. pylori more than NSAIDs, and gastric ulcers with NSAIDs more than H. pylori.

The mechanism resolves the apparent paradox. H. pylori lowers somatostatin and raises gastrin, so the stomach puts out more acid. That extra acid load lands on the first part of the duodenum, which the lecture calls the site of the biggest acid load.

  • A and B place it in the duodenum.
  • C pairs it with the wrong ulcer.

gi-w10-module-q61-61.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastric pathology chart). The chart's PUD pathway ends with: treat H. pylori, then confirm eradication with the C13 urea breath test. The test reads live urease activity, so it turns negative once the organism is gone. It is non-invasive and needs no endoscopy.

  • Serology fails as a test of cure because antibodies stay positive after eradication, as the chart notes.
  • Gastric biopsy works but needs a scope, so it is neither easy nor cheap.

The statement is therefore true.

gi-w10-module-q70-70.html:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs (the antiemetic chart). First-generation antihistamines cross the blood-brain barrier and bind receptors beyond H1. Each off-target receptor explains one side effect:

  • Postural hypotension (i) = alpha-adrenergic blockade (B): loss of the vasoconstriction that supports standing blood pressure, which also causes dizziness.
  • Sedation (ii) = central H1 blockade (A): the on-target effect in the brain, which is why patients are warned about combining it with benzodiazepines.
  • Dry mouth (iii) = muscarinic blockade (D), alongside urinary retention and sinus tachycardia.
  • Weight gain (iv) = serotonin blockade (C), through increased appetite.

gi-w10-module-q77-77.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastroparesis section). Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying without obstruction. The chart names longstanding, poorly controlled type 1 diabetes as the classic cause. Motility lecture 02 explains the mechanism: damage to the vagal (extrinsic) pathway and loss of the ICC pacemakers. Thirty years of type 1 diabetes is the textbook setup for that neuropathy.

  • A. A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic has had no time to develop neuropathy.
  • B. Post-infectious gastroparesis is listed as viral (norovirus, rotavirus), not bacterial Salmonella.
  • C. Codeine does slow gastric emptying, but intermittent use is a weaker, reversible risk than decades of neuropathy.
  • E. The chart lists hypothyroidism as a cause, not hyperthyroidism.

gi-w10-module-q78-78.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastroparesis section). The chart's treatment list settles each option:

  • B. True. Small, frequent meals 4-5 times a day that are low in fat and fibre. Fat and fibre both slow gastric emptying, and a small volume empties more easily.
  • A. False. Promotility drugs go at the lowest dose with drug holidays, and are cycled rather than combined.
  • C. False. Tight glycemic control is part of the treatment.
  • D. False. The monitoring concern is QT prolongation from domperidone, metoclopramide and erythromycin, not QRS widening.
  • E. False. Every item in the treatment list is ongoing symptom control, and none of it offers a cure.

gi-w10-module-q79-79.html:
From 11 - Nausea, Vomiting, and Gastroparesis, and the antiemetic chart in 08. Match the drug to the pathway that drives each cause:

  • Motion sickness (i) = B: inner-ear afferents signal via H1 and muscarinic receptors, so antihistamines and anticholinergics.
  • Gastroparesis (ii) = D: the problem is slow motility, so prokinetics such as metoclopramide and domperidone.
  • PONV (iii) = A: the chart lists post-operative N/V under 5-HT3 antagonists, antihistamines and D2 antagonists (droperidol).
  • Drug- and chemotherapy-induced (iv) = E: blood-borne emetics hit the CTZ and the solitary tract nucleus, so 5-HT3 and D2 antagonists, cannabinoids and NK1 antagonists.
  • Pregnancy (v) = C: doxylamine-pyridoxine (Diclectin) and B6 lead this list.

gi-w10-new-q17-17.html:
From 11 - Nausea, Vomiting, and Gastroparesis, and the antiemetic chart in 08. Cytotoxic drugs act as blood-borne emetics and local irritants on the CTZ and gut afferents. The lecture treats that pathway with 5-HT3 antagonists, dopamine antagonists, anticholinergics and cannabinoid agonists.

  • A. Ondansetron: the chart's first indication for 5-HT3 antagonists is chemotherapy-induced N/V.
  • B. Nabilone: its listed indication is chemotherapy-induced N/V, though not first line.
  • D. Domperidone: a D2 antagonist acting at the CTZ, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
  • C. Benzodiazepines treat nausea from higher cortical centres, such as anticipatory nausea on the drive to the hospital, not the drug-driven pathway itself.
  • E. Diclectin is the pregnancy agent.

gi-w10-new-q19-19.html:
From the GERD section of the GI summary notes (the alarm-feature list behind 09 - GERD). Alarm features are the ones that raise concern for cancer or a complication and send the patient to endoscopy. The list includes new dyspepsia at 60 or older, GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena), iron-deficiency anemia, anorexia or weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, and a first-degree relative with GI cancer.

  • A, B, C and D are all on that list.
  • E. Dental cavities come from acid erosion of enamel. That is an atypical presentation: it shows where refluxed acid reaches, but it says nothing about malignancy or a complication.

gi-w10-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. The four core processes run through the whole lecture:

  • Digestion (A): mechanical and chemical, starting in the mouth, with the stomach as the main site.
  • Motility (B): coordinated by the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
  • Secretion (D): regulated by the submucosal (Meissner) plexus.
  • Absorption (E): mostly in the small intestine, with water absorbed in the colon.

C. Regurgitation is not a function. It is a symptom, the effortless backflow of gastric contents when the lower esophageal sphincter is too relaxed, as in GERD (02 - Gastrointestinal Motility).

gi-w10-new-q20-20.html:
From 09 - GERD, with 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia.

  • C. True. Esophageal manometry measures esophageal pressures, including LES pressure. It is used in refractory GERD or diagnostic uncertainty.
  • A. False. Endoscopy does NOT diagnose GERD and cannot rule it out: 70% of patients have non-erosive disease with a normal-looking mucosa. It screens for complications and alternative diagnoses.
  • B. False. Manometry is exactly how motility disorders are diagnosed. The dysphagia lecture notes that endoscopy does not help much for them.
  • D. False as keyed. The option is garbled as written. The lecture lists ambulatory pH studies as a tool for refractory cases or diagnostic uncertainty, and nothing in it supports the claim.
  • E. False. Barrett's risk factors are an indication for endoscopy. Barrett's is a tissue diagnosis, not a clinical one.

gi-w10-new-q23-23:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's first ultrasound indication is evaluating solid organs such as the liver, spleen and kidney, along with fluid-filled structures (gallbladder, biliary tree) and ascites. The pancreas is the exception, because it lies deep behind bowel gas.

  • A. A full abdominal ultrasound takes about 30 minutes, so it is a poor choice when time is the constraint.
  • B. Large body habitus is a listed disadvantage: extra fat scatters the sound waves.
  • D. Very good spatial resolution belongs to CT, not ultrasound, which is also operator-dependent.
gi-w10-new-q24-24:
From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's obstruction signs on an abdominal series are dilated bowel, differential air-fluid levels, string of pearls, step-ladder pattern, gasless abdomen, and no air beyond the obstructed segment.

  • D inverts the last sign. Gas cannot pass the blockage, so the bowel beyond it is empty, while the bowel before it dilates. “Air only beyond” is the opposite of what you see.
  • A, B and C are genuine signs. String of pearls is specific to small-bowel obstruction.
  • E fails because D is not a sign.
gi-w10-new-q8-8:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. As the testis descends through the inguinal canal it takes a sleeve from each layer it passes through, and those sleeves become the three coverings of the spermatic cord:

  • A. Transversalis fascia becomes the internal spermatic fascia, at the deep ring.
  • B. Internal oblique becomes the cremaster muscle and fascia.
  • C. External oblique becomes the external spermatic fascia, at the superficial ring.

D. Transversus abdominis contributes no layer. The canal passes beneath its arching lower fibres rather than through them, and its aponeurosis instead forms part of the canal's posterior wall as the conjoint tendon.

gi-wb-gi0-q51.html:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Before calling dyspepsia functional, the lecture has you check for red flags: dysphagia, vomiting, nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and onset after age 40.

  • B. Vomiting is on the list, because persistent emesis suggests obstruction, such as gastric outlet obstruction from an ulcer or a tumour.
  • A. Age matters at the older end, so onset under 12 is not a flag.
  • C. Nausea, D. heartburn and belching, and E. upper abdominal pain are the ordinary symptoms of dyspepsia and reflux. They are what brings the patient in, not warnings.

gi-w11-module-q12-12.html:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Read the stem's own lettering, which runs A. PPI, B. octreotide, C. antibiotics, D. tranexamic acid. For variceal bleeding the lecture's regimen is pantoprazole, octreotide, antibiotics (a cephalosporin or quinolone) and band ligation. Its summary singles out antibiotics as the treatment with a mortality benefit.

  • PPI is standard but targets ulcer bleeding.
  • Octreotide lowers portal pressure to control the bleed.
  • Tranexamic acid is not part of the lecture's regimen.
  • An H2 receptor antagonist is not used.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. PPI, B. Octreotide, C. Antibiotics, D. Tranexamic acid). The listed choices A-D are from an unrelated IBD question, so the keyed option C reads “ulcerative colitis” here. It means C. Antibiotics.

gi-w11-module-q14-14.html:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Read the stem's own lettering. The lecture's management rule for a lower GI bleed turns on stability: if stable, proceed with colonoscopy, because bowel prep takes time; if unstable, go to upper endoscopy ± angiography and a surgical consult. So D is true.

  • A is false: "never" is too absolute. Melena marks an upper bleed in the lecture, but a slow bleed from the small bowel or right colon (all distal to the ligament of Treitz) can darken before it is passed.
  • B: the lecture does not rank the two; the usual teaching is that the tagged RBC scan detects slower bleeding than angiography, so it is the more sensitive test.
  • C is reversed: angiography is the one that can treat (embolization); the RBC scan only localizes.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. never presents as melena, B. angiography more sensitive than RBC scan, C. RBC scan both diagnostic and therapeutic, D. stable patient can be prepped for colonoscopy). The listed choices A-D are from an unrelated IBD question, so the keyed option D reads “TB” here. It means D. Prep for colonoscopy.

gi-w11-module-q2-2:
From 04 - Luminal GI Malignancies. The lecture names the cell of origin for each GI malignancy: tumours of the glandular lining, including the stomach, are adenocarcinoma; lymphoma arises from lymphoid cells and is the minority. So C is the false statement.

  • A and E are true: gastric cancer presents with dyspepsia not relieved by antacids or eating, which is easily taken for acid-related dyspepsia.
  • B and D are true: the lecture's own reasoning for right-sided colon cancer applies (a wide organ with thin, distensible walls, "like the stomach"), so a tumour must grow large before it obstructs or is noticed.
gi-w11-module-q21-21:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening. Colonoscopy views the whole colon and can biopsy or remove what it finds; it is the test every other positive screen is referred on to. That is why it is the most sensitive.

  • FIT only detects a lesion that is bleeding (Luminal GI Malignancies), so non-bleeding polyps are missed; it is used q2y because it is cheap and non-invasive, not because it is sensitive.
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy reaches only the distal colon, and misses right-sided lesions such as sessile serrated adenomas.
  • CT colonography is "not recommended" for screening in the lecture's table and is not cost-effective.
gi-w11-module-q26-26:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening. The lecture's average-risk algorithm is explicit: FIT positive → colonoscopy; incomplete → repeat; negative → repeat in 2 years. A positive FIT means blood from somewhere in the colon, and only colonoscopy both finds the source anywhere in the colon and lets you biopsy or remove it.

  • Repeat FIT is for an incomplete test, not a positive one; a negative repeat would not clear the first result.
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy sees only the distal colon, so a right-sided source would be missed.
  • Pill endoscopy is for obscure small-bowel bleeding and cannot take tissue.
gi-w11-module-q27-27:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening. "Increased risk" in the lecture means one or more affected first-degree relatives, defined as parent, sibling, or child. These share half their genes with the patient, and the lecture puts lifetime risk at 9% with one affected relative (15% if diagnosed under 45) and 16% with two, against 4% at average risk. Those patients start colonoscopy at 40, or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis.

  • Grandparent, aunt and cousin are second- and third-degree relatives. On their own they do not move the patient out of the average-risk (FIT) pathway under this lecture's definitions.

gi-w11-module-q29-29.html:
From Summary Notes - Anatomy (appendicitis) and 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. Early appendicitis is visceral pain. The appendix is midgut, and its visceral afferent fibres enter the spinal cord at T10, so the pain is referred to the T10 dermatome, the umbilicus. It moves to the RLQ once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum at McBurney's point.

  • T4 is the nipple line, far above the umbilicus.
  • B: the appendix lies in the RLQ, off the posterior cecum, not deep to the umbilicus. Early pain is referred there, not felt directly.
  • A is garbled ("appendix attached to the appendix"). The meso-appendix is real but does not explain where the pain is felt.

flags.title: Option A is garbled in the bank
flags.html: Option A reads “The appendix is attached to the appendix via the mesoappendix”, which is presumably a typo for the ileum or cecum. It is wrong either way. Also, the lecture this question was matched to (01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut) does not cover the T10 referral. The rationale comes from the anatomy summary notes.

gi-w11-module-q32-32:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Sympathetic presynaptic fibres for the intestines leave T9-L2, pass through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing, and ride the splanchnic nerves to the prevertebral ganglia over the aorta. The ganglion is named for the artery supplying that gut segment. The sigmoid colon is hindgut, fed by the IMA, so the synapse is in the inferior mesenteric ganglion.

  • Sympathetic chain: splanchnic fibres pass straight through it.
  • Gut tube wall is where parasympathetic fibres synapse.
  • Celiac and superior mesenteric ganglia serve the foregut and midgut.
  • Inferior hypogastric plexus serves pelvic structures below the IMA territory.
gi-w11-module-q35-35:
From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. Carbohydrate digestion runs in three steps. Salivary amylase turns starch into oligosaccharides. Pancreatic amylase turns oligosaccharides into disaccharides (lactose, maltose, sucrose). The brush-border enzymes lactase, maltase and sucrase then split those disaccharides into monosaccharides, which enterocytes can take up.

  • Oligosaccharides are pancreatic amylase's substrate, one step earlier.
  • Monosaccharides are the end product; there is nothing left to digest.
  • Transport into the cell uses Na+-glucose co-transporters and fructose transporters, not these enzymes. Exit to the capillaries is a separate step.
gi-w11-module-q36-36: From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. The lecture places protein digestion at three sites, all proximal to the colon. In the stomach, acid denatures proteins and pepsin cuts them into polypeptides. In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases activated by enterokinase (trypsin first) break these into amino acids, di- and tripeptides. On the enterocyte, membrane proteases trim larger peptides before uptake. The large intestine is not a site of protein digestion; it absorbs the remaining water and ferments leftover material.
gi-w11-module-q39-39:
From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. The lecture spells out the mechanism. Cholera toxin holds CFTR open, so Cl- floods into the lumen. To recover Cl-, enterocytes exchange it for HCO3-, and K+ also leaks out. Na+ follows paracellularly, and water follows Na+. The stool therefore carries away HCO3-, Na+, Cl- and K+, and the lecture names the result: severe dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic acidosis.

  • Any alkalosis option is wrong because bicarbonate is lost, not retained. Alkalosis is the vomiting picture, where acid is lost.
  • Any hyperkalemia option is wrong because K+ is lost in the stool.
gi-w11-module-q40-40:
From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. Fat absorption depends on bile-salt micelles. The lecture says bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and recycled to the liver, so after an ileal resection the pool runs down. Micelle formation fails, and so does absorption of fat and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K: steatorrhea.

  • Proteins are digested and absorbed mostly in the proximal small bowel and need no bile.
  • Water and electrolytes are absorbed along the whole small bowel, about 7.5 L a day, and the colon takes the remainder. Losing the terminal ileum alone costs little of that capacity, compared with the bile-salt loss.
gi-w11-module-q41-41:
From 03 - Diarrhea & Malabsorption and the IBD overview chart (08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease). The diarrhea history lists the extraintestinal manifestations of IBD to ask about: mouth ulcers, perianal disease, skin rash, eye symptoms, arthritis. The IBD chart adds PSC (with ulcerative colitis), along with erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum and ankylosing spondylitis.

  • Mouth ulcers, arthritis, eye inflammation and PSC all appear on those lists.
  • Seizures appear on neither. Neurological features in a GI patient point somewhere else, such as B12 deficiency (neuropathy) or hepatic encephalopathy, not an IBD manifestation.

gi-w11-module-q42-42.html:
From 03 - Diarrhea & Malabsorption and 05 - Infectious Diarrhea. Lactase is a brush-border enzyme. When gastroenteritis damages the brush border, the disaccharidase goes with it: a mucosal-cell, osmotic cause of malabsorption. Replacing the missing enzyme exogenously (a lactase supplement) lets lactose be split before it reaches the colon, so D is keyed.

  • A: the Infectious Diarrhea lecture itself advises avoiding milk after gastroenteritis because of transient lactose intolerance. That supports this statement too (see the flag).
  • B: iron deficiency comes with mucosal loss such as celiac disease, not an isolated lactase deficit.
  • C: pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea, not milk-specific symptoms.
  • E: celiac disease is an HLA-DQ2/DQ8 immune response to gluten, not a complication of infection.

flags.title: A second option is also supported
flags.html: Option A (transient deficiency of the enzyme after infection) matches the Infectious Diarrhea lecture's “transient lactose intolerance”. Unless the item intends A to fail on its wording (“lactose enzyme” for lactase), both A and the keyed D are defensible. Check the source before relying on the key.

gi-w11-module-q43-43:
From 03 - Diarrhea & Malabsorption. Chronic pancreatitis destroys acinar cells, so fats and fat-soluble vitamins are malabsorbed. The lecture lists the consequences by system:

  • Tetany: calcium, magnesium and vitamin D deficiency.
  • Amenorrhea: an endocrine effect of malabsorption.
  • Purpura: vitamin K deficiency.
  • Skin rashes: dermatitis from vitamin A, essential fatty acid or niacin deficiency.
  • Keyed hypoparathyroidism has the direction wrong. Poor calcium and vitamin D absorption stimulates PTH, and the lecture says malabsorption causes (secondary) hyperparathyroidism.

gi-w11-module-q44-44.html:
From the IBD overview chart (08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease). The chart's celiac column lists dermatitis herpetiformis under presentation, alongside steatorrhea, weight loss and reduced bone density. It is the itchy, blistering rash of gluten sensitivity, and it improves on a gluten-free diet.

  • Pyoderma gangrenosum is the chart's ulcerative colitis skin manifestation.
  • Erythema nodosum is its Crohn disease one.
  • Sweet syndrome and psoriasis appear nowhere in the celiac material. Neither is its characteristic rash.

gi-w11-module-q47-47:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea. The lecture frames GI defence through what happens when it fails. Reduced gastric acid (PPIs, bypass), reduced peristalsis and disrupted normal flora each let ingested organisms colonize. So acid killing organisms (A), peristalsis clearing them (B) and resident bacteria competing with them (E) are defences. Gut lymphoid tissue making antibodies (D) is the mucosal immune defence.

  • C is not a colonization defence as stated. Vomiting after food poisoning is a toxin effect: S. aureus and B. cereus enterotoxins cause rapid vomiting and diarrhea. It is not a mechanism that senses pathogen numbers.
gi-w11-module-q48-48:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea. Cholera toxin works in the small bowel. It activates adenylyl cyclase, and the rise in cAMP causes Cl- secretion and less Na+ absorption. NaCl builds up in the lumen, water follows it, and the result is massive "rice-water" diarrhea. That is option A.

  • B: cholera contaminates water supplies in developing countries, not Siberia.
  • C: antibiotics are adjuncts. The lecture calls oral rehydration the most important treatment.
  • D: the dehydration comes from the diarrhea itself.
  • E: sanitation is the main prevention. The Dukoral vaccine is listed, but mass vaccination is not the key measure.
gi-w11-module-q6-6:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. The pattern here is patchy: terminal ileum, cecum, descending colon and rectum involved, with the ascending and transverse colon spared. Those are skip lesions, and terminal-ileal plus cecal disease is the lecture's commonest Crohn distribution (30% of patients have ileum and cecum involved).

  • Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum proximally, and it reaches the terminal ileum only through backwash from a pancolitis. It would not skip the mid-colon.
  • IBS is a functional disorder, and its colonoscopy is normal. Visible inflammation excludes it.

gi-w11-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - Constipation. Rome IV functional constipation needs ≥ 2 of 6 features for the last 3 months, with onset ≥ 6 months before diagnosis, plus loose stools rarely present without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS. Shelby has < 3 spontaneous BMs per week (1-2) and incomplete evacuation in > 25%, which makes two features. She has had symptoms for 8 months, and she never has loose stools without laxatives. So no further criterion is needed.

  • A, B, D are additional features she does not need. A's threshold is also misquoted: the criterion is > 25%, not 1/3.
  • C is a required criterion (see the flag).

flags.title: The key assumes Shelby does not meet IBS criteria
flags.html: “Insufficient criteria for IBS” is itself part of the Rome IV definition in the lecture. The stem never mentions abdominal pain, so E is correct only if you read that absence as meaning the IBS criterion is met. Option C names a criterion she must still satisfy.

gi-w11-new-q13-13:
From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. Serotonin promotes gut motility. Prucalopride (the stem misspells it) is a gut-selective 5-HT4 agonist, so it relieves constipation, and diarrhea is its expected side effect.

  • D2 antagonists are metoclopramide (crosses the BBB, extrapyramidal effects) and domperidone (does not, but prolongs QT).
  • A D2 agonist would slow the gut. It is not a prokinetic.
  • Cholinergic agonists increase contraction without coordination, which is why the lecture says prokinetics must act upstream.
  • The macrolide is erythromycin, a motilin agonist.
gi-w11-new-q14-14:
From 09 - Pharmacology of Prokinetics and Antidiarrheal Drugs. The lecture classes bismuth subsalicylate as an antisecretory agent (A): it stimulates fluid and electrolyte absorption across the gut wall. It has antimicrobial actions (C): it binds E. coli toxins and is part of quadruple H. pylori therapy. In the stomach's acid it forms salicylic acid, which inhibits PGE2 production, an anti-inflammatory effect (E).

  • Anticholinergic effects belong to diphenoxylate, which comes with atropine to deter overdose, not to bismuth.
  • Sympathetic activation is not part of any antidiarrheal mechanism in the lecture.

gi-w11-new-q16-16.html:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. Diane (the previous question) has IBS with diarrhea. The lecture's IBS dietary management is: avoid caffeine for anxiety and diarrhea (B); increase soluble fibre, which helps both IBS-C and IBS-D (C); and try a low-FODMAP diet short term (A), because FODMAPs are osmotic and fermented. Regular routines (sleep, activity) are part of the same education, and regular meals (D) fits that. It is also the key's choice, though the lecture does not list meals by name.

  • E: reducing soluble fibre is the opposite of the lecture's advice. The target in the IBD overview chart is 20-25 g a day of psyllium-type fibre.

flags.title: Option D is not in the lecture
flags.html: The Functional Gut Disorders lecture does not mention scheduled meals. Option D is supported only by general principles of IBS routine. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w11-new-q17-17:
From 07 - Functional Gut Disorders. The lecture's dyspepsia red flags are dysphagia, vomiting, nocturnal pain, GI bleeding or anemia, an abdominal mass, weight loss, and age of onset > 40. Any of these means you investigate (endoscopy) before calling it functional.

  • Age of onset < 12 reverses the age flag. It is late onset that raises concern for malignancy, and the Luminal GI Malignancies lecture uses ≥ 60 for new dyspepsia.
  • Nausea, heartburn with belching, and upper abdominal pain are the ordinary symptoms of dyspepsia itself. They are not alarm features.
gi-w11-new-q18-18:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is correct.

  • A: the SMA supplies the colon to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon, not only to the hepatic (right colic) flexure.
  • B: the duodenum (parts 2-4), ascending colon, descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal.
  • D: thoracic, lumbar and sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic. Parasympathetic supply is the vagus (midgut) and the pelvic splanchnics, S2-S4 (hindgut).
gi-wb-gi0-q77:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. Below the pectinate line, the anal canal comes from proctodeum ectoderm. It is lined by squamous epithelium, and its lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Above the line, lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes. So C is correct.

  • A: the SMA supplies the colon to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon, not only to the hepatic (right colic) flexure.
  • B: the duodenum (parts 2-4), ascending colon, descending colon and rectum are retroperitoneal.
  • D: thoracic, lumbar and sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic. Parasympathetic supply is the vagus (midgut) and the pelvic splanchnics, S2-S4 (hindgut).
gi-w11-new-q25-25:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea and the IBD overview chart. Only toxin-producing strains of C. difficile cause disease. The lecture warns that the GDH immunoassay is positive for toxic and non-toxic strains, so confirmation needs evidence of toxin: the chart lists PCR for the C. difficile toxin gene.

  • Abdominal X-ray is for severe disease, looking for toxic megacolon. It does not identify the organism.
  • Colonoscopy (really sigmoidoscopy) can show pseudomembranes, but it is invasive and risks perforating an inflamed colon. It is not the confirmatory test.
  • Stool culture and sensitivity covers the other bacterial causes. It cannot tell a toxigenic C. difficile strain from a carrier strain.
gi-w12-module-q10-10:
From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. This is a hepatocellular pattern (ALT 1500, AST 1200, ALP barely raised), severe at over 15 times the upper limit of normal, with ALT > AST. The lecture's severe list is acute viral, toxic (drug-induced), ischemic and autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease and acute choledocholithiasis.

  • Viral, drug-induced and autoimmune hepatitis are all on the severe list, and all fit ALT > AST.
  • Alcoholic hepatitis fits neither feature. The lecture puts it in the mild (5-10 times normal) group, with AST > ALT, classically 2:1 or more. So it is least likely.
gi-w12-module-q13-13:
From the viral hepatitis table in the IBD, Colorectal Cancer & Liver Disease overview chart (08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease). The table's chronic-infection row gives hepatitis B as < 5% for infection acquired as an adult, which is Mr. Anderson's case: an otherwise well 30-year-old with acute HBV who needs only supportive care. Most such adults clear the virus.

  • 95% is roughly the reverse: clearance in adults, or chronicity after perinatal infection (HBV can pass from mother to child).
  • 40% and 60% match no figure in the table. The 80% chronicity figure belongs to hepatitis C.

gi-w12-module-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Acute Hepatitis. This is acute liver failure: severe hepatocellular injury with encephalopathy (confusion) and coagulopathy (INR 1.6) in a patient with no known liver disease. The Acute Hepatitis lecture states it is most commonly caused by acetaminophen overdose, and a young patient fits. The IBD overview chart gives the mechanism: NAPQI accumulates once glutathione runs out, and the antidote is NAC.

  • Viral and autoimmune hepatitis can cause fulminant failure, but less often.
  • Indeterminate cases exist, but the lecture's answer to "most common" is acetaminophen. Use the King's College criteria to decide on transplant referral.

gi-w12-module-q16-16:
From 06 - Chronic Liver Failure. The lecture gives two mechanisms of portal hypertension, and varices form from both. Increased resistance comes from cirrhotic scarring with arteriovenous anastomoses in the fibrous septa (A) and from contraction of vascular smooth muscle in the sinusoids (B). Increased portal volume comes from splanchnic arterial vasodilation, the hyperdynamic circulation (C).

  • D: hepatic lymph flow into the thoracic duct does rise in cirrhosis, but it is a consequence of high sinusoidal pressure, a route relevant to ascites. It does not raise portal pressure, so it is not a cause of varices.
gi-w12-module-q19-19:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. This is a variceal upper GI bleed in a cirrhotic patient with known varices. After the ABCs (airway, two large-bore IVs, transfusion, correct any coagulopathy), the lecture's variceal regimen gives all three:

  • Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h.
  • Octreotide 50 mcg bolus then 50 mcg/h, which lowers portal pressure.
  • Antibiotics (a cephalosporin or quinolone), which the summary singles out as having a mortality benefit.

Endoscopic band ligation follows. Each single option is part of the answer, so "all of the above" is correct.
gi-w12-module-q20-20:
From the ascites section of the IBD, Colorectal Cancer & Liver Disease overview chart (08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease). A SAAG of ≥ 11 g/L means portal hypertension: a high hydrostatic pressure pushes low-albumin fluid out. The chart's high-SAAG list includes cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari (hepatic outflow obstruction) and cardiac ascites (right heart failure transmits pressure back into the liver).

  • Pancreatic ascites is on the low-SAAG list (< 11 g/L), with peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, biliary ascites and nephrotic syndrome. There the fluid leaks from the peritoneum or from low oncotic pressure, not from portal pressure. So it is the exception.
gi-w12-module-q21-21: From the hepatic encephalopathy section of the IBD, Colorectal Cancer & Liver Disease overview chart (08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease). In cirrhosis the liver cannot clear gut-derived toxins such as ammonia, and anything that adds to the load or sensitizes the brain tips the patient into encephalopathy. The chart's precipitants include GI bleeding (blood is a large protein load in the gut), sedatives, and non-compliance (usually stopping lactulose), with infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance and dehydration. All three options are on the list, so D. Treatment means reversing the trigger and giving lactulose, with rifaximin added if it recurs. Do not follow ammonia levels.
gi-w12-module-q23-23:
From 10 - Approach to Jaundice. Sort by where bilirubin gets stuck. Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises when it never reaches the liver's conjugating step: overproduction, as in hemolysis (high reticulocytes), or impaired uptake or conjugation (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar). Conjugated (direct) bilirubin rises when the liver has conjugated it but cannot get it out.

  • Dubin-Johnson and Rotor are the lecture's genetic excretion defects, which raise conjugated bilirubin.
  • Drug-induced liver injury causes intrahepatic cholestasis. The lecture lists drugs among its causes, and amoxicillin-clavulanate is a classic example. Cholestasis also raises conjugated bilirubin.
  • Hemolysis gives unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, so it is the exception.
gi-w12-module-q28-28:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. A pancreatic mass needs tissue, and the lecture's preferred route is fine needle aspiration during endoscopic ultrasound, which has the higher yield.

  • Biliary brushing (A) and ERCP (C): ERCP brushings are the low-yield, less sensitive way to get cells, and a mass in the body is not sitting in the bile duct to be brushed.
  • CT (B): images and stages the mass but gives no histology, so it cannot provide the diagnosis.
  • Percutaneous core biopsy (E): not the route the lecture teaches; EUS reaches the pancreas from the stomach and duodenum without crossing the peritoneum.
gi-w12-module-q29-29:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. About 90% of acute cholecystitis is calculous: a stone obstructs the cystic duct, pressure rises and blood flow falls, so the wall becomes ischemic and inflamed.

  • Acalculous (A): only about 10%, arising without stones from bile stasis, raised bile viscosity and poor perfusion in patients recovering from major surgery or who are critically ill.
gi-w12-module-q30-30:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Acalculous cholecystitis is the rarer type but the more serious one, with more gangrene and perforation. The reason is who gets it: critically ill and post-operative patients, whose gallbladder is already hypoperfused and whose illness masks the diagnosis.

  • Calculous (B): far more common (90%) but usually occurs in otherwise well patients, is diagnosed on ultrasound and settles with antibiotics then cholecystectomy once stable.
gi-w12-module-q31-31:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. The lecture follows a stone impacted in the cystic duct through time: the gallbladder first distends (mucocele or hydrops), then becomes acutely inflamed if the blockage persists, and if the inflammation persists and fibrosis sets in, chronic cholecystitis results. The scarring then promotes more stones, repeating the cycle. The stem's word prolonged points past the acute stage to that end state.

  • Acute cholecystitis (A): the earlier consequence of the same blockage, not the long-term one.
  • Acute pancreatitis (B): needs a stone at the ampulla, blocking pancreatic outflow.
  • Secondary biliary cirrhosis (D): needs common bile duct obstruction, so bile backs up into the liver; a cystic duct block leaves hepatic drainage intact.
gi-w12-module-q32-32:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Location decides the complication. A prolonged common bile duct obstruction (more than about 6 months) raises intrahepatic duct pressure; bile backs up into the liver, causing bile stasis and fibrosis, which is secondary biliary cirrhosis.

  • Acute (A) and chronic (C) cholecystitis: complications of a cystic duct block, which spares the liver's drainage.
  • Acute pancreatitis (B): an acute event from a stone at the ampulla blocking the pancreatic duct, not the result of long-standing CBD obstruction.

gi-w12-module-q35-35.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Biliary carcinoma is defined in the lecture as adenocarcinoma of the bile ducts (extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma): the ducts are lined by glandular epithelium, and glandular epithelium gives rise to adenocarcinoma. Risk factors are PSC, choledochal cyst, gallstones, IBD (through PSC) and liver flukes in Southeast Asia.

  • Lymphoma (B) and melanoma (C): not tumours of the ductal lining; in the liver they appear as metastases or infiltrates.
  • Neuroendocrine carcinoma (D): a rare exception rather than the rule.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (E): needs squamous epithelium (e.g., the anal canal or the proximal esophagus), which the biliary tree does not have.

gi-w12-module-q37-37:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. Sort by two axes. Epithelial means hepatocytes or bile duct cells, and benign hepatocyte neoplasia is the hepatic adenoma, typically in young women on oral contraceptives, in a non-cirrhotic liver.

  • Bile duct hamartoma (A): benign, but a non-neoplastic lesion (von Meyenburg complex), not a neoplasm.
  • Hemangioma (B): the most common benign liver neoplasm, but of vessels, so non-epithelial.
  • Hepatoblastoma (D) and HCC (E): epithelial hepatocyte tumours, but malignant.
gi-w12-module-q38-38:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. HCC incidence worldwide tracks hepatitis B: highest in Southeast Asia and tropical Africa, low in Western countries because of their low HBV rates.

  • Aflatoxin (A): a real cause (Aspergillus-contaminated food), but it drives HCC in endemic regions, not Canada.
  • Elevated AFP in all (B): only 30-40% of cases have a raised AFP, so a normal AFP never excludes HCC.
  • Never non-cirrhotic (C): 90% arise in cirrhosis, so about 10% do not (hepatitis B can cause HCC before cirrhosis).
  • Smoking not a risk factor (D): an absolute that is false; smoking is an established HCC risk factor, although the lecture's own list does not name it.
gi-w12-module-q39-39:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. Hepatoblastoma is the number one primary liver cancer in children, presenting as an enlarging abdomen or mass with very high AFP; prematurity and low birth weight are associations.

  • Biliary atresia (A): an infant problem, but it presents with jaundice, dark urine and pale stools from obstructed bile flow, not an enlarging mass.
  • Cholangiocarcinoma (B) and HCC (E): adult cancers (HCC mostly men over 40 with cirrhosis; cholangiocarcinoma with PSC).
  • Hemangioma (C): benign and usually an incidental finding, not a growing mass that raises concern.
gi-w12-module-q41-41:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. Focal nodular hyperplasia begins with an arterial malformation; hepatocytes then grow as hyperplastic nodules around a central scar containing large vessels. The lecture says FNH always has a central scar, and it is seen on imaging and in the specimen. It is the second most common benign liver lesion, in women aged 30-50, and needs no treatment.

  • Bile duct hamartoma (A): small, irregular, often multiple white surface lesions, with no scar.
  • Hepatic adenoma (C): a sheet of neoplastic hepatocytes, notable for bleeding when over 5 cm, not for a scar.
  • HCC (D) and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (E): malignancies defined by their risk settings (cirrhosis, PSC), with no characteristic central scar.
gi-w12-module-q42-42:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. Bile duct hamartomas are exactly the lesions sampled at cancer surgery with the question "is this metastatic disease?" A pathologist answers it by comparing the frozen section with the known primary, so they need the site and histologic type of the cancer being resected. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma looks very different from metastatic melanoma.

  • Urgency (A): true of every frozen section and adds no diagnostic information.
  • Infection precautions (B): universal precautions apply to all tissue regardless of history.
  • Lymphoma protocol (C): nothing here suggests lymphoma.
  • Which stains (E): the pathologist's decision, and one that follows from knowing the primary.
gi-w12-module-q43-43:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. The clue is spilled gallstones at cholecystectomy: infected stone and bile left in the peritoneum next to the liver become a septic focus. The lecture's routes to a hepatic abscess include the biliary tree and direct spread from an adjacent septic focus, and the abscess typically presents as a single lesion with fever, RUQ pain and tender hepatomegaly.

  • Angiosarcoma (A): needs thorotrast or vinyl chloride exposure.
  • Hepatic adenoma (C): young women on the oral contraceptive pill, not a 68-year-old.
  • HCC (D): needs cirrhosis or viral hepatitis; there is no such history.
  • Cholangiocarcinoma (E): linked to PSC and ulcerative colitis, and the surgical history does not explain it.
gi-w12-module-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. The lecture separates liver enzymes, which are markers of hepatocyte damage or impaired bile flow, from liver function tests, which measure what the liver actually makes or clears. ALT is a hepatocellular enzyme: it leaks out when hepatocytes are injured and says nothing about how well the liver is working.

  • INR (B): coagulation factors are made almost exclusively in the liver, and their short half-life makes INR a fast marker of synthetic function.
  • Bilirubin (C): reflects the liver's conjugation and excretion of heme breakdown products.
  • Albumin (D): made only by hepatocytes, so it falls when synthetic function fails.
gi-w12-new-q15-15:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion by activated pancreatic enzymes, and each enzyme leaves its own lesion, so all four options are features:

  • Edema (A): from microvascular leakage.
  • Fat necrosis (B): from lipase, forming chalky calcium soaps.
  • Hemorrhage (C): from elastase destroying vessel walls.
  • Parenchymal destruction (D): from trypsin.

An acute inflammatory reaction completes the picture.
gi-w12-new-q17-17:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. IgG4-related chronic acalculous cholecystitis is one expression of a systemic disease:

  • True (A): tissue infiltrates of IgG4-producing plasma cells define it.
  • False (B): serum IgG4 is raised, which is how the systemic disease is recognised.
  • False (C): the infiltrates involve the gallbladder, the biliary tree (IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, often with extrahepatic obstruction) and the pancreas, as well as other organs.
  • True (D): it can mimic gallbladder cancer, and so may be resected as one.

So A and D (E) is the only combination that holds.
gi-wb-gi0-q107:
From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. AST is found outside the liver (muscle, red cells, brain) and falls in mitochondria-heavy, alcoholic, ischemic or vascular injury; ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and dominates in most inflammatory or metabolic hepatocellular injury. The lecture's lists sort each item:

  • i. NAFLD = A (ALT > AST): steatosis and NASH are ALT-predominant.
  • ii. Acute Budd-Chiari = B (AST > ALT): hepatic venous outflow obstruction behaves like ischemic or congestive injury.
  • iii. Alcoholic liver disease = B (AST > ALT): classically at 2:1 or more.
  • iv. Viral hepatitis = A (ALT > AST): acute or chronic.
  • v. Celiac disease = A (ALT > AST): a systemic cause of mild ALT elevation.
  • vi. Ischemic hepatitis = B (AST > ALT), grouped with congestive hepatopathy.
gi-w13-module-q11-11:
From 03 - Abdominal Masses. The lecture's mass-level risk factors for malignancy are gradual onset (so a slow growing mass, C), painless and fixed (B), and its high-risk associated symptoms are jaundice, anemia and weight loss (E).

  • Painful (A): the lecture links pain with a benign cause (inflammatory or infective).
  • Acute febrile illness (D): points to an infective or inflammatory mass such as an abscess, not a tumour.
gi-w13-module-q2-2:
From 02 - Bowel Obstruction. The abdominal exam starts with inspection, and the lecture singles out surgical scars: always look for them, because a prior operation makes an adhesive cause likely and changes both the differential and the management. Palpation, percussion and auscultation come after looking, and palpation needs a relaxed patient lying flat with arms by their sides.

  • Palpating for masses (A): a later step, and the one most likely to make a patient in pain guard.
  • Bowel sounds (B): useful (high-pitched early in SBO, then absent), but never the opening step.
  • Tapping for peritonitis (D): a gentle test of peritoneal irritation that follows inspection; it does not replace it.
gi-w13-module-q25-25:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. Colonic diverticula are acquired, false diverticula. Raised luminal pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa out through focal weak points in the wall, so the outpouching lacks the muscularis propria and does not have all four layers. Contrast the appendix, which is a congenital, true diverticulum with all four layers.

  • True, with muscularis (A): describes the appendix or a Meckel diverticulum, not colonic disease.
  • Congenital (B, D): they are acquired with age and a low-fibre diet, and are rare under 35.
  • False but containing muscularis (E): a contradiction, since having the muscularis is what would make it true.

gi-w13-module-q28-28.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. The lecture's workup for appendicitis is simple labs (CBC, electrolytes, CRP) plus ultrasound. Appendicitis affects a young population (peak age 10-25, including children and possibly pregnant women), so the first image is the one without radiation that can also show ovarian or ectopic pathology. CT abdomen/pelvis is the lecture's first-line image for diverticulitis, where patients are older.

  • Abdominal or pelvic x-ray (A, E): cannot show the appendix; they serve obstruction and free air.
  • CT (C): a good test, but not the lecture's initial choice here, because of radiation in the young.
  • MRI (D): limited availability; reserved for special cases.

gi-w13-module-q29-29:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. Both infections are polymicrobial gut flora: gram-negative rods (E. coli, Klebsiella, other Enterobacteriaceae), gut cocci (Enterococcus, Streptococcus anginosus) and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium). That accounts for B, C, D and E.

  • Streptococcus pyogenes (A): a group A strep of the throat and skin (pharyngitis, cellulitis), not a bowel organism, so it is not the one cultured.
gi-w13-module-q30-30:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. The lecture gives two kinds of regimen for gram-negatives, gut cocci and anaerobes. Combination therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole, because ceftriaxone lacks anaerobic cover. Monotherapy is a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, which cover anaerobes on their own.

  • Ceftriaxone + metronidazole (A): the standard combination.
  • Imipenem (B), meropenem (D), piperacillin-tazobactam (C): appropriate single agents. A 1 cm abscess (under 5 cm) is managed with admission and IV antibiotics, not drainage.
  • Piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole (E): adds a second anaerobic agent to a drug that already covers anaerobes. That duplication makes it the inappropriate regimen.
gi-w13-module-q33-33:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. Neoplasms turn up in 0.5-1% of appendectomies (5-10% of interval appendectomies), and the most common is the neuroendocrine tumour. It is usually cured by the appendectomy alone, although grade determines behaviour.

  • Goblet cell carcinoid (A): the lecture names it among the most common malignant epithelial appendiceal tumours, which is a different superlative.
  • LAMN (C), HAMN (E), mucinous adenocarcinoma (D): recognised mucinous neoplasms of the appendix, but less frequent than NET.
gi-w13-module-q36-36:
From 08 - Anorectal Disease. Painless bright red bleeding seen on the paper or in the toilet water after a bowel movement, in a young man, is the classic internal hemorrhoid. The hemorrhoid sits above the pectinate line, where there is no somatic pain innervation.

  • Colon (A) or rectal (B) cancer: at 25 without red flags (weight loss, anemia, change in bowel habit, family history) they are much less likely, though the history still asks about CRC risk.
  • Infectious colitis (C): would bring diarrhea, cramping and blood mixed into the stool.

A painful bleed with a tearing sensation would suggest a fissure instead.

gi-w10-module-q1-1.html: From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. Follow food down the tract: mouth (1), where mechanical digestion and salivary starch digestion begin; esophagus (2), between the UES and LES; stomach (10), the main site of digestion, behind the pyloric sphincter; then duodenum (5), the first part of the small intestine. The accessory organs sit in the right upper quadrant: liver (3) with the gallbladder (4) tucked beneath it. The colon then runs from the cecum (7) in the right lower quadrant, past the ileocecal sphincter, up as the ascending colon (6), down the left as the descending colon (8), and ends at the rectum (9) before the anal sphincters.

flags.title: Diagram not checked
flags.html: The numbered diagram was not available when this was written, so the explanation gives each structure's position but could not confirm the numbering against the image. Trust the key's number-to-structure mapping over the prose if they seem to disagree.

gi-w10-module-q13-13:
From 02 - Gastrointestinal Motility. CCK is released from the duodenum when fat and protein arrive in chyme, and it slows gastric emptying (it keeps the pylorus more closed) so these nutrients get time to be digested. The lecture's other inhibitors are norepinephrine, leptin, GLP-1 and opioids.

  • Acetylcholine (A): the parasympathetic transmitter, which stimulates emptying.
  • Gastrin (C): released on distension; raises acid and motility.
  • Motilin (D): starts the migrating motor complex, sweeping leftover content onward.
gi-w10-module-q14-14:
From 02 - Gastrointestinal Motility. Option D is half right. Prostaglandins such as PGE2 do increase mucus to protect the small intestine from acidic chyme, but they stimulate motility (clearing the acid faster); they do not inhibit it. That makes D the false statement.

  • A (true): the small intestine is mainly under ENS control, which is why CNS problems spare it relative to the esophagus and stomach.
  • B (true): peristalsis, segmentation, retroperistalsis (the precursor to vomiting) and the MMC are all small-intestinal patterns.
  • C (true): failed motility alters bowel movements, and inflammatory mediators act on it.
  • E (true): CCK slows gastric emptying yet increases small-intestinal motility.
gi-w10-module-q17-17:
From 05 - Development of the GI Tract. Each division of the gut tube carries its own artery through the dorsal mesentery:

  • Celiac trunk (A) = foregut (i): esophagus to the proximal duodenum, plus the liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
  • SMA (C) = midgut (ii): distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The midgut loop rotates around the SMA during physiologic herniation.
  • IMA (B) = hindgut (iii): distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal. Its superior rectal branch supplies the rectum.

This matters clinically: the appendix (midgut) refers pain to the umbilicus, and the sigmoid (hindgut) refers it suprapubically.
gi-w10-module-q2-2:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract and 10 - GI Secretion. Each organ's job follows from what it adds or removes:

  • Salivary glands (A) = saliva with water, electrolytes, mucus and enzymes (v): the secretion itself.
  • Mouth and esophagus (D) = chewing, mixing and initial starch digestion (i): salivary amylase acts during chewing.
  • Stomach (G) = churning, acid secretion and initial protein digestion (ii): HCl plus pepsin.
  • Small intestine (B) = absorption of nutrients and water, and digestion (iii): villi and microvilli make it the main absorptive site.
  • Large intestine (C) = water and electrolyte absorption, and forming and storing feces (iv).
  • Liver and gallbladder (E) = producing and storing bile (vi).
  • Pancreas (F) = enzymes and bicarbonate (vii): bicarbonate neutralises acidic chyme.
gi-w10-module-q33-33:
From 09 - GERD. Most patients with typical symptoms respond to a PPI. That is why an empiric PPI trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this clinical diagnosis; only 10-40% fail standard dosing, and those are the refractory cases.

  • H2 blockers supplanted (A): the lecture keeps H2 blockers as a medical option alongside PPIs and antacids, so they are not obsolete, even though PPIs are more effective.
  • Fundoplication preferred (B): Nissen fundoplication is reserved for select cases, not preferred over medication.
  • Lifestyle limited (D): diet, less alcohol, smoking cessation and weight loss are first-line management.
  • As-needed PPI only (E): PPIs work best taken regularly before breakfast, and poor timing and adherence are a leading cause of apparent refractoriness.
gi-w10-module-q4-4:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract and 10 - GI Secretion. Match each molecule by its signature action:

  • Serotonin (B) = stimulates motility and secretion, and mediates nociception (i): released by enteroendocrine cells on distension; it is also the pain signal from a stretched gut.
  • Gastrin (A) = stimulates gastric acid (ii): from G cells, acting on parietal and ECL cells via CCK2 receptors.
  • Somatostatin (E) = inhibits gastric acid (iii): from D cells when pH falls below 3.
  • CCK (C) = inhibits gastric emptying (iv): released by duodenal I cells in response to fat.
  • Pepsin (D) = breaks down proteins (v): activated from chief-cell pepsinogen by HCl.
gi-w10-module-q43-43:
From 10 - GI Secretion and 02 - Gastrointestinal Motility. The question needs both actions. CCK is one of the intestinal hormones that inhibit gastric acid, and it also slows gastric emptying, so fat stays in the duodenum long enough to be digested.

  • Histamine (A), gastrin (B), GRP (E): all stimulate acid. Histamine acts on H2 receptors on parietal cells; gastrin-releasing peptide acts upstream by releasing gastrin.
  • Prostaglandins (D): inhibit acid, but they increase motility, so only one of the two actions fits.

gi-w10-module-q59-59.html: From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastric pathology chart). The statement is false, because serology stays positive after eradication. Antibodies persist long after the organism is gone, so a positive serology cannot separate cured from persistent infection. Serology is used only for the initial test in a young patient with dyspepsia. Eradication is confirmed, and refractory infection identified, with a test of active infection: the C13 urea breath test (or a stool antigen or biopsy). Only a positive result on one of those tests after treatment defines refractory infection, which is then retreated with a different regimen, such as PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin or rifabutin.

gi-w10-module-q60-60.html: From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastric pathology chart). The statement is true. The lecture's pathway is to treat H. pylori and then confirm eradication with the C13 urea breath test. Checking matters because antibiotic resistance and reinfection make treatment failure common, and residual infection keeps the risk of peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
