The test must detect active infection: serology remains positive after eradication, so it cannot be used to confirm cure.

gi-w10-module-q62-62.html: From 04 - Gallbladder Disease (the gastric pathology chart). The statement is false. The chart lists three ways to test for H. pylori: the C13 urea breath test, serology and gastric biopsy. A biopsy looks for the organism itself, so it detects active infection and can show whether eradication worked. The same applies to the stool antigen test. The test that cannot confirm eradication is serology, because antibodies stay positive after the organism is gone. The chart's routine choice for confirming cure is the urea breath test, since it needs no endoscopy. A biopsy is still a valid test when the patient is being scoped anyway.

gi-w10-module-q68-68.html:
From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs (the antiemetic chart). The chart's rule is to learn each class by which receptors it hits. Its D2-antagonist receptor profile shows benzamides as the most D2-selective, while phenothiazines also block muscarinic and histamine receptors. That is why they cause more sedation and anticholinergic effects.

  • A is true: side effects follow the drug's dopaminergic and off-target receptor affinities.
  • D is true: the agents with the most H1 blockade are the most sedating.
  • B is reversed. Dopamine inhibits prolactin, so blocking D2 raises prolactin, which causes galactorrhea, gynecomastia and impotence.
  • C: dopamine inhibits gut motility, so blocking it is prokinetic. That is the reason domperidone and metoclopramide are used for gastroparesis.
  • E: metoclopramide and the phenothiazines cross the BBB, causing parkinsonian extrapyramidal effects. They oppose antiparkinsonian dopaminergic drugs.

gi-w10-module-q73-73.html: From 07 - Nutrition & Supplements (the nausea and vomiting section). The statement is true. The chart's differential for nausea and vomiting has a CNS arm: benign positional vertigo, migraine and motion sickness. Its workup looks for that arm on purpose. The history asks about headaches, vertigo and other CNS symptoms, the exam includes a neurological exam, and CT head is on the investigation list. Vomiting from raised intracranial pressure or migraine arrives with the neurological symptoms that point to it. That is why a headache with vomiting sends you to the head, not the gut.

gi-w10-module-q74-74.html: From 11 - Acid Base Disturbances and 07 - Nutrition & Supplements. The statement is false. Vomiting loses gastric HCl, so the expected disturbance is metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis. The acid-base lecture lists vomiting as a classic secondary cause. Volume contraction activates RAAS, the aldosterone increase wastes K+ (so hypokalemia comes with it), and a urine Cl- below 10 points to this cause. The N/V chart's acute plan is to treat volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities after life-threatening causes are ruled out. The metabolic causes of vomiting it lists (DKA, uremia) can bring an acidosis with them. The vomiting itself does not.

gi-w10-module-q75-75.html: From 07 - Nutrition & Supplements and 05 - Infectious Diarrhea. The statement is false. The N/V differential's infection arm is bacterial gastroenteritis, foodborne illness, pyelonephritis and viral gastroenteritis, so viruses are listed alongside bacteria. The Infectious Diarrhea lecture names rotavirus and Norwalk (norovirus) among the watery causes. Preformed-toxin food poisoning (S. aureus, B. cereus) is bacterial and vomiting-predominant with a rapid onset. Parasites such as Giardia are also on the list. "Almost always bacterial" ignores the viral gastroenteritis that is the everyday cause.

gi-w10-module-q76-76.html: From 07 - Nutrition & Supplements (the nausea and vomiting section). The statement is true. The chart's physical exam for nausea and vomiting lists abdominal distension/tenderness, succussion splash and a neurological exam. A succussion splash is the sloshing heard with a stethoscope over the stomach when the patient is rocked. It means a large volume of fluid and air is sitting in a stomach that cannot empty, which is the picture of gastric outlet obstruction (e.g., a pyloric ulcer scar or a distal gastric or pancreatic tumour; the pancreatic lecture mentions stenting the gastric outlet as palliation). Severe gastroparesis can give the same sign.

gi-w10-new-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. The lecture's sphincters each separate two compartments. The pyloric sphincter separates the stomach from the small intestine, meaning its first part, the duodenum. The jejunum begins only at the duodenojejunal junction, so C is the false description.

  • UES (A): oral cavity (pharynx) from esophagus. Correct.
  • LES (B): esophagus from stomach. Correct.
  • Ileocecal (D): terminal ileum from large intestine. Correct.

The internal and external anal sphincters complete the list, separating the large intestine from the outside.

gi-w10-new-q10-10.html:
From 10 - GI Secretion. Salivary secretion is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, not the ENS. The lecture's summary says that saliva is primarily under neural (autonomic) regulation, while gastric, pancreatic and biliary secretion depend more on hormones and paracrine signals. So B is false.

  • A is true, and a common trap: both arms stimulate. Parasympathetic input adds enzymes and water; sympathetic input adds mucin, which thickens the saliva.
  • C is true: sleep, fatigue, fear and dehydration all reduce secretion.
  • D is true: the parasympathetic drive is cholinergic, so anticholinergics cause a dry mouth, as the antihistamine side-effect list also shows.

gi-w10-new-q12-12.html:
From 10 - GI Secretion. The lecture names the three major mediators of gastric acid secretion: acetylcholine, histamine and gastrin. ACh (M3) acts on parietal cells directly and also releases histamine from ECL cells and gastrin from G cells. Histamine acts on H2 receptors in a paracrine way. Gastrin acts on CCK2 receptors, both on parietal cells and through ECL histamine release. PPIs block the final step of all three.

  • Somatostatin (A, B): an inhibitor. It is released by D cells when the pH falls below 3.
  • Pepsin (A): an enzyme activated by acid, not a driver of acid.
  • Epinephrine (D): not one of the lecture's stimulants of acid secretion.

gi-w10-new-q21-21.html:
From 08 - Anatomy of the Foregut. The descending colon is retroperitoneal. It is covered by peritoneum only on its front surface and is fixed to the posterior wall, because its mesentery fused with the parietal peritoneum when the gut returned from herniation. The retroperitoneal organs are the SAD PUCKER list: suprarenals, aorta/IVC, duodenum parts 2-4, pancreas, ureters, ascending and descending colon, kidneys, distal esophagus and rectum.

  • Spleen, stomach and ileum (A-C): intraperitoneal and mobile.
  • First part of the duodenum (E): the exception within the duodenum. It is foregut, intraperitoneal, and the site of most duodenal ulcers.

gi-w10-new-q22-22.html:
From 08 - Anatomy of the Hepatobiliary & Portal System. The gallbladder lies under the liver and drains through the cystic duct into the structures at the porta hepatis. The hepatic portal vein runs there, beside the common bile duct and the hepatic artery, and enters the liver at the porta. It is the large non-arterial vessel close to a cholecystectomy dissection (Calot's triangle, around the cystic artery).

  • Splenic, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric veins (A, C, D): they join to form the portal vein. That happens behind the pancreas, away from the gallbladder bed.
  • IVC (E): retroperitoneal. It receives the hepatic veins behind the liver, not in the gallbladder field.

review.t: Anatomy of the Hepatobiliary & Portal System

gi-w10-weekly-q4-4.html:
From 09 - GERD and the vault's Nissen fundoplication note. A Nissen wraps the gastric fundus around the lower esophagus to reinforce the LES. Its listed complications include dysphagia (usually short-term), gas-bloat syndrome, dumping syndrome and vagal injury. A tighter junction makes swallowing harder, so a large improvement in pre-existing dysphagia is the least likely outcome (B). The vault's esophageal dysphagia note even contraindicates the wrap in scleroderma esophagus, where poor motility would be made worse.

  • Inability to vomit (A): the same one-way valve that stops reflux also stops the patient from bringing gastric contents up. This is expected.
  • Bloating and gas (C): gas-bloat syndrome, since swallowed air cannot be belched.
  • Wound infection (D): a possible complication of any incision.

flags.title: Only partly covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The Nissen fundoplication note lists dysphagia and gas bloat. It does not mention the inability to vomit or wound infection, so those two lines are from general surgical principles.

gi-w11-module-q10-10.html:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Read the stem's own lettering. Longstanding UC carries a CRC risk, so surveillance colonoscopy takes regular random biopsies to look for dysplasia, and the lecture lists dysplasia as an indication for surgery. Dysplasia found on random biopsies of flat mucosa means the field is premalignant and cannot be removed endoscopically, so D is of most concern.

  • A. Normal random biopsies: reassuring.
  • B. An adenoma on targeted biopsy: a discrete polyp that can usually be removed at colonoscopy and then followed.
  • C. Chronic active colitis: disease activity, managed medically (5-ASA, steroids, biologics), not a premalignant finding.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. random biopsies normal, B. targeted adenoma, C. targeted chronic active colitis, D. random low-grade dysplasia). The listed choices A-D are from the granuloma question (gi-w11-module-q8-8), so the keyed option D reads “TB” here. It means D. Random biopsies showing low-grade dysplasia. The shared-instructions text above the stem (“Check that the pathologist did special stains”) is also a stray option from that question.

gi-w11-module-q11-11.html:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding and 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs. Read the stem's own lettering. The lecture's non-variceal UGIB regimen is IV pantoprazole (80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/hr), H. pylori testing and endoscopic therapy. Statement A is the false one: PPIs do not block gastrin release. The PUD lecture says the opposite. Lowering acid removes somatostatin's brake on G cells, so PPIs cause hypergastrinemia.

  • B, C and D are the reasons for giving the infusion. A clot forms and holds poorly in acid. Pepsin, which acid activates, digests the clot. Raising the pH therefore stabilizes the platelet plug, reduces clot lysis and stops acid from eroding the ulcer further.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. blocks gastrin release, B. stabilizes the platelet plug, C. less fibrinolysis through less pepsin activation, D. less acid damage to the ulcer). The listed choices A-D are from an unrelated IBD question, so the keyed option A reads “inflammation is transient” here. It means A. Blocks gastrin release.

flags.title: Only partly covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The PUD lecture supports the key (PPIs raise gastrin). The bleeding lecture gives the PPI dose but not why it helps, so the clot-stability reasoning for B-D is from general principles.

gi-w11-module-q13-13.html: Read the stem's own lettering. Endoscopic treatment of a peptic ulcer is for lesions at high risk of rebleeding. An actively bleeding ulcer and a non-bleeding visible vessel are the highest-risk stigmata and are treated with epinephrine injection, cautery or hemoclips, the methods the bleeding lecture lists. An adherent clot sits over one of those lesions, so it is usually lifted and the base treated. Hematin staining, a flat pigmented spot, is old blood on a healing base with a low rebleed risk. It needs a PPI and H. pylori management, not endoscopic therapy, so A is the exception.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. hematin staining, B. visible vessel, C. ulcer covered in clot, D. actively bleeding ulcer). The listed choices A-D are from an unrelated IBD question, so the keyed option A reads “inflammation is transient” here. It means A. Hematin staining.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w11-module-q22-22.html:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening. Risk levels come from the lecture's definitions. Longstanding IBD (Crohn or UC) is placed in the high-risk group, along with FAP, HNPCC/Lynch and prior multiple or large polyps. It is surveyed with colonoscopy every 1-3 years from 8 years after onset, with random biopsies for dysplasia.

  • IBS (B): functional, with no CRC risk. It is not a screening category.
  • Smoking and a high-fat diet (C): lifestyle factors that do not change the screening tier. The patient stays average risk.
  • A cousin with CRC (D): increased risk requires a first-degree relative (parent, sibling or child). A cousin does not count.

gi-w11-module-q23-23.html:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening. The lecture defines a symptomatic patient as one with any new lower GI symptom, especially an unexplained change in bowel habit or new constipation, rectal bleeding, or unexplained iron-deficiency anemia. These patients bypass screening and go straight to colonoscopy, never FIT.

  • Ascites (A): points to the liver, peritoneum or heart. It is not one of the lecture's CRC symptoms.
  • Heartburn (C): an upper GI (reflux) symptom.
  • Hematemesis (D): bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, which calls for an EGD, not colonoscopy.

gi-w11-module-q24-24.html:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening and the vault's sigmoidoscopy note. Flexible sigmoidoscopy views the left side of the colon, up to the splenic flexure. About 65% of CRCs are within its reach. It needs minimal prep (an enema) and no sedation, and in the lecture's screening table it is repeated every 5 years. Its weakness follows from its reach: it can miss proximal cancers.

  • FIT (B): a stool test for human globin that views no mucosa at all.
  • Colonoscopy (C): views the whole colon to the cecum, so it goes beyond the splenic flexure.
  • CT colonography (D): a radiological image of the whole colon, not a direct mucosal view, and not recommended for screening.

gi-w11-module-q28-28.html:
From 11 - Colorectal Cancer Screening and the vault's FIT note. FIT detects human globin, while the older guaiac FOBT detects heme peroxidase activity. Globin is specific to human blood and is digested before it can come from the upper GI tract, so FIT is more sensitive (about 92% for CRC) and more specific for colorectal bleeding.

  • Three samples (A): that describes the gFOBT kit. FIT is a single home sample.
  • Stopping medications first (B): the dietary and drug restrictions (red meat, and in general teaching vitamin C and NSAIDs) belong to gFOBT. FIT needs none.
  • Every 5 years (D): FIT is repeated every 2 years from age 50-74. Five years is the flexible sigmoidoscopy interval.

gi-w11-module-q30-30.html:
From 04 - Abdominal Pain and 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. Early appendicitis inflames only the organ. The pain is visceral: it travels with autonomic afferents that have no somatic map, so it is felt as vague, crampy, midline pain. The appendix is midgut, so that pain is periumbilical. When the inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum of the body wall, the spinal (somatic) nerves that supply the wall carry it. The pain then becomes sharp and localized over the organ at McBurney's point in the RLQ. That is option C.

  • The appendix moves (A): it does not; what changes is which nerves carry the pain.
  • Spread to the abdominal muscles (B): the peritoneal lining, not the muscle, is the source.
  • Mesoappendix detached from the umbilicus (D): anatomically meaningless. The mesoappendix hangs from the ileal mesentery.

review.t: Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall

gi-w11-module-q31-31.html:
From 08 - Anorectal Disease and 06 - Anatomy of the Anterior Abdominal Wall. The pectinate line decides it. Above it the anal canal is hindgut, with autonomic innervation (pelvic splanchnics) and no somatic pain fibres. Below it the canal is proctodeum, with somatic innervation through the pudendal nerve. External hemorrhoids lie below the line, so they hurt: a thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents with sudden, acute pain and a mass at the anal opening.

  • Internal hemorrhoids (A) lie above the line. The lecture's presentation is painless rectal bleeding, with blood on the paper or above the stool, and a lump that may need pushing back in.

gi-w11-module-q33-33.html: From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. The statement is true. The lecture defines digestion as the breakdown of macromolecules by mechanical means (mixing and churning, which is motility) and chemical means (enzymes, which are secretions). Both are needed. Motility mixes chyme with salivary, gastric, pancreatic and biliary secretions and moves it along at a rate that allows breakdown and absorption. The secretions supply the amylases, proteases, lipase, acid, bicarbonate and bile salts that do the chemistry. Too little of either one (gastroparesis, rapid transit, pancreatic insufficiency, biliary obstruction) causes maldigestion.

gi-w11-module-q34-34.html: From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. The statement is false on both counts. Digestion starts in the mouth, where chewing begins mechanical breakdown and salivary amylase begins on starch. Most of it happens in the small intestine, not the stomach. Salivary amylase is destroyed in the stomach, and the stomach's own contribution to protein digestion is limited to acid denaturation plus pepsin. Pancreatic amylase, the proteases (activated by enterokinase) and pancreatic lipase all work in the duodenum. The lecture says the majority of lipid digestion occurs there. Brush-border enzymes then finish carbohydrates and peptides at the enterocyte surface.

gi-w11-module-q37-37.html:
From 02 - Digestion and Absorption and 10 - GI Secretion. Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, and the lecture warns that ileal resection leaves patients unable to maintain enough of them. Without bile salts there are too few micelles, so fat is malabsorbed and steatorrhea follows. That includes cholesterol, which needs micelles to be absorbed and is also excreted in bile. So cholesterol appears in the stool (B).

  • Medium-chain fatty acids (A): small enough to be absorbed directly without micelles, as the lecture describes for short-chain fatty acids. They are the ones spared, which is why MCT oil is used as a supplement.
  • Vitamin A (C): fat-soluble and bile-salt dependent, so its absorption falls.
  • Bile salts (D): their absorption site has been removed, so it decreases.

gi-w11-module-q38-38.html:
From 02 - Digestion and Absorption. The lecture states that the fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E and K, must be carried in micelles to be absorbed, so their absorption is dependent on bile salts. Low bile-salt production therefore hits vitamin A hardest, along with dietary fat (steatorrhea).

  • Glucose (A): absorbed by carrier transport (SGLT1) after amylase and brush-border digestion. Bile is not involved.
  • Vitamin B12 (B): water-soluble. It needs intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum, not bile salts.
  • Amino acids (D): digested by pepsin and pancreatic proteases, then absorbed by active transporters. They do not depend on bile salts.

gi-w11-module-q45-45.html:
From 03 - Diarrhea & Malabsorption and 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. She is already gluten-free, so the gluten-driven tests will come back normal whether or not she has celiac disease. HLA typing does not depend on diet. HLA-DQ2 is present in 95% of celiac patients and DQ8 in most of the rest, but DQ2 is also found in 25% of the general population. So a positive result proves nothing, but absence of both rules celiac out. The Schulich review states this exact use: TTG and biopsy are unreliable once a patient is gluten-free.

  • Normal villi (A) and normal TTG (C): both are expected on a gluten-free diet, so they cannot exclude the disease.
  • Iron improving with supplements (B): happens in iron deficiency of any cause.
  • Ethnicity (E): a risk association (Northern European descent), not a way to exclude the diagnosis.

gi-w11-module-q46-46.html:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease (the celiac column) and 03 - Diarrhea & Malabsorption. Symptoms that return despite strict adherence after decades of celiac disease are a red flag for a complication. The lecture's celiac complications are malabsorption, other autoimmune disease, osteoporosis and small-bowel adenocarcinoma or lymphoma. Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is the one the pathologist must not miss in these biopsies.

  • Abnormal villous architecture (B): expected in active celiac disease, so it does not explain the change.
  • Neuroendocrine tumour (C): typical of the appendix, not a celiac complication.
  • Leukemic infiltration (D): not linked to celiac disease.
  • Decreased intraepithelial lymphocytes (E): reversed. Celiac disease increases them (T-cell infiltration).

gi-w11-module-q49-49.html:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea. The clues are watery, non-bloody diarrhea lasting six weeks after swimming in a lake, with nausea, weight loss and no fever. That is a non-inflammatory, persistent diarrhea from untreated fresh water, the typical story for Giardia. The lecture lists Giardia and Cryptosporidium among the parasitic causes of watery diarrhea, and its investigation list has a separate test for them: stool ova and parasites (E).

  • Colonoscopy (A): invasive, and not the first test for a probable infection.
  • Stool culture (B): finds bacteria, which cause acute illness lasting days, often inflammatory.
  • Blood culture (C): the lecture orders it only if the patient is febrile.
  • C. difficile test (D): needs its risk factors (antibiotics, hospitalization, PPIs), which he does not have.

gi-w11-module-q7-7.html:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Transmural inflammation and deep fissuring ulcers are the Crohn column of the lecture's comparison, together with skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, cobblestoning and fistulas. Inflammation that goes through the whole wall is what allows fissures to track out as fistulas and strictures.

  • Ulcerative colitis (C): mucosal/submucosal inflammation with superficial ulcers and crypt abscesses. It is continuous from the rectum and has no granulomas.
  • IBS (B): a functional disorder with a normal colon on histology. It would not produce this pathology report.

gi-w11-module-q8-8.html:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Granulomas in active colitis suggest Crohn's disease, since the lecture lists non-caseating granulomas as a Crohn feature and UC has none. But granulomas are not specific to Crohn's: infections, tuberculosis above all, produce them too. The lecture's diagnostic column says to use special stains to rule out infection. The next step is therefore to check that the pathologist did those stains, before labelling the patient with Crohn's and starting immunosuppression that would be dangerous in TB.

  • Dismissing it as transient: wrong. Active colitis with granulomas needs a diagnosis.
  • Diagnosing Crohn's and starting treatment: premature until infection is excluded.
  • Diagnosing UC: granulomas argue against it.
  • Diagnosing TB and referring: jumps to the conclusion that the stains are meant to test.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives A, which in this module's option set reads “tell the patient that active inflammation is usually transient, and they need no further work up or treatment.” 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease contradicts that: it asks for special stains to rule out infection, and it treats granulomas as a Crohn feature. The option the lecture supports is the stray “Check that the pathologist did special stains to rule out infection”, which the bank has attached as a preamble to later questions.

flags.title: The answer options are missing
flags.html: The bank lists no options here. This question's choices (transient inflammation / Crohn's / UC / TB / check special stains) were scattered onto the questions that follow it, so this explanation works from that set.

gi-w11-module-q9-9.html:
From 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Read the stem's own lettering. Continuous distal inflammation belongs to ulcerative colitis: it starts in the rectum and extends proximally without gaps, so it cannot be used to identify Crohn's. That makes A the exception.

  • B. Fissure ulcers: deep fissuring ulcers come from transmural Crohn inflammation. UC's ulcers are superficial.
  • C. Perianal fistula: a Crohn complication, and one of its poor-prognosis markers (perianal disease).
  • D. Skip lesions: the defining Crohn pattern, with diseased segments separated by normal bowel and often rectal sparing.

flags.title: The answer options belong to a different question
flags.html: The stem carries its own options (A. continuous distal inflammation, B. fissure ulcers, C. perianal fistula, D. skip lesions). The listed choices A-D are from the granuloma question (gi-w11-module-q8-8), so the keyed option A reads “inflammation is transient” here. It means A. Continuous distal inflammation.

gi-w11-new-q11-11.html:
From 06 - Constipation. The lecture's red flags that call for colonoscopy in constipation are the CRC flags: hematochezia, anemia, weight loss, age over 50, a sudden change in bowel habits, and a family history of CRC. Fever is not on that list. In an adult it points toward an inflammatory or infectious process (e.g., diverticulitis, where colonoscopy is avoided in the acute phase), not toward occult malignancy.

  • Anemia (A), a sudden change in bowel habits (B), hematochezia (C) and age 50 (E) are all listed flags. The Choosing Wisely note adds the converse: do not scope for constipation under 50 without a family history or alarm features.

Fever does appear as a "systemic" red flag in the pediatric constipation chart. That list is for children.

gi-w11-new-q19-19.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Midgut & Hindgut. In the figure the transverse colon is lifted up and the small bowel has been removed. The labelled vessels are:

  • C. Right colic artery: an SMA branch running to the ascending colon on the right. The label and its pointer match, so this is the correct one.
  • A. "Middle colic": the pointer ends on the highlighted loop that runs along the inner edge of the transverse colon. That loop is the marginal artery (of Drummond), which runs the length of the colon. The middle colic is the SMA branch that heads up into the transverse mesocolon.
  • B. "Intestinal arcades": points at the same marginal loop beside the descending colon. The arcades are the loops in the small-bowel mesentery that feed the vasa recta.
  • D. "Celiac trunk": points at the descending colon wall. The celiac trunk is a foregut vessel above the pancreas not shown here.

flags.title: Diagram read at low resolution
flags.html: The bank's figure is small (about 250 px). The readings of where each pointer ends are my interpretation of it, and they agree with the key's C. If the prose and the image seem to disagree, trust the image.

flags.title: The answer options are missing
flags.html: The bank lists no options for this question. The letters A-D are the labels printed on the figure itself.

gi-w12-module-q11-11.html:
From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. The lecture separates primary hepatic disease from liver involvement in a systemic disorder. Hepatitis E is a hepatotropic virus: it infects the liver directly and is listed with viral hepatitis A-E as a primary cause of a raised ALT. So it is the cause that is not a systemic disease.

  • Celiac disease (A): listed under the gastrointestinal systemic diseases (it also appears among ALT-greater-than-AST causes).
  • Amyloidosis (B): its own systemic category. The liver is infiltrated as part of a multi-organ deposition disease.
  • Sarcoidosis (D): the granulomatous systemic category. It is also an infiltrative cause of a cholestatic pattern.

gi-w12-module-q12-12.html:
From 05 - Acute Hepatitis. Acute hepatitis is a clinical diagnosis that usually resolves spontaneously, so it does not need a biopsy. The lecture still lists when one is indicated: doubt about the diagnosis, when the hepatologist needs information about the severity or stage, and post-transplant (rejection vs infection).

  • A: this is one of the lecture's listed indications, so it is a true statement.
  • B: false. Biopsy patterns are nonspecific; the pathology report reads "possible causes include virus, drug-induced liver injury, and autoimmune hepatitis" (02 - Histology & Pathology).
  • D, E: false. Biopsy is not routine in the acute setting, and alcoholic hepatitis is diagnosed clinically.
  • C: overstated. Biopsy is rarely needed, but "no benefit" contradicts the listed indications.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: 05 - Acute Hepatitis says a biopsy is indicated when the hepatologist needs information about the severity or stage of the hepatitis. That makes A true and C ("no benefit for clinical management") false. The key may mean that biopsy rarely changes management in a self-limiting illness, but as written, A fits the lecture better.

gi-w12-module-q14-14.html:
From Summary Notes - GI (acute hepatitis) and 05 - Acute Hepatitis. Transmission splits the hepatitis viruses into two groups. Hepatitis A (and E) are spread fecal-oral and cause no chronic infection and no cirrhosis. The illness is acute only and self-limiting.

  • Hepatitis B (B) and hepatitis C (C): sexual or bloodborne, and both can become chronic viral hepatitis leading to cirrhosis and HCC. They are listed among the viral causes of chronic hepatitis (more than 6 months).
  • Hepatitis D (D): travels with hepatitis B and is also listed as a chronic viral cause.

gi-w12-module-q17-17.html:
From the hepatobiliary chart in 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Raised ALP plus raised (conjugated) bilirubin is the cholestatic pattern. PBC is lymphocyte-mediated destruction of small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts, which causes intrahepatic cholestasis. The chart gives markedly raised ALP, AMA positivity, pruritus and jaundice.

  • Hepatitis B, C (A, B): hepatocellular injury, so the pattern is ALT > AST (03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes), not an ALP-led rise.
  • Steatosis, steatohepatitis (D, E): NAFLD/NASH is also an ALT > AST, mildly hepatocellular pattern. Bilirubin is usually normal until the disease is advanced.

gi-w12-module-q18-18.html:
From the liver overview chart in 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. The chronic hepatitis cause list ends with "cryptogenic (NASH)". Cirrhosis labelled cryptogenic, with no cause found, is most often burnt-out NASH. As fibrosis advances, the fat that marks NAFLD can disappear. The metabolic syndrome that drives NAFLD/NASH is so common that it is the likeliest hidden cause.

  • Alcohol (A): an identifiable cause, found on history and an AST:ALT ratio over 2.
  • Hemochromatosis (B): found by ferritin and transferrin saturation over 45%, then HFE testing.
  • Viral hepatitis (D): found by serology.
  • Wilson's disease (E): found by low ceruloplasmin and 24-hr urine copper.

Each distractor has a specific test, so it would not stay "cryptogenic".

gi-w12-module-q22-22.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Postprandial RUQ pain radiating to the back, all labs normal (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, lipase, bilirubin, INR), and gallbladder stones with no ductal dilatation: this is biliary colic. After a fatty meal the gallbladder contracts and a stone temporarily blocks the cystic duct. Labs are normal and ultrasound shows only cholelithiasis.

  • Choledocholithiasis (B): a stone in the common bile duct raises ALP, GGT and direct bilirubin, and often dilates the duct.
  • Cholecystitis (C): the cystic duct stays blocked, giving inflammation, a Murphy sign, fever and a thickened wall. The notes put cholecystitis among the causes of elevated enzymes.
  • Pancreatitis (D): needs a raised lipase. Lipase here is 30.

gi-w12-module-q24-24.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 06 - Chronic Liver Failure. Extrahepatic cholestasis means the bile ducts outside the liver are obstructed. The lecture's causes are gallstones (most common), strictures, tumours and congenital anomalies. PBC destroys small and medium bile ducts only inside the liver (the 06 table marks it "ONLY intrahepatic"), so it causes intrahepatic cholestasis.

  • Cholangiocarcinoma (A): an extrahepatic bile duct adenocarcinoma is a tumour obstructing the duct.
  • Pancreatic cancer (B): usually in the head of the pancreas (75%). It compresses the distal CBD and causes painless obstructive jaundice.
  • Choledocholithiasis (C): a stone in the CBD. Gallstones are the most common extrahepatic cause.

gi-w12-module-q25-25.html:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. The lecture summary names the most common causes of acute pancreatitis: gallstones and alcohol, and also post-ERCP. Gallstones lead because they obstruct the pancreatic duct at the ampulla. Alcohol causes spasm or edema of the sphincter of Oddi and injures acinar cells. ERCP carries about a 5% pancreatitis risk.

  • Infection (B, E): viral causes (mumps, EBV, CMV, coxsackie) are on the I GET SMASHED list but are uncommon.
  • Hypercalcemia (C) and scorpion sting (D): real causes from the mnemonic, but rare. Each of these options also drops one of the big two.

gi-w12-module-q26-26.html:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies and the pancreas chart in 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion. Digestive enzymes made by the acinar cells are activated inside the pancreas and destroy it: lipase causes fat necrosis, elastase causes hemorrhage by damaging vessels, and trypsin destroys the parenchyma (it also activates the other zymogens).

  • Duct damage from gallstones (A): stones are a common trigger, but the damage is done by the activated enzymes.
  • Fibrosis (B): a feature of chronic pancreatitis.
  • Vascular thrombosis (C): a complication (portal or splenic vein), not the mechanism.
  • Islets (E): endocrine cells that make hormones, not digestive enzymes.

gi-w12-module-q27-27.html:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Alcohol is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults, at 70% of cases. That is why alcohol and smoking cessation are central to management.

  • Cystic fibrosis (B): the most common cause in children. In adults it is in the small "other" group.
  • Gallstones (C): the leading cause of acute pancreatitis, not chronic.
  • Hereditary causes and malignancy (D, E): in the "other" group (autoimmune, CF, genetics, malignancy, divisum, tropical), which sits behind alcohol (70%) and idiopathic (20%).

gi-w12-module-q33-33.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. The common bile duct and the pancreatic duct join at the ampulla of Vater. The lecture's gallstone complications state it directly: a blockage at the ampulla stops pancreatic juice from leaving the pancreas, which causes acute pancreatitis. Duct obstruction is one of its two key pathogenic factors.

  • Acute cholecystitis (A): needs obstruction of the cystic duct, upstream of the ampulla.
  • Chronic cholecystitis (C): recurrent cystic duct obstruction and gallbladder fibrosis over time.
  • Secondary biliary cirrhosis (D): needs prolonged (more than 6 months) extrahepatic bile obstruction, not an acute pancreatic duct block.

gi-w12-module-q34-34.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 10 - Approach to Jaundice. In biliary atresia the extrahepatic biliary tree is obliterated and bile flow is blocked. Unless the Kasai procedure is done early, the process progresses to cirrhosis. It is the #1 reason children need a liver transplant. That ongoing, fibrosing obstruction is what "progressive fibroinflammatory" describes.

  • Always associated with other anomalies (A): false. The notes split it into a fetal form (20%) and an acquired form (80%), so most cases are isolated.
  • Common in older children (C): false. It shows by 2 weeks to 2 months: conjugated jaundice, pale stools, dark urine.
  • Not time-sensitive (D): the opposite. It needs early intervention. Refer any infant whose jaundice lasts beyond 2 weeks, or whose direct bilirubin is more than 20% of the total.

gi-w12-module-q36-36.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease. Adenocarcinoma of the extrahepatic bile ducts carries a poor prognosis. Most tumours are proximal, where the anatomy is too complex to resect. Risk factors are PSC, choledochal cyst, gallstones, IBD (through PSC) and liver flukes.

  • Klatskin for any location (A): false. The name belongs to a tumour at the hilar bifurcation of the hepatic ducts, not to every biliary cancer.
  • Diffuse involvement of the whole tree (B): false. These are usually localized, typically proximal, masses or strictures.
  • Excellent prognosis (D): the opposite of what the lecture says. The intrahepatic form also presents late and is often unresectable (01 - Approach to Liver Masses).

gi-w12-module-q4-4.html:
From 02 - Histology & Pathology of the Liver and Pancreatobiliary System. Liver failure is recognized when its functions fail. Synthetic failure lowers albumin and clotting factors. Excretory failure raises bilirubin. The lecture names the exception: immunoglobulins are not made by the liver, so liver failure does not lower them. In acute hepatitis they actually rise (05 - Acute Hepatitis).

  • Ascites (A) and low albumin (B): less albumin means lower oncotic pressure, so fluid leaks into the abdomen.
  • Bleeding tendency (D): fewer clotting factors, giving purpura, ecchymoses and a raised INR.
  • Raised bilirubin (E): excretory failure, giving jaundice.

review.t: Histology & Pathology of the Liver and Pancreatobiliary System

gi-w12-module-q40-40.html:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. The statement is false. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a rare cancer that usually presents late, so it is often unresectable and has a poor prognosis. Both halves of the statement are wrong.

  • A tumour in the intrahepatic ducts leaves most of the biliary drainage open, so jaundice is not an early warning. Jaundice comes early when the common duct is blocked (e.g., pancreatic head cancer), and even that is not a good-prognosis sign.
  • The overview chart in 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease agrees: "presents late, poor Px", with risk factors of PSC, ulcerative colitis and liver flukes.

gi-w12-module-q5-5.html:
From 02 - Histology & Pathology and the NAFLD section of the overview chart in 08 - Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Steatosis follows fat or metabolic stress. The lecture lists alcohol, diabetes and obesity for macrovesicular steatosis, with NAFLD/NASH driven by metabolic syndrome. The NAFLD causes include rapid weight loss. Autoimmune hepatitis is an immune attack on hepatocytes (high IgG, ANA, anti-smooth muscle Ab, and a portal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate). It is not a cause of fat accumulation.

  • Alcohol (A): steatosis develops in 90-95% of chronic drinkers.
  • Metabolic syndrome (C) and obesity (D): the core NAFLD drivers.
  • Rapid weight loss (E): named in the NAFLD cause list.

review.t: Histology & Pathology of the Liver and Pancreatobiliary System

gi-w12-module-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Histology & Pathology and 04 - Gallbladder Disease. All three statements are in the lectures:

  • Majority in North America (A): cholesterol stones are about 80% of gallstones and the most common type in the Western world.
  • Women more than men (B): Female is the first of the 5 Fs (female, fat, forty, fertile, flatulent). Estrogen and multiparity raise the risk.
  • Cholesterol supersaturation (C): in North America, gallstones are "most often due to supersaturation of bile with cholesterol".

So D is right and E is wrong. Contrast the pigment stones: black stones form in hemolysis or cirrhosis, brown stones in the ducts with stasis or infection.

gi-w12-module-q7-7.html:
From 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. The lecture names exactly two key pathogenic factors in acute pancreatitis: (1) pancreatic duct obstruction and (2) acinar cell injury. Gallstones act by obstruction, and alcohol by sphincter of Oddi spasm plus direct acinar injury. The pancreas chart gives the same histology: acinar cell injury, duct obstruction and fat necrosis.

  • Fibrosis (B, D): the hallmark of chronic pancreatitis, with fibrous stroma and calcification.
  • Plasma cell infiltration (C, E): points to IgG4-related (autoimmune) disease, a separate entity and a cause of pancreatic masses.

gi-w12-module-q8-8.html:
From 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. In systemic IgG4 disease, IgG4-producing plasma cells infiltrate the gallbladder, biliary tree and pancreas. In the pancreas this is autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP). 09 lists "autoimmune" among the causes of a pancreatic mass and names AIP as a diagnostic pitfall that can mimic cancer.

  • Acute pancreatitis (A): acinar injury with a neutrophilic acute inflammatory reaction, not a plasma-cell mass.
  • Reaction to adenocarcinoma (C): the tumour is the mass. Abundant IgG4 cells point to AIP instead, which is why clinical-pathological correlation matters.
  • Multiple myeloma (D): a clonal marrow plasma cell neoplasm, not IgG4-rich pancreatic infiltrates.
  • Pseudocyst (E): a fluid collection with no epithelial lining, which comes after pancreatitis.

gi-w12-new-q16-16.html:
From the pancreas chart in 04 - Gallbladder Disease and 09 - Pancreatic Diseases & Malignancies. Each option is a treatment line in the lecture, so all of the above is right:

  • Stop alcohol (A): alcohol causes 70% of cases. Alcohol and smoking cessation are "important in management".
  • Treat malabsorption (B): pancreatic enzyme replacement and dietary fat restriction for the steatorrhea.
  • Treat pain (C): avoid alcohol and large meals, then non-narcotics, then narcotics (many patients end up on them), then stent or surgery (Puestow).
  • Replace nutritional deficiencies (D): fat-soluble vitamins and B12 are lost with exocrine failure.

gi-w12-new-q20-20.html:
From 01 - Approach to Liver Masses. The lecture supports the core of this. HCC is the most common primary liver cancer ("C = most Common primary liver tumour" in the ABCs). It is most common in males over 40, and 90% arise in cirrhotic livers (aflatoxin, hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis). That makes B and D true, and D's "aged 40" is the lecture's "over 40".

  • "Used to be called a hepatoma" (A): not stated in the vault notes. It is the older name for the tumour.
  • "#8 cause of death worldwide" (C): not in the notes either. It is the question writer's figure.

Because the key is E, A and C have to be accepted as true for this question.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: Only statements B and D are in the lecture notes. Neither "hepatoma" (A) nor "#8 cause of death worldwide" (C) appears anywhere in the vault. The reasoning for those two is not from the lectures, and the worldwide ranking in particular is an unsourced figure. Verify it before relying on it.

gi-w13-module-q1-1.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease and 03 - Abdominal Masses. Location sorts this. The appendix is on the right: midgut, so pain starts periumbilically and migrates to the RLQ. LLQ pain is the least likely fit.

  • Diverticulitis (B): hindgut. Pain moves from suprapubic to LLQ, and the sigmoid is the typical site. It is rare under 35, but at 41 it is plausible.
  • UTI (C): genitourinary causes are on the lecture's systems list for abdominal pain (04 - Abdominal Pain), and they give suprapubic or lower-quadrant pain on either side.
  • Ruptured ovarian cyst (D): an ovarian cyst is listed under both the RLQ and the LLQ, so it fits a left-sided presentation in a woman.

gi-w13-module-q26-26.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease and 04 - Abdominal Pain. The appendix is midgut, supplied by the SMA. Early, only the visceral peritoneum is inflamed, and visceral pain is felt vague and in the midline, at the dermatome of that gut segment. For the midgut that is the umbilicus. The pain moves to the RLQ later, once the parietal peritoneum (spinal nerves, well localized) is irritated.

  • A, E (hindgut): wrong embryology. Hindgut pain is suprapubic, as in diverticulitis.
  • C: it does not begin in the RLQ.
  • D: the migration is real, but it comes from parietal peritoneal irritation, not midgut visceral innervation.

gi-w13-module-q27-27.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease and 02 - Bowel Obstruction. Competing diagnoses for appendicitis produce the same picture: focal RLQ pain and tenderness with fever. The lecture's appendicitis history screens for Crohn's disease and pregnancy for this reason, and the RLQ list includes ovarian cyst.

  • Inflammatory ileocecitis (B): terminal ileal Crohn's is the classic mimic.
  • Ovarian torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess, ruptured ovarian cyst (A, C, E): right adnexal pathology sits next to the appendix and mimics focal RLQ peritonitis.
  • SBO (D): presents differently. It gives colicky central pain, progressive vomiting, obstipation, central distension and air-fluid levels, not a localized inflammatory RLQ picture.

gi-w13-module-q31-31.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. This patient is stable (normal vitals, controlled pain) and has a large (8 cm) walled-off abscess after a delayed, perforated appendicitis. That picture is managed without operating first: IV antibiotics plus percutaneous IR drainage. The lecture uses the same size logic for diverticular abscess (over 5 cm, drain). Appendicitis is still usually treated with surgery "either acutely or post-recovery", so an interval appendectomy follows. Colonoscopy is advised after non-operative management in anyone over 40.

  • IV antibiotics alone (A): an 8 cm collection will not clear without drainage.
  • Immediate laparoscopic appendectomy (B): operating on an inflamed phlegmon is higher risk. There is no peritonitis or instability forcing surgery now.
  • Oral antibiotics or discharge (D, E): too little for a large abscess.

gi-w13-module-q32-32.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease. A 3 cm abscess is complicated diverticulitis below the drainage threshold. The lecture's rule is: abscess under 5 cm, admit and give IV antibiotics; over 5 cm, drain; perforation or shock, go to the OR. Diverticulitis is usually not treated with surgery, but colonoscopy is indicated in follow-up to exclude colorectal cancer.

  • Interval colectomy (A, B): not routine after one attack. The lecture reserves surgery for patients who are actively deteriorating.
  • No colonoscopy (B, D): skipping it is only acceptable for uncomplicated diverticulitis. An abscess raises the concern for an underlying cancer.
  • Discharge on oral antibiotics (E): that is outpatient management, meant for uncomplicated cases.

gi-w13-module-q34-34.html:
From 02 - Bowel Obstruction. The two sites have different leading causes: SBO #1 = adhesions, and LBO #1 = neoplasm. The large bowel obstruction list is neoplasm, diverticular disease and volvulus. Adhesions cause small bowel obstruction, which is why you check for scars.

  • Diverticular stricture (B): after repeated attacks, the scarred colon presents as an LBO (07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease).
  • Cancer (C): the most common cause of LBO.
  • Volvulus (D): on the LBO list, and a classic closed-loop cause.
  • IBD-related stricture (E): a colonic stricture narrows the lumen the same way a diverticular one does.

gi-w13-module-q35-35.html:
From 07 - Appendicitis and Diverticular Disease and 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Diverticular bleeding is painless and happens without a diverticulitis attack. Bleeding comes from a vessel stretched over a diverticulum (diverticulosis), not from the inflamed, obstructed diverticulum of diverticulitis, which gives pain and fever rather than hemorrhage.

  • Diverticulosis (A): the #1 cause of lower GI bleeding, and it can be massive.
  • Angiodysplasia (B): on the lower GI bleed list.
  • Hemorrhoids (C): on the lower GI bleed list. Internal hemorrhoids bleed painlessly.
  • Post-polypectomy bleeding (D): listed. Ask about any recent polypectomy.

gi-w13-module-q37-37.html:
From 02 - Bowel Obstruction and 08 - Anorectal Disease. To localize a low rectal cancer, you have to see the lumen and measure the lesion from the anal verge.

  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy (A) and colonoscopy (B): visualize, biopsy and give the distance of the lesion.
  • Anoscopy (D): done in clinic with an anoscope (about 10 cm), proctoscope or rectoscope (about 25 cm), which reaches the low rectum. The digital rectal exam also finds a low mass.
  • The 3 views of the abdomen (C): upright abdomen, supine abdomen and upright chest. This x-ray series is for obstruction (air-fluid levels, dilated loops) and perforation (free air). It cannot see or localize a mucosal tumour.

gi-w13-new-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea (with 05 - Pediatric Diarrhea). Dehydration is the main complication of diarrhea, and infants are at higher risk. Rehydration should use a balanced electrolyte solution (ORS). Diarrhea loses water and sodium. Replacing that with plain water dilutes the remaining sodium, causing hyponatremia (the same reason tap-water enemas carry a hyponatremia warning in 06 - Constipation). Plain water also supplies no glucose to a child who is not eating, so hypoglycemia is a risk.

  • Taste preference (A): high-sugar drinks worsen osmotic diarrhea. They are not a reason to avoid water.
  • Dehydration is necessary (C): false. Correcting it is the most important treatment.
  • Nutrients for growth (D): ORS replaces fluid and electrolytes. It is not a nutritional supplement.

gi-wb-gi0-q89.html:
From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Active bleeding is a main indication for endoscopy, not a contraindication. After resuscitation, urgent EGD is "both diagnostic and therapeutic" (epinephrine injection, cautery, hemoclips, variceal banding). In lower GI bleeding, stable patients go on to colonoscopy.

  • Suspected perforation (A): insufflating air through a perforated viscus worsens the leak. Free air is a surgical emergency (04 - Abdominal Pain).
  • Obstruction (B): bowel prep cannot pass, and a distended bowel risks perforation.
  • Fixed or redundant colon (C): the scope cannot be advanced safely, which raises the perforation risk.
  • Recent MI (E): sedation and the procedure put stress on an unstable heart.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The vault notes support D: bleeding is an indication for endoscopy. But no lecture lists the contraindications to endoscopy, so the reasons given for A, B, C and E are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

resp-w6-module-q16-16.html:
From the O2–Hb dissociation curve section of 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. A right shift means ↓ affinity and ↑ unloading, and the lecture lists its causes: ↓ pH (↑ H+), ↑ temperature, ↑ PCO2 and ↑ 2,3-BPG, as in exercising muscle.

  • A (↓ pH) and D (↑ [H+]) are the same change stated two ways: the Bohr effect, so both count.
  • C (↑ 2,3-DPG/BPG) stabilises the tense state and lowers affinity.
  • B (↓ temperature) is on the left-shift list: it raises affinity, like ↑ pH, ↓ PCO2 and ↓ 2,3-BPG.

resp-w6-module-q19-19.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia and the V/Q section of 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. Map each lesion to what it does to ventilation, perfusion or the barrier:

  • A – shunt (ii): a plug completely occluding a mainstem bronchus leaves perfused lung with no ventilation (V/Q = 0). The lecture's partial mucous plugs only lower V/Q; total occlusion is a true shunt that 100% O2 will not correct.
  • B – V/Q mismatch (i): PE leaves lung ventilated but not perfused, i.e. dead space (V/Q → ∞).
  • C – hypoventilation (iii): narcotics suppress respiratory drive; PaCO2 rises and the A–a gradient stays normal.
  • D – diffusion impairment (iv): fibrosis thickens the blood–gas barrier (Fick's law), with ↓ DLCO.

resp-w6-module-q22-22.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia and 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. The shared scenario gives a long-haul flight, a swollen tender right calf, acute chest pain, SpO2 88% with a clear chest X-ray, and an ABG with low PaO2 and PaCO2 (33, from tachypnea). The A–a gradient is about 54, far above normal, so the hypoxemia is lung-driven. PE creates ventilated but unperfused lung (dead space, V/Q mismatch), which widens the gradient and leaves the film clear.

  • A (hypoventilation): would raise PaCO2 and keep the gradient normal; here PaCO2 is low.
  • C (MI): chest pain fits, but not the DVT or the wide gradient on a clear film.
  • D (pneumonia): fills alveoli with exudate, so the CXR would show consolidation.

resp-w6-module-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Both diseases narrow the airway lumen, so both can trap gas: incomplete exhalation raises end-expiratory volume. The lecture singles this out as dynamic hyperinflation, worst when demand rises (exercise), in COPD and asthma alike.

  • A: inflammation is the root cause of obstruction in asthma. COPD's cardinal features are loss of alveolar attachments, mucosal inflammation/fibrosis and mucus hypersecretion.
  • B: ICS are first line for all asthma. In COPD they are added only for persistent symptoms despite bronchodilators, frequent exacerbations, or asthma–COPD overlap.
  • C: variable airflow obstruction defines asthma. COPD limitation is persistent.
  • E: alveolar wall destruction is emphysema (COPD), not asthma.

resp-w6-module-q5-5:
From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. The lecture names the costodiaphragmatic recess the deepest recess of the pleural cavity. It runs down beside the diaphragm to about the 8th–10th rib, and the lungs never fully fill it, even in inspiration. In an upright patient, fluid such as blood falls to the lowest point of the pleural cavity and pools there first. That is also why thoracentesis targets this recess.

  • B (costomediastinal recess): a small anterior space between the costal and mediastinal pleura that the lung edges fill during inspiration. It is neither dependent nor deep when upright.
resp-w6-module-q7-7:
From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. Every intercostal puncture must pass the intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior). The bundle runs in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostals. Keep the needle just above the upper border of the rib below.

  • A (diaphragm): rises on exhalation but sits below the recess floor. It is a hazard only if the needle is placed too low, not one met on every pass.
  • B (internal thoracic vessels): run parasternally on the anterior wall, away from a lateral/posterior tap.
  • D (intercostal muscles): must be traversed and are not what you avoid.
  • E (lungs): never fully occupy the costodiaphragmatic recess, and they withdraw further on exhalation.

resp-w6-module-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia (airway structure). The lecture names the right lung the more common site for inhaled foreign bodies because the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical. It continues almost straight down from the trachea, so an object falling through the carina follows it. The left main bronchus leaves at a sharper angle, since the heart and aortic arch push it laterally, and it is longer and narrower.

  • B, D, F are the right bronchus's three features.
  • A, C, E describe the left main bronchus.

review.t: Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax

resp-w6-module-q9-9:
From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. The diaphragm is the major muscle of inspiration, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). It contracts and descends when the patient inhales. On radiograph 1 the patient's right hemidiaphragm (image left, above the liver) sits far higher than the left despite a full breath in. A paralysed hemidiaphragm cannot descend and is pulled up by negative intrathoracic pressure. Radiograph 2 is the normal comparison, both domes low and level.

  • B (left phrenic lesion): would leave the left dome elevated. Here the left descends normally.

Remember films are read as if facing the patient, so the patient's right is on the viewer's left.
resp-w6-new-q13-13:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Each muscle acts on either the cricothyroid joint (pitch) or the cricoarytenoid joint (opening and closing):

  • A – iv: cricothyroid tilts the cricothyroid joint to lengthen the cords (↑ pitch). It is the only one supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
  • B – v: vocalis/thyroarytenoid shorten the cords (↓ pitch).
  • C – iii: posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally. It is the only abductor.
  • D – ii: lateral cricoarytenoid rotates them medially, a pivot adduction.
  • E – i: interarytenoid slides the arytenoids together, a translational adduction synergistic with D.
  • F – vi: aryepiglottic pulls the epiglottis down to close the inlet in swallowing.

resp-w6-weekly-q4-4.html:
From 04 - Pulmonary Function Testing and the IPF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Work the PFTs in order. The FEV1/FVC is 78%, at least 0.7, so there is no obstruction. TLC is 65%, under 80%, so this is restriction. DLCO is reduced, placing the restriction within the parenchyma. The clinical picture matches the chart's IPF profile: insidious progressive dyspnea at 40–70, a non-productive cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, clubbing, and honeycombing on imaging.

  • B (asthma), C (COPD): obstructive, needing a ratio under 0.7. Asthma is also reversible and COPD needs an exposure.
  • D (pulmonary edema): an airspace/fluid process, without 12 months of fibrosis, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing.
  • E: fails because A fits.

resp-w6-weekly-q5-5.html:
From 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. Inspiration is active. The diaphragm and external intercostals expand the thoracic cavity, making intrapleural pressure more negative (a decrease, from about −5 cm H2O toward −8). The lung expands with it, and alveolar (intrapulmonary) pressure falls to about −1 below atmospheric, so air flows in. Both pressures fall.

  • A: intrapleural pressure does not rise on inspiration. It only approaches atmospheric in forced expiration or pneumothorax.
  • B: both rising describes forced expiration.
  • D: alveolar pressure rises only in expiration, when air is pushed out.

flags.title: Option A looks damaged
flags.html: Option A reads “The pressure decreases and intrapleural pressure increases”. A word, most likely “alveolar”, seems to be missing. Read either way it is still wrong, because intrapleural pressure falls on inspiration.

resp-w6-weekly-q6-6.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum (Cardiology, Week 1). On this lateral film the shaded zone sits directly behind the sternum and in front of the trachea and the heart's posterior border, running from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm. That is the anterior compartment. The vault note defines the anatomical anterior mediastinum as the space between the sternum and the pericardial sac, holding the thymus, fat, lymph nodes and internal thoracic vessels. This is where the anterior-mass differential (thymoma, goiter, lymphoma, teratoma) arises.

  • A (posterior): behind the pericardium, against the vertebral bodies: descending aorta, esophagus, azygos, thoracic duct.
  • C (middle): the pericardial sac and heart.
  • D (anterior chest): the chest wall, not a mediastinal compartment.

flags.title: Radiologic versus anatomical compartments
flags.html: The shading extends back over the cardiac silhouette. On a lateral film, radiologic compartment schemes count that zone as anterior. The vault's anatomical definition places the heart in the middle mediastinum and makes the anterior compartment only a thin retrosternal space. The vault does not describe the radiologic scheme, so treat that part as general principle.

review.t: Anatomy of the Heart and Mediastinum

resp-w7-module-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Alveolar Causes of Dyspnea and 02 - Pneumonia. Fever, purulent sputum and new consolidation arising after 2 weeks of ventilation meet the lecture's definition of hospital-acquired disease: onset 48 h or more after admission or intubation, which here is VAP. The lecture separates nosocomial from community-acquired pneumonia by its Gram-negative organisms: aerobic GNRs such as E. coli and Klebsiella (60%), and Pseudomonas. That flora is more resistant, not less, which is why empiric therapy is broad anti-pseudomonal cover (piperacillin/tazobactam + vancomycin) rather than the CAP macrolide/ceftriaxone.

  • A, C: true, as above.
  • D: true. Hand hygiene and clean respiratory equipment block the transfer of hospital flora into ventilated airways. This is an infection-control principle rather than something the notes spell out.

resp-w7-module-q11-11:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. CFTR sits in GI epithelium, so the lecture's GI list is long:

  • A: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, from ducts blocked by mucus, present from birth in most patients.
  • B: CF-related diabetes, i.e. endocrine insufficiency (25% of children, 50% of adults).
  • C: pancreatitis, from the same ductal obstruction.
  • D: DIOS, the adult meconium-ileus equivalent, with RLQ pain mistaken for appendicitis.
  • E: focal biliary cirrhosis, gallstones and portal hypertension.
  • F: rectal prolapse, from chronic malabsorption and diarrhea.

G is the odd one out. The digit sign in CF is clubbing, which the lecture files under skeletal changes (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy), not GI. “Sausage” swollen digits are dactylitis, a feature of psoriatic arthritis and sickle cell disease.

resp-w7-module-q12-12.html:
From the “Other conditions with a positive sweat test” list in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. A raised sweat chloride is not specific to CF. The lecture lists adrenal insufficiency, anorexia, atopic dermatitis (and ectodermal dysplasia), celiac disease, environmental deprivation/failure to thrive, familial cholestasis, G6PD deficiency, glycogen storage disease, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, nephrogenic DI and Klinefelter syndrome. This is why every positive sweat test must be confirmed with a second test and mutation analysis.

  • A, B, C, E are all on the list. Note that malnutrition states (anorexia, failure to thrive) appear there.
  • D (obesity) does not appear. It is the opposite nutritional state and is not a recognised cause.

resp-w7-module-q13-13.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. The newborn heel-prick measures immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) to find babies at risk, who then need a sweat test. The lecture says false negatives are very uncommon but occur with intestinal obstruction in the newborn, which is meconium ileus. Its advice: any baby with a very distended belly should get a sweat test whatever the screen shows. Meconium ileus is itself a classic CF presentation, so a “normal” screen should never reassure you.

  • A (neonatal stress), B (precipitous delivery): perinatal stress tends to raise IRT, a false-positive direction.
  • D (fecal contamination of the spot): a sample-handling error, not the association the lecture names.

The notes do not discuss A, B or D; that reasoning is general principle.

resp-w7-module-q14-14.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. The lecture lists the organisms that prompt antibiotic treatment in CF: S. aureus, H. influenzae, P. aeruginosa, S. maltophilia and B. cepacia. Only Burkholderia cepacia is flagged as carrying particularly bad outcomes. It is associated with rapid lung-function decline, and its person-to-person spread is why CF camps are no longer recommended.

  • A (S. aureus): the common early coloniser in childhood.
  • B (P. aeruginosa): the dominant chronic pathogen, treated with inhaled tobramycin/aztreonam. It drives gradual decline, not the abrupt kind.
  • C (S. maltophilia): on the treatment list but not singled out for prognosis.

resp-w7-module-q15-15.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. The lecture's newborn plan is nutritional and supportive. Start pancreatic enzymes if the baby is pancreatic insufficient, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) against malabsorption. Follow weight gain closely, with early referral to the multidisciplinary CF team. Airway clearance is real CF care: chest physiotherapy, PEP, hypertonic saline and dornase alfa. Nebulised Purell (hand sanitiser) is not.

  • A, B, C: straight from the lecture.
  • E: part of good care. A new diagnosis is still a new baby, and the family needs support alongside the plan.
  • D: pairs a real therapy (physiotherapy) with a toxic, invented one.

resp-w7-module-q16-16:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis (New Frontiers). The lecture's future therapies build on the CFTR modulators. Potentiators such as ivacaftor treat gating class III/IV defects. Correctors such as tezacaftor and elexacaftor, combined in Trikafta, improve trafficking. The next steps it lists are RNA therapy, gene transfer and gene editing.

  • A (gene therapy), D (gene editing), E (mRNA therapy): named in the lecture.
  • B (better modulators): the natural extension of theratyping, i.e. matching drugs to the mutation class.
  • C: invented. Bleach and UV irradiation do nothing about a defective chloride channel.

resp-w7-module-q17-17.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. On room air, PIO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg. With the lecture's alveolar gas equation, PAO2 = 150 − PaCO2/0.8 = 150 − 60/0.8 = 150 − 75 = 75, so the A–a gradient = 75 − 65 = 10. The Schulich shortcut, PaCO2 × 1.25, gives the same 10. Ten is not offered. 13 (B) is the nearest option and is what the full alveolar gas equation gives, since its extra FiO2 term makes the CO2 factor about 1.2: 150 − 60 × 1.2 ≈ 78, and 78 − 65 ≈ 13. Either way the gradient is normal (under age/4 + 4). With a PaCO2 of 60, this is pure hypoventilation.

  • A, C, D: too high for any version of the equation.
  • E (4): too low.

flags.title: The lecture's formula gives 10, not 13
flags.html: 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia teaches PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/0.8, which gives an A–a gradient of 10, and 10 is not an option. The keyed 13 matches the full alveolar gas equation (CO2 factor of about 1.2). Pick the closest option and know which formula produced it.

resp-w7-module-q18-18.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The lecture sorts hypoxemia by A–a gradient. A normal gradient means too little O2 reached the alveoli: ↓ PIO2/FiO2 (altitude) or hypoventilation. Transfer from alveolus to blood is intact, so PAO2 and PaO2 fall together. An increased gradient means O2 failed to cross.

  • B (V/Q mismatch): increased gradient; the most common cause of hypoxemia.
  • C (R→L shunt): increased gradient, and it does not correct with 100% O2.
  • E (diffusion abnormality): increased gradient, as in fibrosis/ILD, often unmasked by exercise.
  • A (hyperventilation): not a cause of hypoxemia. It lowers PaCO2 and raises PAO2.

flags.title: Check option A's wording
flags.html: As printed, option A is “hyperventilation”, which is not a mechanism of hypoxemia, so D is the only answer. If the original read “hypo­ventilation”, A would also have a normal A–a gradient, per 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia, and the question would have two correct answers.

resp-w7-module-q4-4:
From 04 - Pulmonary Function Testing. Fibrosis shrinks and stiffens the lung, giving the lecture's restrictive pattern: TLC < 80%. Because the restriction is parenchymal, DLCO is reduced; that is how it is told apart from extraparenchymal restriction, where DLCO is normal.

  • A (↓ FEV1/FVC): the obstructive signature. In restriction FEV1 and FVC fall together, so the ratio is normal or even increased.
  • B (↑ RV): gas trapping, as in obstruction. The lecture says RV is not raised in restriction.
  • D (↓ FEF 25–75%): mid-expiratory flow reflects small-airway obstruction, which fibrosis does not cause.
  • E (↑ DLCO): the opposite. A thickened barrier lowers diffusion.

resp-w7-module-q6-6.html:
From the Canadian Thoracic Society control table in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Asthma is controlled only when every criterion is met: daytime symptoms < 4 days/week, night symptoms < 1 night/week, normal activity, mild infrequent exacerbations, no absence from school, and reliever use < 4 doses/week.

  • Child A: 1–2 mild exacerbations a year counts as mild and infrequent, so controlled.
  • Child B: symptoms and Ventolin 2–3 times a week, under 4 on both counts, so controlled.
  • Child C: waking about one night a week. The threshold is fewer than one, so uncontrolled.
  • Child D: daily reliever before activity means 7 doses a week, so uncontrolled.

So C and D. F fails because A and B meet the criteria.

resp-w7-module-q9-9.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF mutation-class panel of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. The chart states it outright: not much working CFTR is needed to prevent CF complications. That is why milder mutations with some residual function spare the pancreas, and why modulators that restore even partial function help. E is the false statement.

  • A: true. CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel, a salt channel.
  • B: true. The lecture lists wound healing among CFTR's other functions.
  • C: true. It acts as a tumour suppressor; CF carries ↑ adenocarcinoma risk.
  • D: true in the lecture's sense. CFTR is in all epithelial cells: lung, pancreas, sweat glands, liver, gut, testes, brain.

resp-w7-new-q15-15.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Check each statement against the notes:

  • A: both notes place the CFTR gene on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q), not the short arm. As written, A is false.
  • B: true. ΔF508, a 3-base-pair deletion that loses phenylalanine 508, is the commonest mutation (70–80%).
  • C: true. The chart gives about 2000 known mutations.
  • D: true in substance. CFTR normally secretes Cl− in the airway and gut, and the defective channel cannot.

On the notes, B, C and D are true and A is false, so “all of the above” cannot stand.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: Option A puts the CF gene on the short arm of chromosome 7. Both 07 - Cystic Fibrosis and the CF column of 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease put it on the long arm (7q). That makes A false and “All of the above” (E) indefensible. Either A was mistranscribed (“long” to “short”) or the key is wrong. No other option works on its own, since B, C and D are each true.

resp-w7-new-q4-4.html:
From the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology (Week 7), which carries the acute rhinosinusitis column that 09 - Acute Rhinosinusitis lacks. The chart lists the referral red flags for ABRS as systemic toxicity, altered mental status, severe headache, and orbital swelling or reduced visual acuity. They signal spread beyond the sinus: orbital cellulitis, or intracranial extension such as meningitis, abscess or cavernous sinus thrombosis. Otherwise the default is watchful waiting for 7–10 days with INCS and saline.

  • A, B, C are each on the list.
  • D (A and C): leaves out altered mental status.
  • E: the only complete answer.

resp-w7-weekly-q8-8:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The lecture's mechanisms of hypoxemia are ↓ PIO2/FiO2 (altitude), hypoventilation (both normal A–a gradient), shunt, V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation (all increased gradient).

  • A, B, C, D: each is on that list.
  • E (acidosis): a disturbance of pH, not of oxygen transfer. Acidosis actually shifts the O2–Hb curve right, helping O2 unload to tissue. It can accompany hypoxemia (lactic acidosis from hypoxia, respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation) but does not cause it.

resp-w8-module-q12-12.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology. Most nosebleeds, about 90%, are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area of the anterior septum. There the anterior ethmoid, superior labial, sphenopalatine and greater palatine branches anastomose under thin mucosa, exposed to drying air and fingers. These are the bleeds seen in younger patients, controlled with pressure and cautery.

  • B (posterior septum): Woodruff's plexus, sphenopalatine territory. Less common, but more severe, and seen in older and hypertensive patients.
  • A (cribriform plate), D (olfactory mucosa): the olfactory roof of the cavity, not a vascular watershed prone to bleeding.

resp-w8-module-q13-13.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and the Rhinology chart in 07 - Radiology. The notes group epistaxis causes as local and systemic. Local causes are trauma, including nasal fracture and nose picking, plus foreign body, tumour, drugs such as cocaine, inflammation and dryness. Systemic causes are coagulopathy, hypertension, atherosclerosis, HHT and GPA.

  • B (nasal trauma), C (cocaine): local.
  • D (coagulopathy), E (atherosclerosis): systemic. Stiff, fragile vessels bleed more and stop less, which is part of why posterior bleeds cluster in the elderly.
  • A (low birth weight): appears in neither list and has no mechanism linking it to nasal bleeding.

resp-w8-module-q15-15.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. After ABCs, reversing coagulopathy, 10–15 minutes of firm anterior pressure and unilateral silver-nitrate cautery, the next step is packing, whether nasal tampon or ribbon gauze. The notes do not discuss bilateral packing. The logic is mechanical: the septum is thin and mobile, and a pack on the bleeding side alone can push it across without compressing the vessel. Packing the other side as well gives counter-pressure, clamping the septal bleeding point between two packs. So the statement is true: sometimes needed, not routine.

  • B (false): would mean one pack always suffices, which fails when the septum deviates away from it.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

resp-w8-module-q4-4:
From 01 - Hemoptysis. The lecture gives bronchoscopy several jobs in hemoptysis:

  • A: direct visualisation localises the bleeding site, the first goal in hemoptysis.
  • B: washings/BAL can be cultured, separating infectious causes (bronchitis, pneumonia, TB, aspergillus) from others.
  • C: serial BAL identifies diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. The return gets more bloody with each washout, the opposite of pneumonia.
  • D: it allows site-directed treatment, such as argon plasma coagulation of a bleeding tumour, and guides next steps (embolisation, surgery).

Each is a real role, so E. CT gives anatomy and arteriography can embolise; neither offers all four.

resp-w8-new-q1-1.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Posterior bleeds arise at Woodruff's plexus, where the sphenopalatine artery (maxillary artery, external carotid) enters the posterior nasal cavity. They drip down the throat, are rarely traumatic, are worse than anterior bleeds and cluster in elderly hypertensive patients. When packing fails, the surgical fix is sphenopalatine artery ligation.

  • B (facial artery): reaches the nose through the superior labial branch at the anterior septum (Kiesselbach's).
  • C (anterior ethmoid): supplies the anterior-superior cavity and also feeds Kiesselbach's. It is an internal-carotid branch, so IR must not embolise it.
  • D (ophthalmic artery): the parent of both ethmoid arteries, supplying the roof rather than the posterior cavity.

review.t: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System

resp-w8-new-q2-2.html:
From In Class - Epistaxis and the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. Most bleeds are anterior, from Kiesselbach's plexus, and the lecture's first-aid step is to pinch the soft ala firmly for 10–15 minutes, head tipped forward to protect the airway. After ABCs and reversing coagulopathy, this is the first treatment on the ladder, and it stops most low-volume bleeds on its own.

  • B (cautery): step 4, for a visible vessel that keeps bleeding after pressure. It is unilateral silver nitrate.
  • A (packing): step 5, when pressure and cautery fail.
  • E (tranexamic acid): a topical hemostatic at step 6, used alongside packing.
  • C (embolization): the last step, for refractory bleeding. The note adds that it needs active bleeding to work.

resp-w8-new-q3-3.html:
From the epistaxis chart and stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. When bleeding continues despite packing, the surgical step is to ligate the anterior ethmoid and sphenopalatine arteries. Those two cover the internal- and external-carotid supply to the nose, so E is appropriate for severe bleeding.

  • A: interventional radiology embolizes external carotid branches, not the anterior ethmoid. That is an internal carotid (ophthalmic) branch, so embolizing it risks the eye and brain.
  • B: the plan specifies unilateral silver nitrate cautery. Cauterizing both sides of the thin septum risks a septal perforation (general principle; the notes only say unilateral).
  • C: posterior packs are rare, used mostly in elderly patients, and are not left unmonitored. The notes do not spell this out; it follows from the airway risk.
  • D: juvenile nasal angiofibroma is highly vascular. The chart says do NOT biopsy because of the risk of hemorrhage.

resp-w8-new-q4-4.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis, with 02 - Pneumonia. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most likely to cavitate. As a systemic disease it brings extrapulmonary features: the history asks about bleeding from the nose, ears and urinary tract. D is true.

  • A: the lecture's main cause of cavitary disease is tuberculosis, then fungi (Aspergillus in immunocompromised patients) and vasculitis. The Pneumonia note also lists anaerobic and pyogenic bacteria and NTM. "Fungal or non-tuberculosis" leaves out the most common cause.
  • B: cavities belong to secondary (reactivation) TB at the apices. Primary TB gives a nonspecific lower-lobe infiltrate and hilar nodes.
  • C: this is backwards. In diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (capillaritis), serial lavage gets more bloody with each wash. Returns that clear point towards pneumonia.

resp-w8-new-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis, with the bronchiectasis column in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation after repeated infection or inflammation. Its causes include diffuse ones (CF, primary ciliary dyskinesia) and focal ones (an obstructing foreign body or tumour). The exam finding is localized crackles and the CXR findings are nonspecific, so "only diffuse" is false.

  • A (true): bronchitis is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after other infectious, parenchymal and alveolar causes are ruled out. The CXR is usually normal.
  • B (true): bleeding comes from damage to inflamed airways. Capillary leakage is more likely on blood thinners or with a smoking history.
  • C (true): repeated insults destroy the bronchial walls. This is why bronchiectasis is the most common cause of rapid, life-threatening hemoptysis.

resp-w8-new-q6-6.html:
