From the epistaxis chart in 07 - Radiology, and In Class - Epistaxis. The chart splits causes into local (trauma, foreign body, tumour, cocaine, inflammation, barometric change, nasal dryness) and systemic (coagulopathy, hypertension, atherosclerosis, HHT, GPA). Barometric pressure changes act on the nasal mucosa itself, so D is the local cause and is not systemic.

  • A (hypertension): systemic. The in-class note lists essential hypertension and targets it in outpatient care.
  • B (coagulopathy): systemic. Reversing it is step 2 of management.
  • C (HHT): systemic. It is autosomal dominant, with malformed vessels in the nose and lungs.
  • E: fails because D is a local cause.

resp-w8-new-q7-7.html:
From the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology and In Class - Epistaxis. Epistaxis treatment is pressure, cautery, packing, hemostatics, then surgery or IR. Nasal irrigation is not on that ladder. Saline irrigation is a treatment for acute and chronic rhinosinusitis, and outpatient epistaxis advice is humidity and moisture, not flushing. Irrigation would also dislodge the clot you are trying to keep.

  • B and C (tampon, packing): the same step. The note calls a nasal pack "basically a tampon for the nasal cavity"; ribbon gauze and posterior packs are the alternatives.
  • D (tranexamic acid): a topical hemostatic, step 6.
  • E (pressure): first-line. Pinch the ala for 10–15 minutes, leaning forward.

resp-w8-new-q8-8.html:
From 04 - Approach to Pulmonary Nodules and Masses. Small nodules carry a significantly lower risk of malignancy. The chart calls solitary nodules under 7 mm likely benign: under 6 mm and low-risk needs no follow-up, while ≥ 8 mm gets CT at 3 months, PET/CT or sampling. So C is true. (The note's "< 8cm" in the PET paragraph is a typo for mm.)

  • A: solitary nodules are typically asymptomatic and found incidentally.
  • B: multiple nodules have a broad benign differential (histoplasmosis, TB, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, pneumoconiosis). When malignant, they usually mean metastasis.
  • D: the aim is the opposite. Pick one biopsy site that gives stage and diagnosis in a single procedure.
  • E: M0 means no distant metastasis; M1 indicates metastasis.

resp-w6-module-q1-1.html:
From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. COPD therapy is built on bronchodilation to reduce hyperinflation. The chart's treatment ladder runs from smoking cessation to LABA / LAMA (then dual bronchodilators), then ICS, then O2. If a patient is still breathless on an as-needed short-acting agent, the next step is a long-acting bronchodilator.

  • A (ICS): reserved for moderate–severe disease with persistent symptoms despite optimal bronchodilators, frequent exacerbations, or asthma-COPD overlap.
  • B (oxygen): for hypoxemia (target 88–92%), not for breathlessness alone.
  • C (LTRA): an asthma and allergic-rhinitis drug, not part of the COPD algorithm.
  • E (pulmonary rehab): the notes do not cover it. It is an adjunct and does not replace the missing maintenance bronchodilator.

resp-w6-module-q18-18.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. A low PAO2 triggers hypoxic arterial vasoconstriction. The pulmonary arterioles feeding poorly ventilated alveoli constrict, diverting blood to alveoli that can oxygenate it and restoring V/Q matching. 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology gives the same reflex in bronchospasm: vessels to underventilated regions constrict and vessels to well-ventilated regions dilate. The cost is that widespread or chronic hypoxia constricts the whole bed, which leads to pulmonary hypertension.

  • A: dilation is the systemic vascular response to hypoxia, the opposite of the lung's.
  • B and D: the response is arterial (pre-capillary), where flow is controlled, not venous.

resp-w6-module-q2-2.html:
From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. Inflammation is the root of airflow obstruction in asthma, so an inhaled corticosteroid is first-line controller therapy. The lecture says all patients, from mild to severe, should be on some form of ICS. She has night-time symptoms and persistent obstruction on a SABA alone, which is uncontrolled asthma by CTS criteria, so she needs an ICS added. The SABA stays as her reliever.

  • B and E: never LABA without an ICS. LABA monotherapy increases asthma-related deaths; a LABA is added to an ICS.
  • C: an LTRA is an add-on, a later step after ICS, not the first controller.
  • D: stopping the SABA removes her rescue inhaler for acute symptoms.

resp-w6-module-q21-21.html:
From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. Work through the alveolar gas equation on room air:

  • PIO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) = 150 mm Hg.
  • PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/0.8 = 150 − 33/0.8 = 150 − 41 = about 108–109 mm Hg.
  • A–a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 = 108.5 − 55 = about 53–54 mm Hg.

A normal gradient is age/4 + 4, roughly 10–20 in an adult, so this one is markedly raised. The hypoxemia therefore comes from the lung (shunt, V/Q mismatch or diffusion), not from hypoventilation or low inspired O2. The low PaCO2 reflects tachypnea. With a clear film after a long flight and a swollen calf, this is the pattern of pulmonary embolism (next question).

resp-w6-module-q3-3.html:
From 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 07 - Respiratory Pharmacology. ICS in COPD are indicated for moderate–severe disease with persistent symptoms, or for frequent exacerbations. The pharmacology lecture lists reducing the frequency and severity of exacerbations as a benefit of ICS. So D is true.

  • A: smoking causes over 90% of COPD but not all of it. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, pollution (indoor cooking) and immature lung development are also causes.
  • B: the lecture credits smoking cessation with improving survival. Bronchodilators reduce hyperinflation and symptoms, and no therapy repairs destroyed lung.
  • C: lung function does not normalize once COPD develops. Fixed obstruction, unlike asthma's variable obstruction, is what defines it.
  • E: LTRAs are asthma drugs. COPD escalates to triple therapy (LAMA + LABA + ICS).

resp-w6-module-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax. Fluid pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess, which reaches down to the 8th–10th rib and which the lung never fully fills. You want a site below the lung but above the diaphragm, so in the mid-axillary line (the stem's "mid-axial") that means a low interspace, the 9th. Expiration is the safer phase because the lung withdraws upward out of the recesses. In inspiration it expands down into them, bringing the lung into the needle's path.

  • A and B (5th space): too high. The needle would enter aerated lung rather than the dependent fluid, risking pneumothorax.
  • D: the right level, but at the wrong phase of breathing.

Pass the needle over the top of the rib, because the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the lower border.

resp-w6-weekly-q10-10.html:
From 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation and 01 - Histology of the Lungs and Airway. Surfactant has four listed functions: it lowers surface tension, raises compliance, reduces alveolar edema and aids O2 diffusion. High surface tension would draw fluid from the capillaries into the alveoli, and surfactant opposes that. Without it, as in infant respiratory distress syndrome, the alveoli flood and collapse. So E is true.

  • A: surfactant decreases surface tension (Laplace), keeping small alveoli from collapsing.
  • B: it is secreted by type 2 pneumocytes. Type 1 cells form the thin gas-exchange surface.
  • C: the lecture describes it as a lipid film at the air-liquid interface. It is mainly phospholipid, not simply a protein.
  • D: by raising compliance it decreases the work of expanding the lung.

review.t: Histology of the Lungs and Airway

resp-w6-weekly-q2-2.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System, 02 - Anatomy of the Lungs and Thorax and 01 - Histology. Air passes from the pharynx through the laryngeal inlet into the larynx and "then down into the trachea". The trachea descends from the larynx and bifurcates into the primary and then lobar bronchi. The bronchi branch into bronchioles (terminal, then respiratory) and end in the acinus. So the order is pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles.

  • A: puts the trachea above the larynx.
  • B: puts the larynx above the pharynx and the bronchioles before the bronchi.
  • C: starts at the trachea, below both the pharynx and the larynx.

resp-w7-module-q10-10.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. Thick, inspissated mucus obstructs the small airways. The lecture's list of lower-tract consequences includes atelectasis, emphysema, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, cavitary lesions, respiratory failure and right heart failure / cor pulmonale. Atherosclerosis is a systemic arterial disease and appears nowhere on that list, so E is not a CF lung finding.

  • A (atelectasis): distal to mucus plugs.
  • B (bronchiectasis): from repeated infection, as the bronchial cartilage breaks down.
  • C (abscess): biofilm infection (S. aureus, Pseudomonas) leads to cavitation.
  • D (pulmonary artery hypertrophy): chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction produces pulmonary hypertension and remodelling. That is the path to cor pulmonale.

resp-w7-module-q19-19.html:
From 04 - Blood Gases Interpretation and 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The pH of 7.32 is acidemia, and a PaCO2 of 50 explains it, so this is a primary respiratory acidosis. Is it acute? The rule for acute respiratory acidosis is HCO3 up 1 per 10 rise in PaCO2, so expect about 25. The measured 24 means the kidneys have not compensated yet (that takes about 24 hours). The pH fits too: a fall of about 0.08 for a 10 mm Hg rise. The A–a gradient is 150 − 50/0.8 = 87.5, minus 79, giving about 8, which is normal. That is pure hypoventilation: barbiturates cause CNS depression.

  • B, D, E: a metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3. Here it is normal.
  • C: chronic compensation (HCO3 up 3 per 10) would give about 27 and a nearly normal pH.

resp-w7-module-q2-2.html:
From 02 - Pneumonia. The lecture states that typical and atypical pneumonia are hard to tell apart clinically, so empiric therapy covers both. It is therefore not a criterion for triage. Patients are sorted by setting and severity: outpatient with or without comorbidities, inpatient non-severe, or severe (ICU). CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index are used to decide hospital versus outpatient care.

  • B (severity): separates non-severe from severe/ICU regimens.
  • C (need for hospitalization): the outpatient-versus-inpatient split that CURB-65/PSI decide.
  • D (advanced disease) and E (comorbidities): underlying illness such as COPD, diabetes, malignancy or immunosuppression moves an outpatient from a macrolide/doxycycline to a fluoroquinolone or combination regimen.

resp-w7-module-q20-20.html:
From 04 - Blood Gases Interpretation and 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The pH is 7.22 with a PaCO2 of 60 and a normal HCO3 of 25, so this is an acute, uncompensated respiratory acidosis. Next, the A–a gradient: PAO2 = 150 − 60/0.8 = 75, and 75 − 68 gives about 7, which is normal for age 34 (age/4 + 4, about 12). Hypoxemia with a normal gradient and a high PaCO2 is hypoventilation. The lecture's listed causes start with CNS depression, and in an unconscious patient that points to drug overdose.

  • A, B, C (ARDS, lobar pneumonia, pulmonary edema): shunt or V/Q mismatch widens the gradient, and early on these patients hyperventilate, which lowers PaCO2.
  • E (low FiO2): the gradient is normal, but hypoxia drives ventilation up, so PaCO2 falls (the altitude pattern is respiratory alkalosis).

resp-w7-module-q3-3.html:
From 04 - Pulmonary Function Testing, 03 - Lung Physiology and 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia. The PFT lecture lists early interstitial lung disease as a cause of an isolated DLCO drop, before there is enough fibrosis to cause restriction. The fall in DLCO is therefore early, not "only in very late stages", which makes E the false statement.

  • A: true. Parenchymal restriction is marked by a reduced DLCO, which is what separates it from extraparenchymal restriction.
  • C: true. By Fick's law, a thickened barrier slows diffusion; fibrosis is the example the lecture gives.
  • D: true. Scarring also destroys capillaries, which reduces the surface area and blood volume available to take up CO. The notes imply this rather than stating it.
  • B: true. At high flow during exercise, transfer becomes diffusion-limited. The lecture pairs ILD with hypoxemia on exercise; a scarred bed cannot recruit capillaries, so DLCO rises less than normal.

resp-w7-module-q5-5.html:
From 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. IPF presents with progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles (almost always) and clubbing. Spirometry is restrictive with a reduced DLCO, and the CXR shows lines and nodules, mostly subpleural. Copious purulent sputum is a feature of an airway and infection disease such as bronchiectasis or CF, not of a fibrosing interstitium. B is the exception.

  • A: exertional dyspnea is the headline symptom, because the stiff lung cannot meet demand.
  • C: the thickened blood-gas barrier lowers DLCO.
  • D: bibasilar "velcro" crackles.
  • E: the reticular or nodular subpleural opacities described in the note.

resp-w7-module-q7-7.html:
From the Asthma Predictive Index in 08 - Pediatric Asthma and 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease. The modified API predicts who will keep wheezing into school age. It requires frequent wheezing plus 1 major criterion (a parent with asthma, the child's own atopic dermatitis, or aeroallergen sensitization) or 2 minor criteria (wheezing apart from colds, eosinophilia ≥ 4%, or milk/egg/peanut sensitization).

  • Child B: egg allergy plus wheezing outside viral illness makes 2 minor criteria, so the index is positive.
  • Child A: peanut allergy is 1 minor criterion. The father's eczema does not count, because only parental asthma or the child's own dermatitis is a major criterion.
  • Child C: milk allergy is 1 minor criterion, and maternal allergic rhinitis is not a criterion.

That makes D and E wrong as well.

resp-w7-module-q8-8.html:
From 07 - Cystic Fibrosis. CF is autosomal recessive. The mother has CF, so she carries two mutant alleles and every child receives one mutant allele from her. The carrier partner passes his mutant allele half the time. The child is therefore affected (two mutant alleles) with probability 50% and a carrier otherwise.

  • A (25%): the risk when both parents are carriers, which is the figure the lecture gives.
  • C and D: would need the partner to pass the mutant allele more often than half the time, or to be affected himself (100%).
  • E: the lecture says women with CF have impaired fertility from thick, hostile cervical mucus, but are "not necessarily infertile". It is men who almost always lack a vas deferens.

resp-w7-new-q11-11.html:
From the restrictive-disease chart in 06 - Obstructive Lung Disease and 05 - Interstitial Causes of Dyspnea. The prognosis row for IPF reads: rapid progression, mean survival 4–5 years, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale. All three follow one chain. Fibrosis thickens the barrier and stiffens the lung, and gas exchange fails. Chronic hypoxia constricts the pulmonary arterioles and the scarring destroys the capillary bed, producing pulmonary hypertension. The right ventricle then fails against that pressure, which is cor pulmonale. So E.

  • D (A and B): leaves out cor pulmonale, the end of the same chain.
  • A, B, C alone: each is true but incomplete.

resp-w7-new-q7-7.html:
Partly from the larynx section of Summary Notes - Anatomy. The anatomy notes cover the structure: the vocal ligament is covered by mucosa to form the vocal folds, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts them, and the cricothyroid tenses them to raise pitch. Voice needs three things together:

  • A: the folds approximate (adduct) so that they close the glottis.
  • B: an expiratory airflow builds subglottic pressure beneath the closed folds.
  • C: that airflow sets the mucosal free edge passively vibrating. No muscle contracts for each cycle.

Remove any one and voice fails: open folds give a breathy voice, too little airflow gives no sound, and stiff scarred mucosa gives hoarseness. That makes E the answer. "Forced" overstates B, since conversational speech needs a controlled expiratory stream, not a forced one.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The anatomy notes cover vocal-fold structure and adduction, but no lecture note covers the airflow and mucosal-vibration mechanism of phonation; that part is reasoned from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

resp-w7-weekly-q9-9.html:
From 04 - Blood Gases Interpretation. Hypoventilation raises PaCO2, which lowers pH. The kidneys compensate by retaining HCO3 (1 per 10 mm Hg acutely, 3 per 10 chronically), so HCO3 rises. That gives up PaCO2, up HCO3 and down pH, which is A. The body never overcompensates, so pH stays below normal.

  • B (down PaCO2, down HCO3, down pH): metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing).
  • C (up PaCO2, up HCO3, up pH): metabolic alkalosis, compensated by hypoventilation.
  • D: wrong, because A is correct.

resp-w8-module-q14-14.html:
From the stepwise plan in 07 - Radiology. The ladder specifies unilateral silver nitrate cautery, applied outside in. The septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and is fed by the mucoperichondrium on both sides. Cauterizing opposite points at once can devascularize the cartilage between them and cause a septal perforation. So the statement is false: treat the bleeding side, and if the other side needs it, come back later. The perforation mechanism comes from general principles; the notes only give the unilateral rule.

  • A (true): contradicts the "unilateral" instruction in the management plan.

resp-w8-module-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis and 02 - Pneumonia. Mycoplasma is an atypical organism. It causes an interstitial pneumonia with patchy inflammation of the alveolar walls, an insidious onset and a non-productive cough. It does not destroy parenchyma, so it does not form necrotizing or cavitating lesions.

  • A (M. tuberculosis): the most common cause of cavitary lung disease. It bleeds through capillary leak or erosion into a pulmonary artery (Rasmussen aneurysm).
  • C (Klebsiella): listed among lung-abscess pathogens and in alcohol-associated pneumonia.
  • D (S. aureus): the first-listed abscess pathogen. MRSA is also flagged in abscess plus pneumonia.

resp-w8-module-q3-3.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis. Autoimmune lung disease has several radiographic faces, and the lecture describes each option:

  • A (whiteout): diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from pulmonary capillaritis (e.g. in vasculitis) can look like a complete whiteout and can be life-threatening.
  • B (pneumonia features): alveolar hemorrhage fills airspaces like an infection. The lecture separates the two by serial lavage: returns get more bloody with DAH and clear with pneumonia.
  • C (cavitary disease): granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most often causing cavitary lung disease.

Each is a real presentation, so D. The treatment is steroids for the autoimmune cause, not antibiotics.

resp-w8-module-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis. Massive hemoptysis, a quick bleed of around 100 mL per hour, is an airway emergency. Management starts with ABCs: protect the airway (intubation, an endobronchial blocker), lie the patient on the bleeding side, reverse anticoagulants and consider tranexamic acid. That care belongs in an ICU, not an outpatient clinic. CT is useful, since it localizes the bleed and guides the radiologist, but it is done urgently while the patient is in hospital, never booked as an outpatient scan. So D is the answer.

  • A (ICU): needed for airway protection and resuscitation.
  • B (bronchial artery embolization): arteriography localizes the bleed and treats it by embolization.
  • C (surgical resection): the last resort, for example in tumour or vasculitis.

resp-w8-weekly-q4-4.html:
From 01 - Hemoptysis. Autoimmune lung disease has several radiographic faces, and the lecture describes each option:

  • A (whiteout): diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from pulmonary capillaritis (e.g. in vasculitis) can look like a complete whiteout and can be life-threatening.
  • B (pneumonia features): alveolar hemorrhage fills airspaces like an infection. The lecture separates the two by serial lavage: returns get more bloody with DAH and clear with pneumonia.
  • C (cavitary disease): granulomatosis with polyangiitis is the vasculitis most often causing cavitary lung disease.

Each is a real presentation, so D. The treatment is steroids for the autoimmune cause, not antibiotics.

gu-w14-new-q11-11:
From 13 - IV Fluids. The lecture's own (non-exhaustive) list of indications names every option: ECF hypovolemia (restore hemodynamics and tissue perfusion), ICF hypovolemia (free water to re-expand shrunken cells), replacing deficits and ongoing losses, nutrition in certain instances, and correcting electrolyte and acid-base disturbances.

  • E (A, B and D) is the trap: it leaves out nutrition, which the lecture lists as a valid (if less common) reason.
  • Each of A to D alone is true but incomplete, so F is the only full answer.
gu-w14-new-q22-22:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 30% of the remaining filtered NaCl through the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, and it is impermeable to water, which is how it dilutes the filtrate and builds the hypertonic medulla.

  • A: true; NKCC moves Na, K and Cl in, and the K back-leak drives paracellular Ca and Mg reabsorption.
  • B: true; water-impermeable.
  • C: true ("look" is a typo for loop); furosemide blocks NKCC.
  • D: false; the distal tubule's transporter is the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter, not NKCC.

So E.
gu-wb-gu0-q22:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion and 12 - Potassium Handling by the Kidney. Net K+ secretion happens in the cortical collecting duct, by the principal cells: Na+ enters through ENaC, leaving the lumen negative, which pulls K+ out into the urine. The lecture puts 90-95% of the body's ability to excrete K+ here, and aldosterone turns it up.

  • PCT: bulk reabsorption of Na, water, glucose and HCO3, not K+ secretion.
  • Descending limb: water-permeable, little solute transport.
  • DCT: Na-Cl cotransport and active Ca reabsorption.
  • Medullary collecting duct: the lectures place K+ regulation in the cortical segment.

gu-wb-gu0-q23.html:
From 12 - Potassium Handling by the Kidney. Alkalosis moves K+ into cells: the lecture lists metabolic alkalosis among the causes of shift into cells (a small effect), and the opposite of metabolic acidosis, which is listed under shift out of cells.

  • Digoxin overdose, beta blockers and lack of insulin (undiagnosed type 1 diabetes) are each named under "shift out of cells (or lack of cellular uptake)".
  • Hyperosmolarity is not in the lecture note. By general principle, water leaving cells raises intracellular K+ and drags it out with it (solvent drag), which is why hyperglycemia itself raises serum K+.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The hyperosmolarity distractor is not covered by the lecture note; its rationale is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-wb-gu0-q27:
From 13 - IV Fluids. The lecture sorts IV fluids by what is dissolved in the water. Crystalloids are water with electrolytes and/or glucose; colloids are water with albumin, plasma or large carbohydrates (starches, dextran), which stay in the plasma and pull fluid in from the interstitium.

  • 5% albumin is a colloid, so it is the odd one out.
  • D5W (dextrose in water, effectively free water), normal saline, 3% hypertonic saline and Ringer's lactate are all crystalloids, differing only in their salt and glucose content.

gu-wb-gu0-q85.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The lecture places the apertures as: vena caval foramen at T8 (IVC, right phrenic nerve), esophageal hiatus at T10 (esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks), and aortic hiatus at T12 (aorta, thoracic duct, azygos). Its mnemonic "I ate (8) ten (10) eggs at twelve (12)" reads IVC 8, Esophagus 10, Aorta 12.

The stem asks in the order esophagus, IVC, aorta, which gives T10, T8, T12: option B.

  • A lists the levels in mnemonic order (IVC first), not in the stem's order.
  • C and D misplace the aorta or all three.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives A (T8, T10, T12), but the stem lists the structures as esophagus, IVC, aorta. 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum puts the esophagus at T10 and the IVC at T8, so the answer in the stem's order is B (T10, T8, T12). The key's own mnemonic supports B.

reviews-gu-Q2:
From 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs 100% of filtered glucose (and amino acids), coupled to Na+ entry through Na-glucose cotransporters on its brush border. That is why SGLT2 inhibitors act here, and why Fanconi syndrome, a PCT defect, shows up as glucosuria.

  • Descending limb: water-permeable, almost no solute transport.
  • Ascending limb: NaCl via NKCC, no glucose.
  • DCT: Na-Cl cotransport and Ca reabsorption.
  • Collecting duct: Na via ENaC, K+/H+ secretion and ADH-regulated water; by then no glucose is left to reclaim.
reviews-gu-Q5:
From 08 - Diuretics and 02 - Nephrolithiasis. Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the DCT; Na+ can then enter only through the Na-Ca exchanger, so Ca2+ reabsorption rises and urinary Ca falls. The lecture calls this what makes thiazides a treatment for calcium stones with hypercalciuria.

  • A (loop diuretic): loops increase urinary Ca by abolishing the positive lumen charge that drives paracellular Ca reabsorption, which worsens stones.
  • C: stopping diuretics does nothing for the hypercalciuria.
  • D: potassium-sparing agents act on the collecting duct and have no stated calcium effect.
  • E: the Nephrolithiasis note says low calcium intake predisposes to stones; keep intake normal.
reviews-gu-Q6:
From 08 - Diuretics and 06 - Reabsorption and Secretion. Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC on principal cells of the collecting duct. With less Na+ entering, the lumen stays less negative, so K+ is not pulled into the urine: modest natriuresis with K+ retention. Spironolactone reaches the same channel indirectly, by blocking aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor.

  • A is the loop diuretic target (NKCC, thick ascending limb).
  • B is the thiazide target (NCC, DCT).
  • D and E describe what increases K+ secretion (aldosterone up-regulates ENaC and Na/K ATPase), the opposite of sparing potassium.
reviews-gu-Q7:
From 11 - Acid Base Disturbances. pH 7.29 is acidemia, and the HCO3 is low (14), so the primary process is metabolic acidosis. Check compensation with the lecture's 1:1 rule for metabolic acidosis: HCO3 has fallen 10 (24 to 14), so pCO2 should fall about 10 (40 to 30). It is 30, so the respiratory response is appropriate and no second disorder is needed.

  • Respiratory acidosis needs a high pCO2; here it is low.
  • Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis and mixed alkalosis need a pH above 7.45. The low pCO2 is compensation, not a primary alkalosis.

gu-w15-module-q12-12.html:
From Summary Notes - Anatomy (phrenic nerve) and 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration, driven by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). On inspiration both domes should descend. In this film the right hemidiaphragm sits markedly higher than the left even at full inhalation. The anatomy summary gives exactly this sign of phrenic nerve injury: permanent elevation and paradoxical movement of the paralysed hemidiaphragm on chest x-ray.

  • Left: the left dome is low and flat, as expected on inspiration.
  • Normal: the right dome is normally only slightly higher (liver), not this far.

gu-w15-module-q13-13.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The psoas major lies retroperitoneally, directly behind a retrocecal appendix, and is the main hip flexor. The lecture explains a positive psoas sign as inflammation reaching the fascia of the psoas major. Resisted flexion (active contraction) or hip extension (passive stretch) then moves the inflamed fascia and causes pain.

  • A: the mesoappendix is not attached to the thigh, so extending the hip does not stretch it; the pain comes from the muscle's own sheath.
  • C: hip extension lengthens the psoas rather than squeezing the abdominal contents, so it does not compress the appendix.

gu-w15-module-q14-14:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Kidneys, Ureters, & Adrenal Glands and 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. This is nutcracker syndrome. The left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta but behind the SMA, where it can be compressed. Everything that drains into it backs up: the left testicular (gonadal) vein (hence the varicocele) and the left suprarenal vein, both of which the lectures say drain into the left renal vein rather than the IVC. The duodenum (third part) passes through the same aorta-SMA angle and can be compressed too (general anatomy; the notes do not describe this relation).

  • Left renal, suprarenal and testicular arteries branch from the aorta (or renal artery) and are not trapped in the angle. The findings (varicocele, hematuria) are venous congestion.

gu-w15-new-q11-11.html:
From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease and 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The CKD lecture gives the indications for dialysis as AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia) or encephalopathy, "itis" (uremic pericarditis), Overload, Uremia. In CKD the decline is slow, and hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume are usually managed medically for a long time. What eventually forces dialysis is the uremic syndrome: anorexia, nausea, progressive malnutrition and cognitive change. The RRT lecture lists these as the elective indications.

  • Refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume overload are urgent indications, more typical of AKI.
  • Pericarditis is urgent but uncommon.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The notes list the AEIOU indications but never rank them, so "most common" is reasoned from general principles, not from a lecture. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w15-new-q14-14.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum and Summary Notes - Anatomy (duodenum). The lecture's GI retroperitoneal list is the duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, descending colon and rectum. The sigmoid colon is not on it: it hangs on its own mesentery (the sigmoid mesocolon) and is intraperitoneal.

  • A (2/3 of the duodenum): the anatomy summary makes parts 2-4 of the duodenum retroperitoneal; only the first (superior) part is intraperitoneal.
  • B, C, D are on the retroperitoneal list directly.

gu-w15-new-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum. The lecture's three apertures and their contents: the caval opening (T8) carries the IVC and the right phrenic nerve; the esophageal hiatus (T10) carries the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks; the aortic hiatus (T12) carries the aorta, the thoracic duct and the azygos system ("I ate 10 eggs at 12").

  • A and B swap the contents: the vagal trunks go with the esophagus, the right phrenic nerve with the IVC.
  • C is the only correct pairing.

gu-w15-new-q18-18:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. BUN depends on how much urea is made and how much is reabsorbed, not just on GFR. The lecture's BUN:Cr table puts GI bleeding (a protein load digested from blood) and heart failure (hypoperfusion; a sodium-avid kidney reabsorbs urea with Na) in the high-ratio, pre-renal row.

  • Corticosteroids are not in the table. They raise BUN by increasing protein catabolism, the same mechanism as a high protein load.
  • Protein malnutrition and cirrhosis sit in the low-ratio row: less protein or less hepatic urea synthesis means a lower BUN.
gu-wb-gu0-q94:
From 03 - Hematuria and Proteinuria and 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. Nephritic syndrome is glomerular inflammation: hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, a modest amount of proteinuria, oliguria, and fluid retention with hypertension and edema. Hyperlipidemia belongs to nephrotic syndrome: the liver over-produces lipoproteins as it tries to replace the albumin lost in massive proteinuria.

  • B, E: the lecture's markers of glomerular hematuria (RBC casts; 70% or more dysmorphic RBCs).
  • C: proteinuria is present but below the nephrotic range.
  • D: hypertension from salt and water retention.

gu-w16-meds2024-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis. Each hip bone (os coxae) is three fused bones: the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. The two hip bones meet anteriorly at the pubic symphysis and join the sacrum posteriorly; with the coccyx they make up the bony pelvis.

  • Femur, tibia: bones of the lower limb, not the pelvis.
  • Ileum (with an e) is the small bowel; ilium (with an i) is the bone, a classic spelling trap.
  • Symphysis is the joint between the two pubic bones, not a bone.
  • Coccyx is part of the pelvis but not of the hip bone.

gu-w16-module-q10-10.html:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. Step one in managing stage 1 pediatric hypertension is to rule out white coat hypertension. Home readings in children are error-prone (wrong cuff, poor technique), so the lecture calls 24-hour ABPM the better, more accurate method.

  • B: the lecture does not discuss cost. In general, ABPM is thought to save money, because it spares children with white coat hypertension from work-up and treatment they do not need.
  • C: the secondary-cause work-up (CKD, renal artery stenosis, thyroid) is step two, once hypertension is confirmed as real.
  • D: the lecture lists white coat hypertension under "when NOT to treat".

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The lecture does not discuss the cost of ABPM, so the rationale for rejecting B is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w16-module-q11-11:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture's stage 2 sequence is: 1. clinical evaluation, 2. medication, 3. rule out a secondary cause. It stresses: do NOT wait for repeat readings at later encounters. At the same visit, decide whether this is hypertensive urgency (asymptomatic) or emergency (seizure, encephalopathy, heart failure, AKI), because that sets how fast and by what route BP is lowered.

  • B: ABPM is the first step for stage 1, to rule out white coat hypertension.
  • C: the secondary work-up is step 3.
  • D: non-pharmacological treatment with outpatient referral is the stage 1 approach, too slow for stage 2.

gu-w16-module-q12-12.html: From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture's approach to renal edema rests on three renal causes, each with a lab signature. AKI raises creatinine and BUN (edema always follows the rise). Nephritic syndrome means hematuria. Nephrotic syndrome means massive proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia. So A, B and C all hold. D is the false one because of "all" and "mild". Hematuria is the defining nephritic feature, but the degree of proteinuria varies: it can be absent, and some nephritic lesions (e.g. membranoproliferative GN) can reach nephrotic range.

flags.title: The lecture lists mild proteinuria as a nephritic feature
flags.html: 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology lists "small amounts of proteinuria" among nephritic features, so D reads close to the lecture. It is false only because of the absolute "all", and that reasoning comes from general principles.

gu-w16-module-q13-13.html:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture treats MCD and FSGS with the same steroid protocol: prednisone 2 mg/kg/day (60 mg/m2/day) for 4-12 weeks. Both are usually steroid-sensitive, which is why steroids are started without a biopsy.

  • A: the majority is MCD (80-90%), with FSGS second. Membranous is a cause in adults.
  • C: not in the lecture. In general, a first episode gets a longer course than a relapse, which is treated only until remission and then tapered.
  • D: the most common approach is steroids without a biopsy.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The lecture does not compare steroid duration for a first episode against a relapse, so the rationale for rejecting C is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w16-module-q14-14.html:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture's treatment ladder: steroids first; for the 10-15% who are steroid-resistant, cyclosporine (so A is correct). For frequently relapsing/steroid-dependent disease it lists several options: cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, rituximab or cyclosporine. Cyclosporine is one choice among these, not the first line, so D is the incorrect statement.

  • B, C: not stated in the note. In general, steroid resistance and onset before age 1 both make MCD unlikely (FSGS, congenital or genetic nephrotic syndrome), so a biopsy is done before treatment.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The biopsy indications in B and C are not in the lecture note, so their reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

gu-w16-module-q2-2.html:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. The lecture comes back to one point: scrotal ultrasound is very helpful in sorting out a scrotal mass (hydrocele, hematocele, torsion versus epididymo-orchitis, tumour) and directing the next step.

  • A is garbled ("on a hernia ... but not a hernia"). The lecture's sign is that you can get above a hydrocele but not above an indirect inguinal hernia.
  • B: varicoceles are typically left-sided; a right-sided one should prompt imaging of the retroperitoneum.
  • E: the lecture separates hernia from hydrocele by getting above it, not by reducibility (a communicating hydrocele can also empty).
  • C: see the flag.

flags.title: Option A is damaged
flags.html: Option A says "on a hernia ... but not a hernia", so one of the two words was transcribed wrongly. As written it cannot be assessed.

flags.title: C may also be true
flags.html: The varicocele-infertility link is well established and is a standard indication for repairing a varicocele. The lecture note does not mention it, so this rests on general knowledge. If the question is single-best-answer, D is the lecture's emphasis, but C is not clearly false.

gu-w16-module-q36-36.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis. Visceral pain afferents travel back along autonomic nerves, and the pelvic pain line (the inferior limit of the peritoneum) decides which ones. Structures above it (ureter, superior bladder) send pain with the sympathetics to T11-L2, which is the stone's loin-to-groin pain. The urethra lies below the line, so its afferents run with the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4). Pain is then referred to the S2-S4 dermatomes: perineum and back of the thigh.

  • C describes the ureteric phase, not the urethra.
  • A and D mismatch the pathway and the spinal level: parasympathetics are sacral, sympathetics thoracolumbar.

gu-w16-module-q4-4:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture separates pre-renal from intrinsic renal AKI at the bedside. Pre-renal means hypovolemia, with urine that is appropriate for it. Renal AKI means edema (fluid overload), so edema is the feature that does not fit.

  • A: preceding diarrhea is the classic route to volume depletion.
  • B: dehydration on exam defines pre-renal.
  • C, D: high urine osmolality and low urine sodium show intact tubules conserving water and Na+.

Management follows the distinction: fluids for pre-renal, fluid restriction for renal.

gu-w16-module-q5-5.html:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. HUS is a hemolytic anemia. The lecture lists schistocytes, raised LDH, bilirubin and reticulocytes, and low haptoglobin. Red cells are sheared in thrombosed small vessels; they are not under-produced for lack of iron. So C is false.

  • A, E: HUS is a common cause of AKI in children, typically after E. coli infection with diarrhea.
  • B: thrombocytopenia is the lecture's "evidence of systemic thrombi".
  • D: true. HUS injures the kidney directly (thrombotic microangiopathy), so it is intrinsic renal, not pre-renal, AKI.

flags.title: Options A and E are damaged
flags.html: Options A and E begin "coli ..."; the "E." of E. coli was lost in transcription, probably read as an option letter.

gu-w16-module-q6-6.html:
From 12 - Potassium Handling by the Kidney. Hyperkalemia treatment runs in the lecture's four steps: confirm, stabilize, shift, eliminate. Potassium-binding resins (sodium polystyrene/Kayexalate, patiromer, zirconium cyclosilicate) eliminate K+ by binding it in the gut, so C is correct.

  • A: calcium gluconate "doesn't do anything to the potassium level". It stabilizes the myocardial membrane, and shifts no K+.
  • B: insulin-dextrose shifts K+ into cells. The cardioprotective drug is calcium.
  • D: the dangers the lecture names are arrhythmia and neuromuscular dysfunction (weakness), not seizures.

gu-w16-module-q7-7:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. Under the 2017 AAP guidelines, children 13 years and older use fixed adult-style cut-offs instead of percentiles: normal <120/<80, elevated 120-129/<80, stage 1 hypertension 130-139/80-89, stage 2 140/90 or more. A 15-year-old is hypertensive at 130/80 or above.

  • B is the stage 2 threshold, not the definition of hypertension.
  • C, D: percentile definitions apply to ages 1-13 (the 90th percentile is only "elevated").
  • E: pediatric BP percentiles are indexed to height, age and sex, never weight.
gu-w16-module-q8-8:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. Pediatric BP thresholds are based on auscultation, and oscillometric readings can differ by 5-10 mmHg. So an elevated oscillometric reading is confirmed by auscultation, not the other way round. D reverses the rule, so it is the incorrect statement.

  • A: if BP is at or above the 90th percentile, re-measure twice at the same visit.
  • B: confirm on separate encounters (three in all, at least 1-2 weeks apart) before diagnosing.
  • C: the cuff is chosen by mid-arm circumference, not age, weight or sex.
gu-w16-module-q82-82:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. On contrast CT the kidneys enhance brightly. The mass here (in the right kidney, on the left of the image) is a solid, heterogeneous, space-occupying lesion that takes up contrast and distorts the renal contour. The lecture: the majority of solid enhancing masses are renal cell carcinoma, and any solid mass warrants urology referral.

  • B: a fatty angiomyolipoma would show fat attenuation (dark, like the surrounding retroperitoneal fat), which this lesion does not.
  • C: a complex cyst is fluid with septae or calcifications, not a solid enhancing mass.
  • D: the right kidney is visibly abnormal compared with the left.
gu-w16-module-q83-83:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. Nephron-sparing surgery (partial nephrectomy, ablation) is for smaller masses, and whenever kidney tissue is precious. The lecture names a solitary kidney, multifocal bilateral tumours, pre-existing CKD, and conditions that predispose to CKD such as diabetes or hypertension. That covers A, B and D (a 2 cm tumour in a hypertensive man).

  • C: a large tumour with renal vein invasion and IVC thrombus is locally advanced disease. The lecture reserves radical nephrectomy for larger tumours or suspected locally advanced disease, so partial resection is not an option.
gu-w16-module-q84-84:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. The lecture says a renal mass biopsy is not always necessary. Consider it only if it will change management, or when a history of another cancer makes you want to confirm where the tumour came from. Most solid enhancing masses are RCC and go to surgery or surveillance either way. The diagnostic yield is only 80-90%, so a biopsy that would not change the plan adds risk without benefit.

  • A, B: blanket rules in either direction ignore that biopsy is case-specific.
  • D is a joke distractor.
gu-w16-module-q86-86:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. Subtype matters because behaviour and prognosis differ. The lecture singles out collecting duct carcinoma as very rare and very aggressive, and type 2 papillary RCC (in HLRCC) as more aggressive than type 1. It also notes that late metastases depend on the primary's driver mutations. Subtype also points to hereditary syndromes (clear cell with VHL, chromophobe with Birt-Hogg-Dube), which changes counselling and surveillance for the family.

  • B, C, D are joke distractors.
gu-w16-module-q87-87:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. Multifocal, bilateral tumours are the lecture's clue to a hereditary syndrome, and each syndrome has its own histology. Hereditary papillary renal cancer syndrome (MET gene) gives type 1 papillary RCC.

  • A: von Hippel-Lindau gives clear cell RCC.
  • B: Birt-Hogg-Dube gives chromophobe RCC and oncocytoma.
  • C: succinate dehydrogenase (SDHB) deficiency is not in the lecture; in general it causes its own SDH-deficient RCC, not type 1 papillary.

(HLRCC, the fourth syndrome in the lecture, gives the more aggressive type 2 papillary.)

gu-w16-module-q88-88.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. The lecture says only that von Hippel-Lindau raises the risk of clear cell RCC, with increased angiogenesis, and that hereditary syndromes give multifocal, bilateral tumours. Beyond that, VHL is a multisystem tumour syndrome: CNS and retinal hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, and pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumours, as well as renal cysts and RCC.

  • A: the kidney is only one of many organs.
  • C: it affects both sexes equally.
  • D: it is autosomal dominant (a germline hit in the VHL tumour suppressor, then a second somatic hit).

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The lecture note covers VHL only as a clear cell RCC risk. Multiorgan involvement and autosomal dominant inheritance are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

gu-w16-module-q89-89:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. A paraneoplastic syndrome is a systemic effect of a hormone or protein the tumour makes. For RCC the lecture lists hypercalcemia (PTH-related peptide, or lytic bone metastases), SIADH with hyponatremia, erythropoietin with polycythemia, and thrombocytosis. It adds that paraneoplastic syndromes are common in metastatic disease.

  • C (hematuria): a local sign of the tumour itself, not a remote hormonal effect.
  • A (headache) and D (alopecia) are not RCC paraneoplastic syndromes.
gu-w16-module-q9-9:
From 08 - Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology. The lecture's list of when not to treat hypertension includes white coat hypertension: BP raised in clinic only, confirmed by 24-hour ABPM. Persistent clinic readings do not change that; the ambulatory numbers decide.

  • A: repeating twice at one encounter screens the reading; the diagnosis needs 3 separate encounters, at least 1 week apart.
  • B: kidney disease is a secondary etiology, and a diagnosed secondary cause is an indication for medication, not a lifestyle-only trial.
  • C: step 2 of stage 1 management is checking target-organ damage, i.e. left ventricular hypertrophy.
gu-w16-module-q93-93:
From 07 - Urothelial Cancer. The lecture stresses a wide spectrum of biological behaviour: from low-risk superficial tumours followed by cystoscopy, to high-grade invasive disease needing cystectomy. Presentation varies too (hematuria, an incidental mass, clots, UTI, metastases), so "uniform and predictable" is false.

  • B: true; low-grade tumours can recur every few months, and frequent recurrence defines the medium-risk group.
  • C: true; the lecture warns against treating hematuria repeatedly as UTI with antibiotics.
  • D: true; the field effect is why upper-tract disease gets the whole kidney and ureter removed.
  • E: true; medium-risk disease gets prophylactic intravesical BCG.
gu-wb-gu0-q116:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A varicocele is a dilated network of gonadal veins, the pampiniform plexus, from back-flow (raised abdominal pressure or defective gonadal vein valves). It feels like a "bag of worms".

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q117:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A hematocele is blood between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, almost always after trauma, and may involve testicular rupture; scrotal ultrasound confirms it and rules rupture out. The contrast to learn is with a hydrocele: the same space, filled with fluid rather than blood, and it transilluminates.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q118:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. In testicular torsion the gubernaculum fails to anchor the testis, which lies horizontally and can swing and twist on its cord. It presents as sudden severe pain in adolescents and young adults, with a rock-hard testis (arterial inflow, no venous outflow), and needs surgery within 6-8 hours.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q119:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. An adult hydrocele is fluid in the enclosed space lined by the tunica vaginalis (in infants it is usually a hernia sac communicating with the peritoneum). It transilluminates, and you can get "above" it on pinching the top of the scrotum, which a hernia does not allow. Blood in the same space would be a hematocele.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q120:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. A spermatocele is a multilocular, semen-filled sac from a seminal fluid leak off the epididymis. It feels like a "third testicle" and is seldom symptomatic unless large.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q121:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. Orchitis is infection of the testis, and the lecture presents it with the epididymis as epididymo-orchitis. Unlike torsion, the pain is usually gradual, Doppler shows blood flow, and there are signs of infection (fever, raised WBC). It is treated with antibiotics, not surgery.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-wb-gu0-q123:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses. In an indirect inguinal hernia bowel protrudes through the inguinal canal and can reach the scrotum, where it mimics a hydrocele. Pinch the top of the scrotum: you cannot get above a hernia, but you can get above a hydrocele.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.
gu-w17-module-q10-10:
From 02 - Nephrolithiasis. The lecture's secondary-cause table lists malabsorption (IBD, short bowel) causing hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones: unabsorbed fat binds gut calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed. The other secondary causes are hypercalcemia, medullary sponge kidney/RTA, and drugs (topiramate, indinavir).

  • A: it is hypercalcemia (e.g. hyperparathyroidism) that causes stones.
  • B: potassium citrate is a treatment; citrate inhibits stones.
  • C and E: not on the list. Pancreatitis would count only through the fat malabsorption that D already names.
gu-w17-module-q11-11:
From 02 - Nephrolithiasis. Low calcium intake is a risk factor: dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut, so cutting dairy leaves more free oxalate to be absorbed. The lecture's review point is to keep calcium intake normal, and the vault's calcium oxalate note prefers low-fat dairy.

  • A: more fluid means more dilute urine.
  • B: salt drives urinary calcium excretion.
  • D: high protein intake is a risk factor (it raises urinary uric acid and calcium).
  • E: less oxalate means less to precipitate with calcium.

gu-w17-module-q12-12.html:
From 02 - Nephrolithiasis. Uric acid stones form because of low urine pH, often with normal serum and urine uric acid; about 80% of patients are not hyperuricosuric. Uric acid cannot precipitate above pH 6.5, so alkalinizing the urine with potassium citrate (or sodium bicarbonate) is the core treatment.

  • D: allopurinol helps only the ~20% with raised urinary uric acid.
  • A: thiazides treat hypercalciuria in calcium stones.
  • C: a low oxalate diet targets calcium oxalate stones.
  • E: not a uric acid measure; the option text looks truncated.

flags.title: Option E looks damaged
flags.html: Option E reads "Daily intake with meals", which names no substance. It was probably something like "calcium intake with meals" (a calcium oxalate measure). Check it against the source module.

gu-w17-module-q15-15:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. Stage 5 CKD is GFR <15, so a GFR of 15 is a staging threshold, not a reason to dialyse. The lecture's GFR indication is <5 mL/min, and it is only an elective one.

  • A, B: nausea and anorexia (with progressive malnutrition) are elective indications.
  • C, E: pericarditis and uncontrollable hyperkalemia are urgent indications, alongside seizures, coma, confusion, severe neuropathy, acidosis and fluid overload.
gu-w17-module-q16-16:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The lecture ranks vascular access with the surgically created AV fistula as optimal. It is the patient's own vessels, so it has the fewest infections and clots.

  • A, E: the lecture's defining problem of the AV graft is increased thrombosis, not infection.
  • B: a permcath is a tunnelled line into the internal jugular. Catheters carry the highest infection risk, so a permcath is not ideal for anyone who can have a fistula.
  • C: infection is mainly a catheter complication.
gu-w17-module-q17-17:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The lecture lists five hemodialysis complications: infection (worst with catheters), cardiovascular disease (the #1 cause of death on dialysis), thrombosis of the access, fluid overload and electrolyte problems, and bone disease (vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate). Liver disease is not among them.

  • A, B, C, E: all on the lecture's list.
gu-w17-module-q18-18:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The lecture lists four peritoneal dialysis complications: peritonitis, catheter infection (which may force a switch to hemodialysis), domestic stress (the cycler alarming at night), and cardiovascular disease. Inflammatory bowel disease is not one of them.

  • A-D: all on the lecture's list. Domestic stress is the one most often missed, since it is a home-based therapy.
gu-w17-module-q19-19:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. A pre-emptive transplant is done before the patient ever starts dialysis. It gives better survival and fewer complications, so it is preferred where possible.

  • A: reversed; transplant is the optimal RRT, with better survival and quality of life.
  • B: the lecture does not rank donor types, but living donation is what makes pre-emptive transplant possible, and in general living-donor grafts do better.
  • C: many dialysis patients are unsuitable because of comorbidity and frailty.
  • E: most living donors are related, but unrelated donation is accepted. The ethical problem the lecture names is paid donation.
gu-w17-module-q3-3:
From 01 - Incontinence & Voiding Dysfunction. Voiding symptoms mean trouble getting urine out, remembered as WISHED: weak stream, intermittency, straining, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, double-voiding. Storage symptoms mean trouble holding urine.

  • A, B, D: frequency, incontinence and nocturia are all storage symptoms, along with urgency. They point to the bladder rather than the outlet.

Hesitancy points instead to outlet dysfunction, such as BPH or a urethral stricture in men, or prolapse in women.
gu-w17-new-q10-10:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. The AV fistula is the optimal access. A permcath is simply a tunnelled line into the internal jugular, and catheters carry the highest infection risk, so ease of set-up does not make it optimal.

  • A: true; pericarditis and uncontrollable fluid overload are urgent indications.
  • B: true; anorexia and GFR <5 mL/min are elective indications.
  • D: true; with a machine, training and tested home water, patients can dialyse at home.
gu-w17-new-q11-11:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. As with hemodialysis, most patients on peritoneal dialysis eventually die of cardiovascular disease. That is the sense in which it is the "main" complication: peritonitis is the commoner acute one.

  • A: PD is less expensive than hemodialysis and home-based.
  • B: the filter is the patient's own peritoneum, not skin. Hypertonic glucose dialysate draws fluid across it by osmosis.
  • C: it increases patient autonomy.

gu-wb-gu0-q29.html: From 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. True. The lecture ranks the major causes of CKD as #1 diabetes (diabetic nephropathy), #2 essential hypertension, #3 glomerulonephritis, with polycystic kidney disease the commonest genetic cause of ESRD. The Renal Replacement Therapies lecture adds that rising type 2 diabetes is driving the growth in chronic dialysis. The statement concerns chronic renal failure. For acute kidney injury the commonest renal cause is tubular injury (ATN), not diabetes.

gu-w15-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - Diabetic Nephropathy and 05 - Chronic Kidney Disease. The lipid target is LDL <2, so an LDL of 4 is not a goal; it is hyperlipidemia left untreated.

  • A: 130/80 is the BP target in diabetic patients (<140/80 in non-diabetics), usually with an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • B: protein restriction is advised only for those already on a high-protein diet. High protein dilates the afferent arteriole and raises glomerular pressure.
  • D: tight glycemic control, HbA1c <7%.

gu-w15-new-q19-19.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. The lecture's contraindications include a solitary kidney (a bleed could cost the only kidney) and end-stage renal disease (small scarred kidneys; the diagnosis no longer changes management). The others on the list are an uncooperative patient, coagulopathy, severe uncontrolled hypertension, severe anemia, cystic kidney, hydronephrosis, acute pyelonephritis, renal artery aneurysms and suspected cancer.

  • B: a transplanted kidney is not a contraindication. In general it is biopsied routinely to diagnose rejection, even though it is a single kidney.
  • D: hyperkalemia is not on the list.

gu-wb-gu0-q106.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. The lecture says WBCs in the urine should make you think of UTI first, especially with bacteria on microscopy; interstitial nephritis is the other cause. What separates the two is whether the WBCs are free or packed into casts.

  • A: glomerulonephritis gives RBC casts.
  • B: hyaline casts are the nonspecific, possibly normal finding.
  • C: ATN gives muddy brown granular casts.
  • E: AIN needs WBC casts, not free WBCs.

gu-wb-gu0-q107.html:
From 02 - Measurement of Renal Function. A cast forms in the tubule, from Tamm-Horsfall protein precipitating in the distal tubule and collecting duct. WBCs wrapped in that protein therefore localize the inflammation to the kidney itself, and the lecture links WBC casts to interstitial nephritis. The AKI lecture pairs sterile pyuria and WBC casts with drug-induced AIN.

  • D: a lower UTI gives free WBCs and bacteria, not casts.
  • A: RBC casts; C: muddy brown casts; B: hyaline casts.

gu-wb-gu0-q109.html:
From 04 - Acute Kidney Injury. Muddy brown granular casts are made of sloughed, necrotic tubular epithelium, and the lecture ties them to ATN, the commonest renal cause of AKI (ischemic or nephrotoxic). They contrast with the hyaline casts and low FENa of pre-renal AKI.

  • A: glomerulonephritis gives RBC casts.
  • B: hyaline casts are the nonspecific finding.
  • D: UTI gives free WBCs and bacteria.
  • E: AIN gives WBC casts.

gu-w16-module-q3-3.html:
From 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses (its embedded testicular cancer note). That note says trauma is NOT a predisposing factor; it only prompts men to examine themselves and find a mass. The risk factors are cryptorchidism, atrophic or dysgenetic testes, and prior contralateral cancer. So D is the incorrect statement.

  • E: true. The lecture's key message is that prognosis is good even with metastases, because the tumour is very sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation.
  • A: true; peak age is 13-35.
  • B: true; diagnosis is delayed by 4-6 months on average, since the mass is usually painless.
  • C: true; testes drain to lumbar and preaortic nodes (Anatomy of the Pelvis).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives E, but 05 - Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses states that prognosis is "usually quite good - even with metastatic disease", which is option E almost word for word. The testicular cancer note it embeds says trauma is NOT a predisposing factor, which makes D the incorrect statement. The answer the material supports is D.

gu-w16-module-q79-79.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. The lecture's renal mass history asks about prior cancer and family history, smoking, occupational carcinogens, and comorbidities such as obesity and hypertension. Hereditary syndromes (von Hippel-Lindau, HPRC, HLRCC, Birt-Hogg-Dube) carry a high risk of renal cancer, and a known carrier is a reason to refer.

  • B: sunlight is a skin cancer risk.
  • C, D: vaccination and work in education carry no carcinogen exposure.

gu-w16-module-q80-80.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. The lecture's summary: CT (or MRI) is required to fully characterize a renal mass, unless ultrasound has already shown a simple cyst. Contrast CT shows shape, density, exophytic growth and enhancement of 20 HU or more. Measurement of Renal Function adds that CT is very good at characterizing kidney cancers.

  • A: creatinine measures function, not the mass.
  • B: urine cytology screens for urothelial malignancy.
  • C: cystoscopy looks inside the bladder and is considered only for gross hematuria.

gu-w16-module-q81-81.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. Simple renal cysts are round and smooth-bordered, with no nodularity or solid elements. They are very common (40-60% of adults) and rarely cause problems, and the lecture is explicit that no further testing is needed. This incidental 2 cm simple cyst therefore calls for reassurance only.

  • A: refer only a mass that is not a simple cyst or a dromedary hump.
  • B: CT is needed only when ultrasound has not shown a simple cyst. Septae, calcification, irregular borders or enhancement would change that.
  • D: a simple cyst needs no surveillance.

gu-w16-module-q85-85.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses and the vault's renal cell carcinoma note. RCC arises from the renal tubule. Its most common subtype, clear cell, and type 1 papillary both arise from the proximal convoluted tubule; chromophobe comes from the distal tubule. The lecture adds that most solid enhancing renal masses are RCC.

  • A: the glomerulus gives glomerular disease, not RCC.
  • C: renal medullary carcinoma arises in the medulla but is rare.
  • D: juxtaglomerular tumours (reninomas) are rare curiosities.

gu-w16-module-q90-90.html:
From 06 - Approach to Renal Masses. The lecture: metastatic RCC is usually fatal and cure is very rare, so the goals are to minimize harm and maximize quality of life. Systemic therapy (immunotherapy, TKIs, VEGF inhibitors) is the mainstay, with bisphosphonates, analgesia and steroids for symptoms.

  • A: cure is the goal only for localized disease.
  • B: surgery helps only select patients (palliation of hematuria or pain, or low-volume metastases), not universally.
  • C: high-dose vitamin C is not a treatment.

gu-w16-module-q91-91.html:
From 07 - Urothelial Cancer. The lecture's risk factors are age, smoking including second-hand smoke, occupational or environmental exposures (petroleum compounds, aniline and hair dyes, textiles, paints, plastics, leather, the automotive industry), geography, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide, and chronic irritation. Family history is not on it.

  • A: beauty salon = hair dyes.
  • B: plastics.
  • C: second-hand smoke.
  • E: oil refinery = petroleum compounds.

Contrast this with the renal mass history, where family history does matter.

gu-w16-module-q92-92.html:
From 07 - Urothelial Cancer. The lecture's work-up is urinalysis with cytology, blood work, renal ultrasound, contrast CT (CT urogram) for the upper tract, and cystoscopy for the bladder. Abdominal MRI plays no part in it.

  • A: the lecture calls IVP "somewhat outdated", but it still outlines the collecting system for filling defects, which is the question here.
  • C, D, E: the core tests; cystoscopy after referral to urology.

gu-wb-gu0-q122.html:
From 09 - Special Issues in Pediatric Urology. Cryptorchidism is failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum: 3% of term and 30% of premature infants. Most descend within 3-6 months; orchidopexy by 17 months if not. Untreated, it raises cancer risk 3-8x, and bilateral cases compromise fertility.

  • Other options: hydrocele = fluid within the tunica vaginalis; hematocele = blood there; varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus; spermatocele = epididymal cyst; torsion = poorly anchored, twisted cord; orchitis = infection; cryptorchidism = undescended testis; inguinal hernia = bowel in the canal.

gu-w17-module-q9-9.html:
From 02 - Nephrolithiasis (its embedded kidney stones note). The prevalence table: calcium oxalate 80%, uric acid 15%, struvite 4%, cystine <1%. Only B pairs the top two.

  • A, C: struvite (infection stones) is third.
  • D: cystine (not "cysteine") is the rarest.

A useful corollary: uric acid stones are radiolucent on KUB but visible on ultrasound and CT.

gu-w17-new-q13-13.html:
From 03 - Renal Replacement Therapies. True. The lecture's transplant complications are rejection, surgical anastomotic problems, infection (CMV, herpes), cancer from immunosuppression (lymphoma, skin cancer), cardiovascular disease, and drug side effects. Calcineurin inhibitors cause hypertension, hyperlipidemia and CKD, and the immunosuppressants can cause diabetes and bone disease. The original disease can also recur in the graft.

The underlying trade-off is between too much immunosuppression (infection, cancer) and too little (rejection).
